comments.content: Data-integrity bug: when ReviseInPlace throws after File.Copy has succeeded, the `using` block in ReviseInPlace auto-saves the partial state on dispose, so outPath is left as a truncated/possibly-corrupt .docx. The fallback then calls `WordprocessingDocument.Create(outPath, ...)`, which throws `OpenXmlPackageException` on an existing path, so the user gets NO output at all. The catch for the File.Copy failure deletes it, but this catch does not. Either re-clean outPath before falling through, or wrap the in-place path in a way that ensures outPath doesn't exist before the fallback Create runs.

Correctness gap: InnerRuns only enumerates direct child `Run` and `Run`s wrapped in `Hyperlink`. Runs nested inside an existing `w:ins` / `w:del` / `sdt` / `fldSimple` are NOT direct children of the paragraph, so they are silently excluded from both `ParaText` (unit text) and the run-map used by `ReviseParagraph`. If the input .docx already contains unaccepted tracked changes or structured-content wrappers, `oldText`/`ParaText` will be a strict subset of the model-provided original lines, the consistency check inside `ReviseParagraph` (`pos != oldText.Length || string.Concat(...) != oldText`) fires, and every affected paragraph silently degrades to "整段删 + 整段增" — the user can no longer see which characters changed. Either yield runs inside w:ins/w:del too (and mark them as pre-existing, not as new revisions), or accept this limitation and document it loudly via Console.Error before falling back.

Correctness gap: unit collection only iterates `body.Elements<Paragraph>()` and `body.Elements<Table>()`. Any paragraph or table nested inside a `TableCell` (nested tables, sub-paragraphs), inside `SdtElement` (content controls), inside `CustomXmlInsRangeStart`, or under the section properties container is silently skipped. Their text never enters the diff, so they never get revisions, and any structural insert that should land inside a nested region is impossible. The in-place path is essentially usable only for flat documents. Either document this limitation explicitly, or recurse via `Descendants<Paragraph>()` / `Descendants<TableRow>()` with proper ancestor tracking so nested rows/paragraphs can also receive revisions.

OOXML well-formedness risk in `ReviseParagraph`: only `Run` and `Hyperlink` children are removed before re-inserting the rebuilt content. `BookmarkStart` / `BookmarkEnd` / `CommentRangeStart` / `CommentRangeEnd` / `CommentReference` / `PermStart` / `PermEnd` and similar markers remain as siblings of the new runs. If a bookmark previously enclosed text that has now shifted to a different position (or been deleted entirely), Word will open the file but log "bookmark not defined" / "comment range not closed" errors and may drop the orphaned references or refuse to save cleanly. Either drop the orphaned markers together with their runs, or move them to bracket the new content of the same character range.

Data-integrity bug in `DeleteUnit` RowUnit branch: `trPr.AppendChild(new Deleted { ... })` is unconditional — it never checks whether the row already has a `w:del` element. Per OOXML, `trPr` may contain at most one `w:del`/`w:ins` row-marker pair, so appending a second one produces an invalid row that Word typically refuses to save ("Cannot add a new element to the trPr; it already contains one"). The risk is real because: (a) the same row could be in the diff twice if the original document already had tracked deletions on it (e.g. someone re-runs this tool on an already-revised doc), and (b) running the tool twice on the same original would double-mark every deleted row. Either check for an existing `Deleted`/`Inserted` child and remove/replace it, or use `GetFirstChild<Deleted>()` and only insert when null.

Resource leak: `JsonDocument` returned by `JsonDocument.Parse(...)` is `IDisposable` and is never disposed. The buffered JSON content stays in memory until GC. The previous `File.ReadAllTextAsync` also doesn't dispose its implicit handle in the same expression. Wrap the parse in `using` so the document is released deterministically at the end of `Main`.

comments.content: `.nm-input:focus` uses `:focus` while every other interactive component (`.nm-btn`, `.nm-icon-btn`, `.hold-confirm`, `.save-btn`, `.exec-bar`) keys the focus ring off `:focus-visible`. The effect: clicking into any input flashes the brand-color border + focus-ring every time (`:focus` fires on mouse-click, `:focus-visible` does not), which is the exact noisy pattern the project's `:focus-visible` discipline elsewhere is guarding against. Switch to `:focus-visible` (and add an explicit `outline: none;` to suppress the global `:focus-visible` outline when keyboard-tabbing, just like the sibling classes do).

The `--now` pill text falls below WCAG AA on **both** themes: light `--now:#e5484d` with `#fff` text → ~3.72:1 (fails AA normal 4.5:1 at 10.5px), and dark `--now:#ff6b62` brightening actually makes it worse → ~2.79:1 (fails AA Large 3:1). The dark `--now` was lifted in saturation/brightness without re-balancing the white foreground. Either pick a darker `--now` for dark mode (e.g. a deeper red), or use a dark text color on the bright red pill (the file already does this for `.chat-bubble-user` in dark, suggesting `--now` was missed).

The blanket `*, *::before, *::after { transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; ... }` under `prefers-reduced-motion` is intentional, but the `!important` plus universal selector makes it impossible to selectively opt any low-risk feedback animation back in — most notably the `save-btn__spin` (loading indicator on a save action), `hold-confirm-shake` (destructive-action confirmation feedback), and `exec-pulse` (status signalling). If a future product requirement asks "show the spinner even under reduced-motion, just slower", this rule silently swallows it. Consider scoping reduced-motion overrides to a known list or using `:where()` so individual components can re-arm.

`.hold-confirm-ring-fg { transition: none; }` documents an rAF-driven JS contract in CSS alone — if the React driver stops pulsing `stroke-dashoffset` (pointer cancel mid-press, component unmount, prop change before reset), the ring silently stalls or stays at whatever offset the last frame set, with no visible failure. This is a hidden CSS↔TS contract that will only surface as a bug. Either (a) gate the JS reset to also zero `stroke-dashoffset` on cancel/unmount in a place reviewers see, or (b) drop `transition: none` and let CSS tween on top of rAF (which the comment says was tried and rejected — capture the rejection criteria next to the declaration).

`.exec-bar__inner--over` hardcodes both the foreground `#ffffff` and the shadow `rgba(6, 78, 59, 0.4)`. The shadow is a fixed dark-green darkening that bypasses the `--success` token — if `--success` is ever themed differently (or replaced with a brand-derived color in a future mode), this shadow will be wrong. The rgba(6,78,59) is approximately `--success: #16a34a` darkened; replace with `color-mix(in srgb, var(--success) 25%, black)` (or a similar token expression) so it tracks the theme.

There are three separate `:root { ... }` blocks scattered through the file (theme tokens at the top, scrollbar `color-scheme` mid-file, timeline `--accent`/`--now`/plan palette later). They are functionally fine, but it makes the token surface area harder to audit for unused vars and prevents anyone from grepping "what defines `--now`?" in one pass. Consolidating all root-level tokens into the top `:root` block (and the `.dark` overrides likewise into the single `.dark` block) would make the theme surface auditable.

Tauri shim's `transformCallback` returns the callback function itself, but the real Tauri API contract returns a numeric callback ID (and registers the callback internally for later dispatch). Returning the callback means any `invoke` that ships a `handler`/`callback` field will receive a function where the real runtime expects a number; downstream code that validates payloads or re-dispatches by ID will silently misbehave. At minimum the shim should mint a stable numeric ID (e.g. an incrementing counter) to match the contract, and ideally store the callback so event dispatch can actually invoke it.

comments.content: Failure path is invisible: unmocked commands `console.warn` + `Promise.reject`, and the only sink is `window.__errors`. A render that fails (e.g. an unmocked but optional `task_*` command rejecting at mount) will leave `#root` empty / partially rendered and the screenshot will look like a successful empty graph. The smoke runner must read `window.__errors` to notice the failure; add a visible DOM indicator (badge, banner, or `#root` overlay) that surfaces count + first error, so a human or CI diffing the PNG can spot a broken render.

The mock inventory only covers `workflow_list`, `people_list`, and `tag_similar_pairs`. GraphPage almost certainly needs additional commands (tasks, task-graph, edges, focus, etc.) to actually populate the graph; the comment block does not list them, and there is no allow-list/registry that documents the contract surface this demo is meant to satisfy. Either expand the mocks to cover the full command surface GraphPage touches (per a shared constants file), or maintain an explicit allow-list of expected commands and assert against it in the smoke runner, so a future command addition cannot silently regress this screenshot demo.

The error sink pushes only `String(e.message)` / `String(e.reason)`, dropping stacks, component stacks, source file/line, and the originating Tauri command name. For a screenshot smoke test whose whole purpose is "find regressions visually", the post-mortem path is much weaker than the vitest setup this file claims to mirror (which would normally capture full Error objects). Capture `{message, stack, source}` objects instead of pre-stringified values so the runner can format/serialize them losslessly.

The `<title>` is still the unmodified Vite scaffold string "Tauri + React + Typescript". This is what shows in the Tauri window title bar / OS taskbar on the shipped desktop app — it leaks the framework stack and reveals nothing about the product. Replace with the real product name before any release build.

In Vite dev this resolves fine, but in a packaged Tauri build the bundle is served from `tauri://localhost/<asset>` and the asset is only emitted if it's in `public/`. comments.content: The `catch (e)` block silently swallows every error from `localStorage.getItem`. In Safari private mode, when third-party storage is blocked, when Storage Foundation is disabled, or when a future browser removes the synchronous storage API, this just falls back to the light theme with zero observability — making storage-related bug reports hard to triage. At minimum branch on the known `SecurityError` / `QuotaExceededError` cases so the "ignore" stays narrow; ideally `console.warn` once on cold start so the support team can correlate real failures with user complaints.

Drag-from-pool duplicates blocks and loses sync between pool and grid. `blocks.push(B(d, min, min + 60, p.t, p.c, ...))` adds a new block without checking whether a block for the same task already exists, and the pool item stays in the pool. Re-dragging the same pool item creates duplicate blocks at each drop, while `p.at` is overwritten each time so the pool label no longer reflects any real block. Either de-duplicate by task identity, update the matching block in place (like the block-drag path does), or remove the pool item on drop.

Drag/resize relies on column geometry captured at pointerdown, so any window resize, panel toggle, or vertical scroll between start and drop maps coordinates against stale rectangles and can snap blocks to the wrong day or wrong time. `locate()` is called with the captured `rects` on every move/up. Recompute `colRects()` inside `move`/`up` (or at least on resize) so dragging remains accurate.

Dynamic data is interpolated into innerHTML without escaping: block titles (`b.t`), pool titles (`p.t`), legend labels, and the ghost element's title/time are all concatenated raw into a string. The demo data is static today, but this is exactly the XSS pattern that will bite the moment titles come from user input, the agent, or an external API. Switch to textContent or build elements with `document.createElement` / DOM APIs (or escape with a small `escapeHtml` helper) before this gets reused as the real product.

comments.content: `locate()` extends hit detection ±20px outside each column's vertical bounds. This was likely intended as a usability buffer, but it also makes the hit area overlap the gaps between stacked columns and bleed into the hour axis. Combined with the X-first loop in `rects`, a drop near the top/bottom of one column can be mis-attributed to the adjacent one. Either remove the buffer or apply it only when the cursor is over the column's horizontal range.

`renderGrid()` inserts the nowline into today's column right after `gridbody.innerHTML = html`, but `renderBlocks()` is called immediately after and overwrites every column's innerHTML, including the just-inserted nowline. The nowline insertion inside `renderGrid` is dead code. Either drop the renderGrid-side insertion and rely on `renderBlocks` (which already appends `nowlineHtml()` for `d === jsDay`), or have `renderGrid` not initialize column contents at all.

`renderBlocks(f, keepFresh)` declares two parameters that no caller ever supplies, and `startDrag` keeps a `last` variable that is written but never read. Dead state/parameters suggest an incomplete refactor. Either wire them up (e.g. expose filtering, persist the fresh flag) or drop them so the intent of the renderer is unambiguous.

comments.content: Every pool drop, block move, and grip resize triggers `renderBlocks()`, which rebuilds every column's innerHTML and rebinds click/pointerdown handlers on every block. With 12 blocks this is fine, but the pattern (full HTML teardown + `bindBlockEvents` re-walk on every interaction) will not scale. Consider a single delegated `pointerdown` listener on `gridbody` that reads `data-id` and routes to the right block, and update only the affected column on changes.

Both pool and block drag handlers attach an extra `pointerup` listener just to clear `dragging-src`, while `startDrag`'s own `up` handler runs `payload.onDrop` which also removes the class. Two listeners fire on every drop and the cleanup is split across them, making it easy to introduce leaks if one path is changed. Have `startDrag` own the source-element cleanup (pass the source element through `payload` and clear the class in `up`), and drop the duplicate listeners.

comments.content: Design tokens are copy-pasted into this mockup rather than imported from src/ui/main.css. The opening comment claims they are '同源' (in sync), but any change to main.css will silently diverge from this preview. For a long-lived design doc this is a maintenance hazard — either @import the token block or at minimum annotate each value with its source path so drift is detectable.

Ribbon blocks set `cursor: grab` (and a translate-on-hover transition) implying drag-to-reschedule, but they are plain <div> with no role, no tabindex, no aria-label, no mousedown/pointer/keyboard handlers, and no script wiring. Keyboard users cannot reach them at all, and mouse users get a misleading affordance. Either wire up the drag interaction with proper accessible semantics (role="button" or role="listitem" + tabindex + aria-label + keyboard handlers) or remove the grab affordance until the feature lands.

Visual scale mismatch inside the time ribbon: the .ribbon-grid has 8 vertical separators and the axis spans 8:00–22:00 (a 14-hour range, so the rightmost line sits at 100% = 22:00), but every .ribbon-blk left/width percentage and the .now-line position are computed on a 16-hour scale (8:00–24:00). For example, the now-line at left:47.9% is labelled '15:42' — in the 14-hour scale that position is ~14:42, i.e. roughly an hour off; block '09:00' sits at 6.25% which is 9:00 only in the 16-hour scale. Pick one scale and align grid/labels/blocks/now-line.

comments.content: Patterns are raw strings re-compiled by `re.finditer` for every scanned file, and line numbers are derived via `cleaned.count("\n", 0, m.start()) + 1` which scans from offset 0 for each hit. Combined cost is O(files × patterns × file_len + hits × file_len) per run. On a small repo this is invisible; on a large codebase it scales poorly. Compile each pattern once at module load (or store a list of `(compiled_re, label)` tuples) and precompute line offsets per file (e.g. iterate `enumerate(cleaned.splitlines())` or cache a list of `\n` positions for O(log n) bisect lookup per match).

Each call performs a `sorted(SRC.rglob("*"))` walk over the source tree. Pass the already-computed list from `main()` into `run_checks(files)` (or have `run_checks` return the list and the file count) to drop the duplicate traversal. Minor on small repos, but the structure makes it easy to forget the second walk if either function is extended later.

Global `LOG_WRITE` mutex is held across `rotate_log_if_large`, `OpenOptions::open`, and `writeln!`. Every rate-limited request is serialized on a single process-wide mutex through blocking filesystem I/O; under concurrent traffic this turns log-write latency into latency for every API call and creates a contention hot spot. Consider a per-file lock, opening the file once and caching the `File`, or moving appends onto a bounded background worker that owns the mutex.

Poisoning recovery in `rate_check` calls `into_inner()` and immediately continues with whatever `(timestamp, count)` the panicking thread left behind. Both individual writes are atomic, so the tuple is never torn, but a panic mid-window can pin `g.1` at `RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN` and silently throttle every subsequent caller until the next window expiry — only an `eprintln!` signals the operator. Reset to a known-safe `(now_ms(), 0)` on the recovery path (or call `clear_poison` after re-initialising the state) so a poison doesn't degrade availability.

Fixed-window semantics admit up to `2 * RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN` requests in the ~2 s straddling a minute boundary; the doc-comment accepts this for "runaway scripts" but the same function is now fronting every authenticated handler, including ones that may trigger expensive work. If any consumer of `rate_check` is security-sensitive, switch to a sliding-window (e.g. token-bucket / `governor`) — at minimum add an integration test that pins the worst-case burst so the trade-off can't silently regress.

`let _ = h.join()` discards `Result<T, Box<dyn Any + Send>>` from `JoinHandle::join`. If the accept thread panics (e.g., an unwinding bug inside the API server), the panic payload is silently lost — there is no audit_event and no log line. Given how aggressively this file audits other failure modes (HTTP start failure, SSE leaks, recovery rollback), hiding thread panics here is a notable observability gap. At minimum, log via `audit_event!(app, AuditLevel::Error, "api_thread_panic", ...)` when join returns Err, and consider re-panicking so the process exits rather than reporting a healthy stopped service.

Same `let _ = h.join()` issue as in `api_start_locked`: the panic from the accept thread during a user-initiated stop is silently swallowed. The accept thread is the long-running server task; if it died due to a panic, the user thinks the stop succeeded but the cause of death is invisible.

All `state.0.lock()` sites in this file convert `PoisonError` to `e.to_string()`, which destroys the wrapped guard (`PoisonError<MutexGuard<…>>` carries the original lock state and backtrace). The user-visible message becomes a generic `"poisoned"`-style string with no actionable context. Prefer a typed conversion via `From<PoisonError<_>>` for `CommandError::Internal`, or at least preserve the original error via `format!("{e:?}")` (note `{:?}` is used here but is only printed to stderr, never threaded into the returned error). Also, `audit_event!` would be more consistent than `eprintln!` for a critical failure class the rest of the module audits explicitly.

Same `PoisonError → String` flattening as the start path. Even more importantly, this lock failure is *not* audited via `audit_event!` (only `eprintln!`-ed), unlike the structured audit used for HTTP start failures, rotate rollback failures, and SSE writer leaks. A mutex poisoning on the status path is at least as severe as those and should be reported through the same channel.

comments.content: `load_or_create_token(&app)` is invoked on every `api_status` call when the service is enabled. This performs a filesystem read on each UI status poll (and on first-ever call, also creates the directory and writes the token file). Since the token is immutable between rotations and the running service already holds an authoritative copy in `RunningApi.token`, the status handler should expose the in-memory token from `g.as_ref().map(|r| r.token.clone())` instead of touching the disk. The disk file can be used as a fallback only when `g` is `None` (e.g., after a rotation completed while the service wasn't running).

In Phase 3 recovery, if the lock itself is poisoned (`state.0.lock()` returns `Err`), the code only logs via `eprintln!` and continues, then returns the original `Err(e)` to the caller. There is no `audit_event!` for this critical failure (unlike every other failure branch in the file), and the recovery is silently abandoned. Two issues: (1) observability gap — the user gets the original error but the system may be in a worse state than reported; (2) the function still returns `Err(e)` which is correct behaviorally, but should at least emit an audit event so logs distinguish "Phase 2 failed and recovery skipped because of poison" from "Phase 2 failed and recovery succeeded". Same poisoning-handling inconsistency as the start/status paths.

`service_present` returns `Option<bool>` (None on poison) but the three callers interpret `None` inconsistently: `api_start` writes the flag (`!= Some(false)`), `api_status`'s cleanup branch does NOT clear the flag (`!= Some(true)` evaluates true so it WOULD clear — wait, `!= Some(true)` means clear unless it's Some(true), so poison=clear), and the comment in `api_start` calls this "conservative". The asymmetric treatment of poison between start (write flag) and stop (clear flag) means a poisoned lock state can leave the on-disk flag and memory state pointing in different directions across an outage. Pick one direction (preferably "no disk write on poison — trust neither side until re-bootstrapped") and apply uniformly to avoid silent flag/memory drift.

`write_enabled_flag` 与 `should_autostart` 的状态机不自洽：`std::fs::write` 是非原子写（无 tmp+rename，无 fsync），而 `should_autostart` 又以 `b == b"1"` 严格比较内容。若进程在 `api_start` 之后、`std::fs::write` truncate 与单字节落盘之间被 kill/OOM，flag 文件会处于空文件状态——下次启动 `should_autostart` 直接返回 `false`，自动静默地丢失「上次退出时 API 是开的」这条盘上事实源。建议改用与 `write_token_file` 一致的 tmp+rename 原子写（甚至「先写 flag 再启服务，启失败再删 flag」的顺序倒装），并把失败从 `eprintln` 升级为可观测的错误返回。

token 落盘没有任何 `sync_all`，是个 durability 缺口：`create_token_file_atomic` 的 `create_new + write_all` 与 `write_token_file` 的 tmp+rename 都假设写完即落盘，但断电/内核崩溃后 token 文件可能为空或残缺。一旦发生，调用方有两个后果：（a）`load_or_create_token` 读到空文件 → 重新生成 UUID → 静默吊销用户手里那个仍在使用的 token；（b）并发首跑输家满循环 500ms 仍拿不到非空内容 → 同步阻塞返回 `Err`，调用方拿不到可用 token。token 等价于密码，对持久性要求高于普通 flag，至少应在 `write_all` 后调用 `f.sync_all().ok()`（或对 tmp 调一次再 rename），并在 `load_or_create_token` 启动时区分「首次启动」与「正常启动」——前者允许生成，后者空文件应直接报错而不是覆盖。

`verify_bearer` 的 `split_once(' ')` 与 RFC 7235 §2.1/2.2 不一致：scheme 与 credentials 之间的 OWS（可选空白，可以是 SP/HTAB）只接受单 SP；同时 B 段对比走 `ct_eq(rest, token)`，如果客户端按 RFC 拼接了尾随 OWS（如 `Bearer <token>\r\n` 被代理剥剩 `Bearer <token> `），整段都会因为长度不同被判定不等。这是单纯的 interop 问题而非安全洞（反而收紧了 attack surface），但既然注释里引用了 RFC 7235，就值得在文档或实现里明确「仅接受标准单空格分隔，OWS 不放行」，免得未来按 RFC 修一发又把大小写敏感度破坏了。

存量 0644 token 文件的读—紧权顺序留了 TOCTOU 窗口：先 `read_to_string` 拿到明文 token 返回给调用方，*之后* 才 `tighten_token_permissions`，而 chmod 还是 best-effort（失败仅 `eprintln`，调用方照样拿到 token）。窗口虽小，但语义上「读取合法 token」和「token 文件权限收紧」不应解耦——同机其他用户/进程能在收紧前用旧权限读到明文。建议把 tighten 提前到 read 之前，或在 tighten 失败时直接 `return Err(...)`（密码文件权限不达标就不要返回明文），并在 `tighten_token_permissions` 内把 chmod 失败也归类为「应阻断读」的硬错。

`write_token_file` 的两处 tmp 清理 `if let Err(cleanup_err) = std::fs::remove_file(&tmp)` 没有按 `ErrorKind` 过滤，`NotFound`（tmp 已不存在，例如 OS 重启清理 / 同名 tmp 提前被别的进程 unlink / 自己上一轮 rename 后留下的 inode 已经被回收）也会触发「清理失败（请手动删除）」的告警日志，让运维误以为有真实残留。建议过滤为「仅在错误不是 NotFound 时打 eprintln」，或干脆把 NotFound 归 Ok；同样的模式还有前面 `write_result` Err 分支里的那一份。

Public fields on both stores break the very abstraction the file exists to enforce. `MemStore.tasks`, `MemStore.hub`, `TauriStore.app`, and `TauriStore.hub` are all `pub`, so external code can mutate `MemStore.tasks` directly (e.g. `store.tasks.lock().unwrap().push(...)`) and never go through `upsert` + `notify_change`. The whole point of moving the EventHub into the store (A5) is that writes flow through one method and the SSE broadcast is automatic — `pub` fields silently desynchronise that contract. Make the fields private (or `pub(crate)`) and expose only constructor + trait methods; the `#[allow(dead_code)]` on `MemStore` already signals the struct is only constructed from tests, so visibility can be tightened without API churn.

The two adjacent comments above `if let Some(expected) = t.expected_updated_at` are stale and contradict each other: line 67 reads "与 db.rs upsert 的基线比对对齐——忽略" (align with db.rs upsert baseline — ignored) while line 68 says "expected_updated_at 会让 API 层 409 冲突路径在 MemStore 下不可测（测试基建空洞）". The code below them *does* implement the conflict check, so "ignored" is misleading; and the second comment openly admits the 409 path under MemStore is untestable. Either the conflict check is correct (delete the comments and replace with a one-liner explaining the BASELINE_NULL_ROW semantics) or it diverges from `db::db_upsert` and needs a TODO + test. Leaving both contradicts each other in source will trip the next reader.

`MemStore::upsert` and `load` both `lock().unwrap()` on a `Mutex`, and `upsert` additionally holds the guard across *both* the O(n*m) batch conflict-check loop and the follow-up write loop (the comment "整批比对基线…批量写必须原子成败" makes the long hold intentional). Two consequences: (1) any panic in a holder permanently **poisons** the mutex — every subsequent `load`/`upsert` returns `Err(PoisonError)` carrying no context about what poisoned it, turning a single bad write into a permanently broken API; (2) the conflict-check loop + write loop are bounded only by `tasks.len()` × `tasks.len()`, so a hostile or pathological batch can stall all readers. Recover from poison with `lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())` (or surface the original panic context), and at minimum avoid `unwrap()` on user-reachable paths.

`MemStore::load` allocates a fresh `Vec<db::Task>` on every call (full clone under the mutex) and uses `Mutex` even though the dominant workload is reads. For tests this is fine, but the trait return type `Vec<db::Task>` forces the clone — there is no way to return a snapshot or an iterator without copying. If `MemStore` is ever reused outside test fixtures, or if a future trait consumer is added, this will become a hot-path allocation. Consider `RwLock<Vec<db::Task>>` for reads, or change the trait to return an `Arc<Vec<db::Task>>` snapshot (clone the `Arc`, not the `Vec`).

Two `expect("静态 header 字节不可能失败")` calls panic on `Header::from_bytes` failure in an HTTP response helper invoked on every successful and error response. Even with ASCII-validated bytes, a panic here tears down the whole server thread and leaves the request half-processed. Replace with a precomputed `OnceCell<Header>` (or `Lazy<Header>`) built once at module init, so the failure mode is a startup-time abort (or a logged, contained error) instead of a per-request panic in a production HTTP path.

Reference: `Header::from_bytes` returns `Result<Header, _>` precisely because header token/byte validation can fail; the rule against `expect()` in production paths applies regardless of how safe the call appears today.

Every handler uses `let _ = req.respond(...)` which silently discards `tiny_http`'s `io::Result`. Client disconnects, broken pipes, half-closed connections, and full TCP buffers all disappear without a log line, masking real delivery failures and conflicting with the rule against swallowing `Result`. The API_RMW_LOCK scope intentionally stops before `respond`, so the only blocking work left is the socket write — there's no cost to logging the failure.

Suggestion: at minimum `eprintln!("[api] respond failed for {method} {path}: {e:?}")` on `Err`, or factor a `respond_or_log(req, resp, method, path)` helper and route every call site through it.

Reversing a task from `Done` to any non-Done status unconditionally wipes `completed_at` and `archived`, losing the original completion timestamp and any explicit archive state the user set previously. Only `updated_at` survives, so the audit trail loses "first completed at" data the model otherwise preserves. The forward branch (`→ Done`) similarly overwrites any pre-existing `completed_at`.

This is a data-integrity hazard on the dual-write surface: the RMW lock only protects within the API path, so a UI/bot-driven change to `archived` between two API calls can be silently erased by a Done→Todo transition.

Suggestion: keep `completed_at` as the first completion timestamp (only set on first transition into Done), and never auto-clear `archived` here — let the explicit `archived` field on `UpdateReq` carry that intent.

The handler manually mirrors `file_path`/`file_is_dir` into `files: Vec<TaskFile>` in both `create_task` and `update_task`, with three branches (set, clear, change `is_dir` only). The synchronization is implicit and the invariant "after this handler returns, `files[0]` equals `file_path` if either is `Some`" is not enforced anywhere. Any future code path (UI handler, bot path, migration, future field like `file_aliases`) that writes one side without updating the other silently desynchronizes the legacy single-binding and multi-binding representations, and the next API write through here will overwrite the orphan with stale data.

Suggestion: centralize the dual-write in a single helper on `db::Task` (e.g., `fn sync_file_bindings(&mut self)`) and call it from every write site, or — better — make `files` the source of truth and derive `file_path`/`file_is_dir` only at serialization time so the two cannot drift.

`ApiStatus` encodes an invariant ("`token` is `Some` only when `enabled` is `true`") only in a Chinese comment, while the type still permits the four combinations `enabled: {true,false} × token: {None, Some(_)}`. Per the type-design guidance to "make invalid states unrepresentable", this should be a single enum, e.g. `enum ApiStatus { Disabled, Enabled { port: u16, token: String } }`, so that a disabled status with a leaked token (or an enabled status without a token) cannot be constructed in the first place.

The doc comment claims the field is skipped to "避免泄露空串" (avoid leaking empty string), but `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` only omits `None` — `Some(String::new())` will still be serialized as `"token": ""`. Either tighten the predicate (e.g. a helper that also rejects empty strings) or rephrase the comment to match what the code actually does, otherwise a caller that constructs `token: Some("".into())` while `enabled` is `false` (which the type system allows) will silently leak an empty token to the client.

Both `ApiInfo` and `ApiStatus` carry a bearer credential as a plain `pub token: Option<String>` that is serialized verbatim. The `skip_serializing_if` attribute only governs JSON output; nothing here prevents the struct (and therefore the token) from being captured by `Debug`, `tracing`, `log`, error reports, panic messages, or audit trails constructed by callers. Consider documenting this risk (or providing a custom `Debug` impl that redacts the token, e.g. `format!("Some(\"***\")")`) so callers are nudged toward not logging the structured value.

comments.content: Per-request Vec<&str> allocation whose only purpose is `len() > 1`. Since declared_len is read from `content_length_headers.first()` right after, only the *count* and the *single value* are needed. A counter with an early `return BodyRead::Malformed` on the second CL avoids the heap allocation entirely. The subsequent Transfer-Encoding scan iterates headers a second time and can be merged into the same pass (one loop, one field-equiv check), avoiding the double traversal on every body-reading request.

`Vec::new()` grows from empty up to MAX_BODY_BYTES via `extend_from_slice`, which means multiple reallocation/copy rounds on every accepted request. The upper bound is already known at this point (declared_len, clamped to MAX_BODY_BYTES), so pre-allocating the buffer once removes the hot-path reallocations.

This test inlines the loopback/server/stream setup that `request_with_raw_body` already abstracts for the other two tests, so any future change to the helper (extra headers, keep-alive, HTTP version, request-line tweak, etc.) will silently drift out of this one. Extract a shared setup that takes the pre-built raw request bytes (or a header list + body) and route both `valid_utf8_body_reads_back` and `duplicate_content_length_is_malformed` through it, leaving only the JSON `{}`-with-CL form as a small wrapper if convenient.

SabotageStore::upsert is fragile by design (already acknowledged inline): it relies on MemStore's per-row baseline-compare-then-replace to surface 409 after the sabotage increments `updated_at`. If MemStore's upsert ever changes to whole-table replace, trusts task.updated_at directly, or drops `expected_updated_at` handling, this test silently changes meaning (or returns the wrong status) instead of failing with a clear diagnostic — the test for the production conflict path would then be guarded by an external invariant that is not enforced anywhere. Consider adding a self-check (e.g., a non-sabotaged PUT returning 200 in the same flow) so a MemStore refactor that bypasses the baseline path causes a hard, localized test failure rather than a silent regression.

Box::leak permanently leaks the mock Tauri App on every run of exit_drains_in_flight_handler_then_refuses_new; CI loops and local debug reruns accumulate leaked App state (and any resources it owns). Tauri's mock_app exists specifically to be discarded at end of test — prefer leaking only the handle (or wrapping mock_app in a OnceLock/scope) so the app itself goes out of scope.

Test spawns a 30-second-sleep thread on purpose to exercise the detach-after-join-timeout path, but stop_sse_writers returns within ~300ms leaving the spawned thread alive in the background for the remaining ~27s. Subsequent tests in the same process run with that zombie thread still holding its stack, which can surface as flaky timing or thread-count warnings unrelated to the system under test. Consider lowering the sleep to just-over the SSE_STOP_JOIN_TIMEOUT (e.g., 2s) so the thread exits soon after the test returns.

Both SSE read loops in sse_receives_change_events treat any non-zero read as success and `unwrap_or(0)` collapses real socket errors to EOF. A genuine mid-stream error or a server-side crash would surface as a missing 'tasks-changed' substring and a flaky timeout, not a localized diagnostic. Distinguish `Ok(0)` (clean EOF) from `Err(_)` (propagate) and report the partial buffer on unexpected closure so SSE delivery regressions are easy to triage.

The comment claims `sync_channel(256)` overflows by dropping events with "广播不阻塞" (broadcast does not block). That is wrong for `sync_channel`: when the buffer is full, `Sender::send` *blocks* the producer thread until there is room. So if `EventHub::broadcast` (in api_server.rs) calls `tx.send(...)` for every client in `clients`, a single stuck SSE writer (slow TCP socket, paused client, half-open connection that hasn't tripped the 30s write timeout yet) will pin the broadcast loop at 256 pending items and back-pressure every other subscriber behind it — the exact opposite of the documented contract. Either:
  1. switch the broadcast side to `try_send` and treat `TrySendError::Full` as the documented "drop, client will replay by `since`" path, or
  2. replace `sync_channel` with a primitive that genuinely drops on overflow (`tokio::sync::mpsc` is not an option here, but you could keep a `VecDeque<(u64, Vec<u8>)>` behind a `Mutex`/`RwLock` with a cap, evicting the oldest on overflow, and have each writer thread drain that buffer under its own short-lived lock — which also aligns better with the out-of-order/dedup logic already present).

Either way, the comment and the primitive must agree, otherwise a single slow client can stall the entire hub.

```rust
// sync_channel(256)——单客户端最多积压 256 条，超出则丢事件（广播不阻塞）；
let (tx, rx) = sync_channel::<(u64, Vec<u8>)>(256);
```

`check_field` returns `Option<String>` where `Some(_)` carries the error message and `None` means "no error" or "skip". The doc-comment even has to spell out the caller pattern `if let Some(e) = … { respond(400, &e); return; }`. The type does not communicate that `Some` is an error — at a call site, it reads like an optional value. Prefer `Result<(), ValidationError>` (or a typed `FieldTooLong { label, max, actual }`) so the error-vs-empty distinction is expressed in the type system and reviewers cannot accidentally treat `Some` as a value.

The actual length comparison is delegated to `super::util::over_limit`, but only the `check_field_counts_chars_not_bytes` test pins the "counts chars, not bytes" contract. If someone "fixes" `over_limit` to use `s.len()` (a very common Rust reflex for length limits), every other test in this module still passes because none of them care about char-vs-byte semantics at the boundary. Consider asserting the contract at the helper's definition site (a doc-comment `/// counts Unicode scalar values, not bytes` plus a unit test on `over_limit` itself), or fold the comparison into `check_field` so the contract lives here.

comments.content: `str::trim` only strips Unicode `White_Space`-property code points. It does NOT strip zero-width space (U+200B), zero-width joiner, BOM (U+FEFF), directional marks (U+200E/F), or other "invisible" characters, and performs no NFC/NFKC normalization. Combined with the char-counted length cap, an attacker can submit thousands of zero-width spaces — passing length validation (each is one char) while rendering as an "empty" task name in the UI, or being used to evade duplicate-name / denylist checks downstream. If the API surface is human-entered task names/descriptions, consider also rejecting (or stripping) the invisible-format-category characters before the length check.

`take_trimmed_string` and `check_field` independently run `Option<&str> -> trim() -> empty-check`. The inline comment correctly notes that `check_field` skips `to_owned` to avoid an allocation on the happy path, but the two paths must stay behaviorally identical (both must treat `None`, `""`, and all-whitespace as "skip"). Any future change to one (e.g. adding NFKC normalization, stripping zero-width chars, or normalizing line endings) must be mirrored in the other — there is no single source of truth. Consider extracting a tiny private helper such as `fn trimmed_view(raw: Option<&str>) -> Option<&str>` that both call.

Add a `// SAFETY: ...` comment so a future reader does not weaken the contract (e.g. by passing a non-string array or an arbitrary type string).

comments.content: `over_limit` counts Unicode scalars (`chars().count()`) and labels the message as "字" (characters), but the caps are propagated from `crate::bot::MAX_*` and the downstream storage (SQLite TEXT, file paths, etc.) is byte-bounded. If `MAX_TITLE`/`MAX_NOTE`/`MAX_DUE`/`MAX_TAG_LEN` are meant as byte caps (the usual convention for storage limits), a string of multi-byte characters will sail past the guard and still overflow the column. Conversely, if they are genuinely char caps, the user-facing message is correct but the storage layer must independently enforce a byte cap. Decide the contract on the `MAX_*` constants and either count bytes (`v.len() > max`) or rename the label/unit so it cannot silently disagree with the byte-bounded storage path.

On a system with a skewed/far-future clock this produces bogus `created_at`/`updated_at` stamps with no log line. Use `i64::try_from` so overflow is observable.

comments.content: Side-effect ordering is wrong for the stated contract. `store.notify_change` (SSE broadcast) and the audit log are emitted *before* `emit_fn` runs. If the user-supplied callback panics, returns Err, or simply blocks the calling thread, connected observers have already received the broadcast and the log line claims the change succeeded — yet the front-end callback never fires, leaving SSE listeners and the embedded webview out of sync. Either run `emit_fn` first (so a callback failure aborts the broadcast), or document and enforce the current order as load-bearing. The synchronous call into user code on the handler thread is also worth flagging — if the callback ever does IO it will block whatever thread invoked `after_change`.

Both error-path helpers do `let _ = req.respond(...)`, silently dropping the `Result`. Under load, broken pipes / dropped clients leave no trace and the `Request` is consumed unconditionally, so connection-level failures (e.g. tiny_http I/O errors, write back-pressure) are invisible. At minimum, log the respond error so we have an observability signal when a 5xx never reaches the wire; ideally wrap respond in a helper that logs and counts failures. The same pattern exists in `upsert_err`'s 409 branch.

Request DTOs have no size or shape guards at the deserialization boundary. `tags: Option<Vec<String>>` accepts an unbounded vector, `title`/`note`/`file_path` strings are unbounded, and there is no `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` so extra/unexpected fields are silently dropped. A single oversized payload allocates the full structure in memory *before* `over_limit` ever runs in the handler — a classic DoS surface for a JSON API. Enforce a request-body byte cap in the tiny_http handler (or `serde_json::Deserializer::from_reader` with a bounded reader), and consider `deny_unknown_fields` plus a max-length custom deserializer for `Vec<String>` tags.

comments.content: FALLBACK is a single per-process `OnceLock<AppState>`. The header comment acknowledges that integration tests (`tests/*.rs`) cannot inject the `pub(crate)` `AppState`, so every test in a single test binary funnels into this one shared instance. Cargo runs test functions concurrently within a binary by default, so tests that touch `pending` / `confirm_requests` / `question_waiters` / `subagent_stops` / `stop_registry` / `trace_registry` via the accessors will race and cross-contaminate (a `oneshot::Sender` taken in test A can never resolve in test B, leftover StopTokens get cancelled by test A's StopGuard drop, etc.). Consider making the accessors take an explicit `&AppState` (no fallback) and exposing a test-only `pub` constructor on `AppState`, or shard FALLBACK by thread/test name.

Lock-poisoning handling is implemented in exactly one place (`trace_id_for_session`, with an explicit `[mutex_poisoned]` log + `into_inner()` recovery). Every other accessor (`skill_runs`, `artifact_registry`, `confirms`, `question_waiters`, `ask_contexts`, `sched_running`, `stop_registry`, `chat_running`, `exec_running`, `pending_map`, `subagent_stops`, `trace_registry`) hands back an `Arc<Mutex<...>>` clone or `&Mutex` and leaves poison handling to the caller. If some callers `lock().unwrap()` and panic while others silently `.lock().ok()`, a single poisoned lock yields inconsistent behavior — and because FALLBACK is shared across tests, a lock poisoned in one test can silently corrupt queries in the next. Pick one convention (e.g. always `lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!(...); e.into_inner() })`) and either enforce it via a small helper (`MutexExt::lock_or_recover`) or at least document the required behavior on each accessor.

`NEXT_STOP_ID` is a process-global `AtomicU64`, but `stop_registry` lives inside `AppState` (per-instance). The doc claims the split is intentional, but in the FALLBACK path the global counter and the FALLBACK-shared registry are both global in practice, while in injected unit tests the counter is still global even though each test injects its own `AppState`. A unit test that registers `StopGuard`s against an injected `AppState` will see `NEXT_STOP_ID` continue from values used in earlier tests / FALLBACK paths, and any cross-binary integration check that compares numeric stop ids will be off-by-N. Either reset `NEXT_STOP_ID` in `AppState::default`/`new` for tests, or hand each instance its own `AtomicU64` next-id field.

comments.content: Long-held `clients` mutex spans file I/O (`db::atomic_write`) and a nested `history.lock()` acquisition. Any sync I/O stall (slow disk, antivirus scan, fsync latency) blocks every concurrent broadcast and SSE client iteration. The comment justifies this trade-off ("人级频率, 锁内文件 I/O 开销可忽略"), but a single slow write holds up all publishers — consider moving `atomic_write` outside the critical section using a separate id-persistence mutex (clients→history order still holds; only the file write exits the lock). At minimum, document this as a known scalability ceiling.

Per-client heap allocation in the broadcast hot loop: `msg.as_bytes().to_vec()` copies the entire SSE frame into a fresh `Vec<u8>` for every connected client on every event. With many clients and frequent broadcasts this is significant allocator traffic on the publisher path. Share the payload across clients via `Arc<Vec<u8>>` (or `Arc<[u8]>`) — `SyncSender::try_send` takes `T: Send`, so an `Arc<Vec<u8>>` flows through unchanged and avoids the per-client copy.

Inconsistent mutex-poison recovery: `clients` recovers via `into_inner()` and continues with whatever state the panicking thread left behind, while `history` rolls back the id and bails (`fail-closed`). Two policies for the same kind of failure in the same critical section is a smell. Worse, after a successful `atomic_write` (id persisted to disk), a poisoned `history` lock rolls back the counter but leaves the higher id on disk — restart will resume from an id that no client ever saw, and the dropped event is silently lost. Either recover both (with a documented invariant that the persisted id and in-memory history can diverge across the poison boundary) or fail-closed on both.

`replay()` silently swallows a poisoned history lock (`Err(_) => Vec::new()`) with no logging or telemetry. If history is poisoned, every reconnecting SSE client will silently receive zero replay events — a debugging nightmare. Either log the poison (matching the `clients`/`history` paths in `broadcast`) or propagate a typed error so the SSE writer can at least surface a 5xx. At minimum, log to the same audit channel as `broadcast` so operators can correlate.

`EventHub.clients` and `EventHub.history` are declared `pub Mutex<...>`, contradicting the module-level intent that only `hub_id()` is externally accessible ("只读访问一律走 hub_id() getter"). External callers can bypass `broadcast()`/`replay()` invariants — pushing clients without their `Weak` token, breaking id monotonicity by mutating `history` directly, or popping history entries mid-replay. Make these `pub(crate)` (or private with accessor methods) to keep the encapsulation promise stated in the doc-comment.

comments.content: BOT_LOG_LOCK is declared `pub`, not `pub(crate)`. This exposes the global sync mutex to the entire crate graph, allowing any external module to hold the audit log lock across arbitrary blocking work. Combined with `write_at` spanning rotate+open+write under the lock, this is an external starvation vector. Should be `pub(crate)` at most, or hidden behind a typed enqueue API.

`write_at` holds BOT_LOG_LOCK across rotate + open (with chmod) + writeln. The doc comment explicitly forbids calling from tokio/延迟敏感 paths, yet `frontend_event_report` (a `#[tauri::command]`) calls `write_event` → `write_at` directly on the runtime worker. This both violates the documented contract and means one slow disk operation stalls every audit write globally. Either enqueue from `frontend_event_report` via `std::thread::spawn` (as the comment demands), or convert to a channel-based async writer.

`open_log_append` opens new files with mode 0o600, but for existing files `mode()` doesn't apply and the follow-up chmod is best-effort — failure is only `eprintln`'d and the write continues. If chmod fails (FS without POSIX perms, read-only mount, etc.), bot.log keeps whatever umask allowed (commonly 0o644) while still receiving user commands/paths/tool output, contradicting the stated invariant that sensitive data must not be world-readable. Either refuse to write (return Err) when chmod fails on a pre-existing file, or skip the write and surface the failure to the caller instead of eprintln-only.

`tool_call_failed` advertises per-tool failure logic via the `name: &str` parameter but discards it with `let _ = name;`. Callers in DSL/PREVR/hallucination guard may reasonably assume the tool name is consulted (e.g., "this tool-specific message format only applies to tool Y"). The dead parameter is a leading indicator that an intended per-tool branch was lost during refactor. Either remove the parameter (and update all call sites) or implement the documented per-tool logic.

Doc comment claims panic_message handles "&str / String / 其他三种情况" (three cases), but the implementation has only two typed `downcast_ref` branches plus one catch-all that collapses every other payload (including an empty `Box<dyn Any>` from `panic!()` with no args) into the misleading string "non-string panic payload". Either distinguish the common payload types more precisely (e.g., `&'static str`, `String`, numbers via formatting) and explicitly handle the empty case, or correct the comment to match the actual two-type coverage.

`write_event` takes `&[(&str, String)]` and immediately allocates a second `Vec<(&str, &str)>` from it on every call before passing to `write_at`. Since `audit_event!` always produces owned `String`s via `format!`, the caller already pays for that allocation; the second `to_vec` doubles the cost on a hot audit path. Either change `write_event`'s public signature to `&[(&str, &str)]` (the macro can still produce `String`s via temporary variables) or have `write_at` accept `&[(&str, String)]` directly so the slice can be iterated without reallocation.

TOCTOU race on cache miss: two concurrent invocations of `bing_daily` (e.g., multiple Tauri windows or rapid frontend polling) will both observe an empty cache and both issue network requests to cn.bing.com, doubling API load and producing two `write_cache` writers. There is no per-day in-flight guard, no file lock, and the daily file does not yet exist so neither write can be detected as redundant. Add a per-day `Mutex<()>` / `tokio::sync::OnceCell<BingDaily>` keyed on `today`, or use `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` on a lock file as an in-flight marker that `read_cache` consults and `write_cache` removes on completion.

Sync `std::fs` calls in async context: `bing_daily`, `read_cache`, `write_cache`, and `prune_old` are all reached from an async command but use blocking filesystem syscalls (`create_dir_all`, `read_to_string`, `read`, `write`, `remove_file`, `read_dir`). Even on the cache-hit fast path (file reads of an ~150-400KB jpg plus a base64 encode) this can block the Tokio/tauri worker thread that drives other Tauri commands and tasks. Either move the filesystem work to `tokio::fs` / `spawn_blocking`, or, since this is purely a disk-cache command, drop the `#[tauri::command]` `async` and return a sync `Result` — Tauri's command handler will run sync ones on a blocking worker already.

Round-trip base64 encode/decode on every write: `fetch_today` reads the image as raw bytes, immediately base64-encodes it into `data_url`, then `write_cache` calls `decode_data_url` to recover the very same bytes just to write them back to disk. The encode+decode is pure waste and grows peak memory by ~33% during the round trip. Refactor `fetch_today` to return `(bytes, title, copyright, image_url)` (or pass a writer closure) so the raw jpg is written directly; build the data URL only at the IPC boundary.

Re-base64-encoding the cached image on every hit: the whole purpose of the disk cache is to avoid recomputation, but `read_cache` re-reads the .jpg into memory and runs `to_data_url` on each call. If the frontend polls / re-invokes `bing_daily` on window focus or rerender, this pays a full base64 encode of a 150-400KB jpg (≈ 200-540KB output string) per call. Either (a) precompute and persist the data URL alongside the .jpg (write the base64 blob once), or (b) cache the last-served `BingDaily` in an in-memory `OnceCell<BingDaily>` / `Mutex<Option<(String, BingDaily)>>` keyed on date so repeated same-day calls short-circuit before touching the disk and the encoder.

Stringly-typed error wrapping discards the project's structured error codes. `req_err` and the four direct `CommandError::from(format!(...))` sites funnel every error (network failure, HTTP status, JSON parse, empty list, image too large, prefix mismatch, base64 decode) into a generic string. Per `src-tauri/src/error.rs` the crate exposes typed `CommandErrorCode` variants (`IoError`, `LlmRequestFailed`-shaped network errors, `InvalidArgument`, `PayloadTooLarge`, …) with stable codes that the frontend `hintForCode` table dispatches on — losing that signal means the UI cannot distinguish "network blip, retry" from "input corrupted, surface as fatal" from "image over size cap". Pick a real variant per failure mode (e.g. wrap `reqwest::Error` into a `CommandError::IoError`/`Internal` carrying URL + status, image-cap into a typed payload-too-large variant, empty-list into a domain-specific error) instead of pre-formatting into a string.

`file_date` is too permissive: it only inspects the first 10 bytes of the filename, with no check that the 11th character is non-alphanumeric (e.g. `.`). The current file set is fine (`.json`/`.jpg` always have `.` at position 10 or later), but a future file like `2026-10-11abc.json` (11 chars before the extension) would be silently picked up by `prune_old` as a cache file — and worse, anything written directly with `2026-10-11` plus an arbitrary suffix would be swept away. Tighten the matcher to require `name.len() == 10 || !name.as_bytes()[10].is_ascii_alphanumeric()` (and ideally also reject path-separator characters) so only true date prefixes are pruned.

`MAX_IMAGE_BYTES` is enforced *after* the full body is buffered into a `Vec<u8>`. With a pathologically large or slow response the runtime can accumulate up to the 8 MB cap (or more, if there's a malicious redirect) before rejecting. Switch to a streaming `client.get(...).body().await` with `Body::with_max_length` / `reqwest::Response::chunk()` capped to `MAX_IMAGE_BYTES` so an over-cap response aborts on the first oversize chunk instead of buffering. Same applies to `read_cache` which `std::fs::read`s the whole file unconditionally — `to_data_url` could stream-encode from a `BufReader<File>` so cache hits don't pin a full 150-400KB `Vec<u8>` plus the ~200-540KB `String` simultaneously.

Consider reducing these to `pub(crate)` (or moving them under a `#[doc(hidden)]` path) unless an external caller genuinely depends on the literal string values.

comments.content: Lock-held invariant is enforced via `debug_assert!`, which is compiled out in release builds. If a future caller forgets to acquire `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK` (e.g., from a new write path), `migrate_config_file_locked` will silently perform read → mutate → atomic write → `SCHEMA_MIGRATION_CHECKED.store(true, …)` unsynchronized, racing concurrent writers (the very property the lock exists to prevent) and potentially corrupting state with no diagnostic. Either upgrade to a runtime check (`assert!`/returns-Err/poison-on-misuse), or encode the invariant in the type system (e.g., pass a `ConfigWriteGuard` token into the locked fn).

Same `debug_assert!`-only invariant problem in the schema-migration locked entry point. In release builds, calling this without holding `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK` is unsanctioned and silent — concurrent migration of `bot-config.json` + premature `SCHEMA_MIGRATION_CHECKED.store(true)` = permanently skipped future migrations for the session. Pair with the other `_locked` fn fix.

Check-then-act / "让路" race: on `try_lock` `WouldBlock` the function returns `Ok(())` on the assumption that the lock-holder has already invoked `migrate_bot_config_schema_locked`. If the holder is any write path that does NOT call the migration (or fails before doing so), schema migration is silently skipped for the session — `SCHEMA_MIGRATION_CHECKED` stays false but every subsequent call also hits `try_lock` and yields, so retries never recover. The atomic only protects against double-execution by this path, not against permanent silent bypass. At minimum, when `WouldBlock` is observed, record an audit event / set a "pending-migration" flag and re-attempt after a short backoff (without try_lock) on the next call, rather than blindly trusting the holder.

Security-sensitive ordering coupling enforced only by docstring: the migration writes back the entire JSON (still containing any plaintext `apiKey` left over from pre-keyring configs), with a comment stating that redaction is `migrate_legacy_key` / `migrate_search_keys`'s responsibility and "调用顺序不能反". A new boot path, retry loop, or future test harness that invokes schema migration without first running the legacy-key redaction will atomically persist credentials to disk. Consider (a) running the redaction inside the same locked critical section before re-serializing, (b) at least refusing to write back if a known plaintext-shape `apiKey` field is detected, or (c) replacing the convention with a typed "safe-to-write" marker from the redaction pass.

Two combined risks in the file-migration reader: (1) `std::fs::read_to_string(path)` has no size cap — a corrupted or attacker-controlled multi-GB `bot-config.json` will be fully slurped into memory and then re-serialized, exhausting memory / wedging the migration. Add an explicit size pre-check (e.g., `metadata().len()` against a sane upper bound like a few MB) before reading. (2) `serde_json::from_str` errors are collapsed to `Ok(None)` with no `eprintln!` / `audit_event!`, leaving the corrupt file in place. The next `load_config` will then fall back to in-memory defaults and, on next save, atomically overwrite the user's settings with empty ones — silent, unlogged data loss. At minimum, log the parse error and consider renaming the bad file to `.corrupt.<ts>` before returning.

Vendor label is derived by raw substring search on a lowercased URL: `contains("openai")`, `contains("anthropic")`, etc. This has no notion of hostname boundaries, so URLs like `https://my-openai-compatible-proxy.local`, `https://anthropic-clone.example.com`, or any path containing the substring (e.g., `/v1/openai-compat`) will be silently labelled as the official vendor. The resulting label is then persisted via `migrate_legacy_models` and shown to the user in settings — misleading attribution of credentials to a non-official endpoint. Prefer matching on hostname only (parse with `url::Url` or split on `/` and take the host) and on a more specific token (`api.openai.com`, `api.anthropic.com`, etc.), or require exact host equality against a small allow-list.

Substring check and label value disagree: the match arm checks `u.contains("minimaxi")` but returns `"MiniMax"`. Any URL whose host happens to contain the trailing characters that produce the same string will be labelled as that vendor — but if the actual vendor token in the URL is the same as the label, the check itself is too permissive (matches unrelated substrings). Make the check token match the returned label, and ideally pin to the official hostname (or document why a substring is intentional).

`migrate_legacy_models` checks `models_by_provider.is_some()` up front but then assigns `cfg.models_by_provider = Some(mbp)` unconditionally at the end without re-verifying. Today the early-return guarantees this, but the pattern is fragile: any future code added between the two sites that re-mutates `models_by_provider` could desync the contract. Either drop the early return and unconditionally overwrite (idempotent), or add an assertion / `debug_assert!(cfg.models_by_provider.is_none())` at the end. Same applies to `active_model_id`.

`derive_legacy_fields_from_active` clones `entry.base_url` and `entry.model` into `cfg` even when they are already equal to the existing values. On the chat/main-loop hot path this is two unconditional `String::clone`s per call. Add an `if cfg.base_url != entry.base_url { cfg.base_url = entry.base_url.clone(); }` (and similarly for `model`) to skip the allocation when nothing changed — common case after first save.

The doc on `migrate_config_value` says "v0→v1 只补版本号字段本身；后续版本在此按 from 分支改字段" — but the current implementation has no version-branching at all: it unconditionally writes the current `BOT_CONFIG_SCHEMA_VERSION` and returns `(from, to)`. Either remove the misleading forward-looking comment, or implement the per-version branching now and gate the `(from, to)` audit so the reported `from` matches the version actually applied (currently `from` is the *file's* pre-migration version, which is fine for audit, but the branching story the comment promises doesn't exist yet).

The acknowledged HIGH-severity lost-update window is real and the load here is unlocked: `let _g = super::io::lock_config_write(); let disk = super::io::load_config(&app);`. The guard only protects `write_bot_config_file_locked`; the `load_config` read happens without the lock, so any concurrent writer (e.g. `persist_last_run`, or another `bot_set_active_model`) that lands between the unlocked load and the locked write will be silently overwritten by this save. The same pattern is repeated in `bot_set_active_model` with the misleading comment "读改写全程持 CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK——与 bot_set_config 同锁，消除并发丢更新" — `io::load_config(&app)` is again unlocked, so the comment promises a guarantee the code does not deliver. Fix by introducing and using a locked load variant (e.g. `io::load_config_locked`) that takes the same `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK`, or document explicitly that this race is accepted (and then drop the misleading HIGH comment).

Inconsistent with the file's own documented policy ("keyring 真实故障透传 KeyringError，不静默拿全局 key 去探测") and with the sibling `has_api_key()?` / `has_search_key()?` calls in `bot_get_config` which propagate keyring errors with `?`. `.unwrap_or_default()` collapses a real keychain fault (locked, denied, backend unavailable) into `""`, so the probe sends an unauthenticated request and the vendor returns a misleading 401/403 — the user sees "vendor unauthorized" instead of "keychain locked". Propagate the error (or audit-log it the way the `migrate_*` failures are logged) so the diagnostic matches the policy stated in the function's docstring.

When the id is found in BOTH protocols the code silently leaves `cfg.api_provider` unchanged, contradicting the function's own stated principle earlier ("用户点的是哪一个就该切哪一个") and the loud failure it already returns for the not-found case. Downstream effect is also non-obvious: only the kept-protocol slot of `active_model_id` is updated, so the OTHER protocol's `active_model_id` becomes stale and the very next `bot_get_config` view will show an inconsistent active pair. Either return `InvalidArgument` here (matching the not-found branch, and actually the only branch consistent with the rest of the function), or — if the dual-hit is truly unreachable — drop one of the `.iter().any(...)` checks and assert/inline the result.

The explicit `drop(_g); bot_get_config(app)` only works because `bot_get_config`'s `migrate_legacy_key` / `migrate_search_keys` helpers ALSO grab `CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK` and the lock is non-reentrant. This is a hidden cross-function coupling that a routine refactor (e.g. moving migration into `load_config`, or adding any other helper inside `bot_get_config` that locks) can silently turn into a self-deadlock that takes the Tauri command runtime down. Either extract the view-build half of `bot_get_config` into a pure function and call it directly while the guard is still held, or make `lock_config_write` reentrant (per-thread re-entry count) so callers no longer have to know which helpers take the lock. The current state is "one bot_get_config refactor away from a deadlock".

comments.content: `s.replace("| ", "|  ")` unconditionally allocates a fresh `String` of size `s.len()` for every audit line, even when the input contains no `"| "` (the common case). On the cold path this is wasted allocation + scan; fold the `| `→`|  ` doubling into the same char loop using a `prev_was_pipe` flag, so a single allocation (`escaped` with `with_capacity`) and a single pass over `s` is enough. Drop the intermediate `String` from `replace`.

comments.content: Truncation does three passes over `escaped`: full char-by-char build, full `chars().count()`, then another `chars().take(max).collect()`. On long inputs that is `O(2n)` extra work for every log call. Merge counting into the escape loop and break once `max` chars are emitted, appending `…` if and only if the input actually exceeded the limit. This also lets you skip the trailing allocation when nothing was truncated.

`read_log_tail` always loads the entire file via `std::fs::read_to_string` and then builds a `Vec<&str>` over the full contents before slicing the last `limit` lines. With a 5 MiB rotated log this allocates ~5 MiB of buffer plus a full-file `Vec<&str>` and only keeps ~200 of them. Stream the file with `BufReader::lines()` into a fixed-size `VecDeque<String>` ring of length `limit` (or read tail-only by seeking backwards in pages for the larger files) — both avoid the upfront full-file allocation and keep memory proportional to `limit`, not file size.

`audit_log` returns `()`, but `append_bot_log_line` already returns a `bool` indicating whether the line was actually persisted. `let _ = ...` then silently drops that signal — an audit-writing failure is only observable via the side-channel `eprintln!`, which neither callers nor the audit_event pipeline can see. For an "audit log" entry point, propagating a `Result<(), AuditWriteError>` (or at least a `bool`) lets callers and tests distinguish a successful append from a dropped line, especially under mutex-poisoned + disk-failure conditions where `e.into_inner()` may happily keep appending to a half-broken state.

`audit_log_hook` is a one-line unconditional forwarder that differs from `audit_log` in nothing but its name (same generics, same signature, same body). The pub doc-comment claims this exists for `bot_skills` callers while `bot.rs` uses `audit_log` directly, but exposing two identical public surfaces makes the API larger to audit and easier to drift (e.g., one caller getting new validation while the other is forgotten). Either `pub use audit_log as audit_log_hook;` in the module root, or merge the callers onto a single name; keeping two trampolines adds review surface with no behavior to show for it.
comments.suggestion_code: pub use audit_log as audit_log_hook;

comments.content: Function could be `const fn` to match the convention already established in `db/tasks.rs::TaskStatus::as_str`, which is also a pure enum-to-`&'static str` mapping marked `pub const fn`. Making this `const fn` enables compile-time evaluation in static contexts (e.g., building a `static STATUS_LABELS: [&str; 3] = [...]` table, or `const X: &str = status_label(TaskStatus::Doing);`) and signals to readers that this is a pure, side-effect-free mapping. `TaskStatus` derives `Copy`, so the change is trivial and there is no runtime cost difference.

comments.content: The doc comment claims these label strings must stay aligned with `src/format.ts` if a same-name function is introduced there. Currently `src/format.ts` has no such function (verified — searching for `statusLabel|status_label|TaskStatus` returns no matches in that file), so there is no actual drift today. However, the cross-stack contract is fragile: when the frontend equivalent is added, a label change here (e.g., "待办" → "待处理") will silently diverge from any future `src/format.ts.statusLabel` and produce inconsistent text in bot tool-result summaries vs. the main UI. Consider either (a) co-locating both label tables in one shared definition via a build-time codegen, or (b) at minimum adding a short comment in `src/format.ts` pointing back here so the next editor of either side knows about the contract.
