comments.content:
Code-drift hazard: 34-column `task_from_row` and `TASK_SELECT_COLS` are positional-index-coupled. Adding/removing/reordering a column requires synchronized edits at both sites AND updating the 34-argument `INSERT ... VALUES (?1..?34)` in `upsert_tasks`. There is no compile-time check that the indices match the projection order — a single reordering silently reads the wrong column.

Recommend one of:
1. Generate the projection list with `format!("SELECT {} ...", COLS.join(","))` where `COLS` is the single source of truth, and use `row.get::<_, T>(col_name)` (rusqlite supports column-name lookup) so reorders are safe.
2. At minimum, add a `const _: () = assert!(/* all columns covered */)` compile-time check that the projection list count matches the row.get count.
3. Switch to a small derive-based row mapper to eliminate the index bookkeeping entirely.

REDUNDANT DB WRITE LOCKS in `db_load_for` / `db_upsert_for` / `db_delete` / `tasks_export` / `tasks_import`. All of these take `lock_db_write()` even when their workload is read-only (`db_load_for` is purely `SELECT` except for the migration branch which already gates on `p.exists()` outside the lock).

`db_load_for` (lines 1240-1262) holds the write lock during the full `load_all` call, blocking every writer on the app for what is essentially a SELECT. Even the `migrate_data_json` branch's need for write access is satisfied before `load_all`; the lock could be released as soon as migration completes.

For read-only paths, downgrade to a shared/read lock (introduce `lock_db_read`) — single-process SQLite has no real concurrent readers benefit, but the principle of holding the *minimum* lock needed documents intent and lets future migrations to a multi-process backend (`WAL` mode + separate processes) work without API churn.

At minimum, add a doc comment at each `lock_db_write()` call site clarifying WHY that specific operation needs exclusive access, since the current blanket use makes the contract invisible at call sites.

JSON corruption in `subtasks`/`files`/`budget`/`result`/`depends_on` is logged via `eprintln!` but the corruption message is unparseable for log scraping: no task-id prefix that disambiguates between thousands of tasks in a busy session, no column name, no DB connection hint. Worse, the field name printed is bare `id` — which collides with whatever Rust identifier is in scope at log emission time.

The TODO of this code is to keep the row readable after partial corruption. The current log line fulfills the don't-crash contract but fails the forensics contract ("which column of which row on which DB at which time was bad?"). Format the line as `[db] task_id={id} col={col_name} row_json_corrupt (raw_len={len}): <err>` and route through `crate::audit::write_event` (Warn level) so it lands in the structured audit log alongside other write-path events.

parse_tool_call slices args using `find('(')` (first paren) and `line.len() - 1` (last char, expected `)`), with no depth/balance walk or quote awareness. Inputs like `foo())` yield args="`)`", `foo({)})` yields args="`{)}`", and `foo({}) extra)` yields args="`{}) extra`" — all malformed JSON that only fails downstream at the JSON parser (so the user gets a runtime execute-tool error rather than a clear authoring-time message). Even well-formed tool calls whose args string contains a literal `(` (e.g. a regex pattern inside a JSON value) are sliced correctly only because the trailing `)` happens to be the outer close — a fragile coincidence. Replace the open/find/last-char slicing with a paren-depth walk that ignores parens inside balanced double/single-quoted runs and surfaces `None` on depth imbalance.

Multi-line JSON tool calls (e.g. `foo({\n  "a": 1\n})`) fall through every arm of the parse_skill_steps loop: the open line `foo({` doesn't end with `)`, the body line `  "a": 1` doesn't end with `)`, and the close line `})` has no `(`. So `parse_tool_call` returns `None` on each, the lines silently disappear past the final `else if`, and the step is pushed at the next `## Step` heading with an empty `tool_name`. Two complementary gaps let this slip through: (a) the loop has no fallthrough rejection under a step heading, and (b) the post-loop validation below only checks duplicate/sequential indices and never tests `s.tool_name.is_empty()`. The net effect is Skills that parse cleanly but ship to the scheduler as no-tool steps. Add an `else` branch that returns `Err` for any unrecognised non-blank, non-`#` line under an unfilled step, and add an empty-tool_name check alongside the sequential-numbering check.

The single-line allowed-tools branch uses `s.trim()` only, while the analogous intents branch strips both double and single quotes (`s.trim().trim_matches('"').trim_matches('\'')`). A line like `allowed-tools: "foo","bar"` therefore produces [`"foo"`, `"bar"`] with literal quote characters preserved. Those entries never match the tool registry, so the N7-⑤ gating silently degrades to a no-op — exactly the opposite of what the field is supposed to enforce (作者主动限权). Mirror the intents transformer so quoted single-line values are unquoted consistently.

Both `strip_frontmatter` and `parse_meta` use `find("\n---")` to locate the closing fence, with no awareness of YAML quoting and no signal when the fence is missing. Two concrete breakages: (1) any scalar field whose value contains a `---`-only line — common in multi-line descriptions with separator blocks — is misidentified as the fence, silently truncating frontmatter and dropping all subsequent fields without diagnostic. (2) When no closing fence exists at all, the `None` arm returns the original `text` (including the opening `---` prefix), so `parse_skill_steps` sees the bare `---` as free text and proceeds — silently producing a Skill that "parses" but contains no DSL body. Consider adopting a real YAML frontmatter parser (`serde_yaml`/`yaml-rust`) and changing the return to `Option<&str>` or making `strip_frontmatter` return an empty slice when the fence is missing so callers can detect the malformed input.

The inner while-loop under `intents:` (when the value is empty) breaks on the first line that does not start with `- `, including `#` comment lines and blank separator lines between items. After the break, the outer loop re-feeds these lines through the top-level scanner: a `#` comment line has no `:` and is silently skipped by the generic `let Some((k, v)) = line.split_once(':') else { continue; }` arm, and a subsequent `- bar` line also has no `:` and is silently skipped. So intent entries after a comment/blank are silently swallowed with no diagnostic — particularly treacherous for regex patterns with quantifier commas that legitimately need the multi-line form. Continue over blank/`#`-comment lines inside the inner loop instead of breaking on them, and only break when the line looks like the start of a new top-level key.

`unknown_tool_names` uses `out.contains(&s.tool_name)` for dedup inside an outer O(n) iteration over chained steps+rollback, yielding O(n²) lookups. The same pattern in `parse_meta`'s `allowed-tools`/`intents`/multiline path also uses linear dedup but those are bounded. For Skills that reference the same tool across many steps this gets quadratic. Use a parallel `HashSet<String>` for the seen-set and push only when `.insert()` returns `false` — same dedup semantics, linear scan, and avoids the `s.tool_name.clone()` for already-seen entries.

Synchronous `std::fs::write` runs on the Tokio async task after the blocking thread has already returned. For large audit exports (full-history JSON of every run × node), this performs file I/O on the async runtime, blocking other Tauri commands. Move the `std::fs::write` call into the `spawn_blocking` closure (pass `path` into the closure alongside the DB work) so the actual disk write happens off-worker like the comment above says it should.

comments.content: `wa_prune(keep_runs == 0)` unconditionally executes `DELETE FROM workflow_audit`, wiping every audit row across all workflows. The doc comment relies on an external `5..=100` clamp in `workflow_settings`, but the function itself enforces nothing, so any future caller, misconfigured setting, or test that bypasses the clamp silently destroys the audit history. Add an explicit guard (`if keep_runs == 0 { return Err(...) }`) or remove the branch entirely and require callers to use `wa_clear_all`.

`wa_prune`'s DELETE filters by `run_started_at NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT ... LIMIT)`. The inner SELECT is a snapshot that is not evaluated atomically with the DELETE, and the whole statement is not wrapped in a transaction. Concurrent `wa_insert` calls landing between SELECT evaluation and DELETE commit can cause newly inserted rows with an older `run_started_at` to be retained when they should be pruned (or vice versa). Wrap in a `conn.transaction(...)` and, ideally, materialize the keep set into a temp table inside that transaction so the DELETE sees a stable view.

Nearly every DB call is flattened to `String` via `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())?` before crossing the function boundary. This discards the structured `rusqlite::Error` (SQLSTATE, primary/secondary code, embedded SQL) at exactly the layer where it is most useful for diagnostics, and forces the caller to wrap the resulting `String` into `CommandError::DbError` later. Consider keeping `rusqlite::Error` (or a thin newtype around it) inside this module and only stringifying at the Tauri command boundary with `e.to_string()` plus contextual information (e.g. the SQL statement name).

`kind` and `level` are documented as an 11-value enum and a small fixed set (`info`/`warn`/`error`) respectively, but `wa_insert` only `chars_truncate`s to 40 chars and never validates membership. Any short string round-trips as a legitimate `AuditEntry` and downstream filters (e.g. `kind = "review"`) silently miss typos like `"reivew"`. Consider a `Kind` newtype with a `FromStr`/`TryFrom` that rejects unknown values, or at minimum a debug-assert against the known constants in debug builds. Same applies to `level`.

The serialize-failure placeholder interpolates the `serde_json::Error`'s `Display` directly into a JSON string literal: `format!("{{\"_serialize_error\":\"{e}\"}}")`. If `e`'s display contains a literal `"` (e.g. `"expected `"`...`), the resulting column value is malformed JSON, which then trips `row_to_entry`'s degradation path and silently masks the original failure. JSON-escape the message (e.g. `serde_json::Value::String(e.to_string()).to_string()`) instead of raw interpolation.

comments.content: behavior_deviation: `case_total` is only a zero-guard but the metric it gates is silently distorted. When `case_total > 0` and `hit_fractions` is empty, `avg` is forced to `1.0` and the function returns `0.0` deviation — i.e. zero feedback is reported as *perfect* behavior. Also, any slice shorter than `case_total` silently drops the missing cases from the mean, so a 5-case evaluation with only 1 hit_fraction entry gets 0% deviation instead of being treated as 4 missing. Per the docstring this is intentional ("缺反馈按 1.0 计"), but the contract is dangerous: it lets a misconfigured caller (no feedback wired in) show "perfect behavior" in a dashboard. Either weight missing cases explicitly (treat them as 0 hits) or have callers be required to pre-fill the slice with the right length.

pollution_survival_days silently drops records where `now_ms < applied_at_ms` (clock skew, replay of old `applied.jsonl`, or future-dated entries). The negative durations are filtered by `if days >= 0.0` with no log, no counter, no telemetry — mis-timestamped pollution just disappears from the metric. Either emit a structured warning / counter when a negative-day record is skipped, or count it as `0` days so the bias is explicit rather than silently lost.

`compute` hardcodes `case_passed_placeholder: true` regardless of whether real case-level judgment is being supplied. Today there is no case-level signal, so this is technically correct, but the field's purpose is to tell consumers "this value is a placeholder". The moment any caller adds a real `case_passed` derivation and forgets to flip this flag (or it stays `true` because nobody owns the flag), `task_success_rate` will keep being flagged as a placeholder and silently misrepresent real outcomes. Make it derive from the inputs (e.g. a dedicated `case_passed_source` enum / bool parameter) instead of a constant, so the placeholder flag is data-driven and reviewed in the same code path as the metric itself.

`rollback_count` builds a `HashMap<&str, ()>` to test set membership; only key presence is read. This allocates an unused unit value per entry and obscures intent. Use `HashSet<&str>` (or, more cheaply, sort + `binary_search`/`starts_with`-style scanning given small live sets) — clearer API and avoids the wasted value slot.

`read_applied` flattens `io::Error` and `serde_json::Error` into Chinese `String` messages at the first failure boundary and drops the original error type. Callers cannot distinguish "file unreadable" from "malformed line" programmatically, the chain/source is gone, and down-stream code cannot attach retry/parsing logic. Return a typed error (or at minimum wrap with `anyhow::Error` / `thiserror` enum preserving `source()`) so the underlying cause is reachable.

`wa_export_list` reads the entire audit history for a workflow into a `Vec<AuditEntry>` with no pagination and then `serde_json::to_string_pretty` materializes the whole JSON in memory inside `spawn_blocking`. The retention policy (`wa_prune`) is supposed to bound this, but if pruning is misconfigured, skipped, or `wa_prune(0)` is ever invoked this returns, the export can allocate hundreds of MB and stall the worker thread. Stream rows to the file instead (e.g. use `std::io::Write` with `serde_json::to_writer_pretty` over a `BufWriter<File>`) so memory stays bounded by the write buffer.

comments.content: `workflow_audit_clear_all` is named identically to the helper `wa_clear_all` and duplicates its body. More importantly, `crate::audit::write_event` is called after the DB op with no return value observed; if `write_event` ever returns a `Result` (or in tests where it's stubbed to panic), failure here silently goes unnoticed. Either capture and log the error, or document explicitly that audit-write failures are tolerated.

Critical: Mutex poisoning is silently recovered via `e.into_inner()` after an `eprintln!`. If any prior task panicked while holding `DB_WRITE_LOCK` mid-transaction, the SQLite connection state may be torn (uncommitted transaction, partially-applied WAL page, etc.). Continuing to issue writes against that state risks persisting inconsistent workspace data with no caller-visible signal. Consider propagating the poison to the caller (return a typed `PoisonedDb` error from `CommandError`) so the IPC layer can fail-closed, or at minimum force a `conn.rollback()`/integrity check on the recovered guard before any new write. The same pattern repeats in `workspace_delete` and `workspace_import`, so a single bad panic poisons every subsequent workspace write.

Security: `workspace_import` reads `std::fs::read_to_string(&path)` with no path gate, while the symmetric `workspace_export` runs `check_export_path_gate(...).await?` first. The asymmetry means any caller (including a compromised frontend/JS bundle, or a misconfigured IPC permission) can supply an arbitrary filesystem path — including symlinks pointing outside the user's intended workspace dir, oversized files causing OOM, or unrelated sensitive JSON whose parsed shape happens to deserialize into `Vec<WorkspaceItem>`. Reuse the same gate (or an equivalent `check_import_path_gate`) before opening the file, and bound the read size to avoid unbounded allocation in the blocking thread.

Data-loss / fail-closed semantics in `workspace_import_merge_unchecked`: the merge decision uses `it.updated_at.unwrap_or(0) > ua`, which silently turns any imported item lacking `updated_at` into a no-op for every existing non-NULL row — i.e. importing older or freshly-edited items that lost their timestamp will never overwrite the current row. The block comment explicitly acknowledges this ("永不覆盖非 NULL 行") but does not defend against it (e.g. reject items with `updated_at = None` early, or surface a per-item warning instead of silently dropping). Additionally, `Some(None)` returns Err mid-loop with a Chinese-only message; the rollback via `tx` drop is correct, but the error is unstructured and only actionable for CJK-locale users — consider a typed `CommandError::AmbiguousImportTimestamp { id }` variant with an English fallback message.

comments.content: **Concurrency: `std::sync::Mutex` guard held across notification I/O, audit log, and file I/O.** The lock acquired here at the top of `run_round` is intentionally held through `plan_round` (which mutates `state`), then through the per-task `app.notification().builder()...show()` call and `crate::bot::audit_log(...)`, and finally through `save_state` (which does disk I/O via `db::atomic_write`). The intent comment "全程持锁…原子完成" makes the over-serialization explicit. Concrete problems: (1) the notification builder and audit log are Tauri/IPC paths whose latency is unbounded — holding a sync Mutex blocks any future reader (e.g. a diagnostics command, tests) for the full round; (2) `run_round` is `async fn`, so if any of these callees are ever made `async` (Tauri commands commonly are), holding a sync lock across `.await` becomes a compilation error and silently breaks shutdown; (3) on `save_state` failure the mutex is still held while the function returns, leaving no opportunity for a higher layer to retry. Scope the lock to just the in-memory mutation phase, drop it before `for p in &pending`, then re-acquire briefly only around the final `save_state`.

**Error handling: `save_state` silently swallows `serde_json::to_string` failures after in-memory flags have already been flipped to "sent".** When `to_string` fails, the function returns early with only an `eprintln!` missing; the in-memory `state` retains the post-`plan_round` mutations (`h1 = true`, `t0 = true`, due rearm resets, etc.), but nothing reaches disk. On next process start the file is re-read with those flags still false, and the notifier will re-fire H1/T0 for the same tasks — exactly the storm this module was built to suppress. Either fall back to logging the in-memory map size / a hash, or propagate the error up to `run_round` so the caller can decide to retry the disk write before dropping the guard.

**Correctness: `crate::bot::audit_log` is called from an `async fn` without `.await`, and its return value is discarded on both branches.** `run_round` is declared `async`, but the call sites `Ok(()) => crate::bot::audit_log(app, &format!(...))` and `Err(e) => crate::bot::audit_log(app, &format!(...))` treat the result as a tail expression with no `.await`. If `bot::audit_log` returns a `Future` (a common Tauri command pattern), that future is constructed and immediately dropped — the audit record is never persisted. If it is in fact synchronous, that assumption is undocumented and any future refactor that makes it async will silently break auditing without a compile error here. Either confirm and document the sync contract, or properly `.await` the future.

**Performance: `state.retain(|id, _| valid.iter().any(|(vid, _, _, _)| *vid == id))` is O(state × active) on every 30s tick.** For each entry already in `state` we walk the entire `valid` slice to check membership. With non-trivial task counts this becomes the only quadratic site in the hot loop. Build a `HashSet<&String>` (or `HashSet<String>`) from `valid` once before `retain` so cleanup is linear, and the same set can be reused if you later need to skip duplicates across `entry().or_insert_with` paths.

**Data integrity: corrupt `due-notify-state.json` is mapped to an empty `HashMap` and then `save_state` writes that empty map back, destroying prior `h1`/`t0` suppression on disk.** The comment "宁可重发不丢通知语义" acknowledges re-sending, but the actual behaviour is worse for non-stale tasks: `plan_round` first calls `state.retain(...)` (which against an empty map empties everything), then enters the `overdue >= 0 && overdue <= T0_WINDOW` branch for any task whose due falls in the last 24 h — those tasks' `t0` flag was previously suppressed and is now false, so they will be re-notified on the next tick after corruption. Even tasks outside the 24 h window lose their `t0 = true` until the next scan sets it again, but only if they survive `state.retain` (i.e. still in `active` and parseable). Consider preserving a backup or recording a `corrupted_at` tombstone so the corruption can be quarantined without wiping historical suppression.

**API design: `T0_WINDOW` is used for both the T0 resend window AND the H1 stale-suppression cutoff, but the constant name only reflects T0.** Inside the `overdue > T0_WINDOW` branch both `entry.h1 = true` and `entry.t0 = true` are set, so the constant also bounds H1 suppression for stale tasks. Renaming (e.g. `STALE_WINDOW` or `RESEND_WINDOW`) and/or splitting into two named thresholds would make the dual role explicit, and document why both flags are flushed together for tasks older than 24 h.

comments.content: The atomicity invariant claimed in this doc comment is incorrect for realistic entry sizes. POSIX guarantees O_APPEND atomicity only for `write()` calls <= PIPE_BUF (typically 4096 bytes on Linux), but `std::io::Write::write_all` is documented to 'call write in a loop until all bytes are written' — so it may issue multiple `write()` syscalls for buffers above that threshold. A serialized `ProposalEntry` (with 6-layer fields, refs, summary, etc.) can easily exceed 4KB, so concurrent readers from another process can observe a partial line. The downstream 'skip corrupt middle line' behavior in `read_jsonl` masks the symptom rather than preventing the torn write. Either (a) downgrade the claim to 'atomic only for entries <= PIPE_BUF' and document the size limit, (b) implement chunked append with a final fsync and an explicit size check, or (c) hold a cross-process `flock` on the file for the duration of the write.

`pub status: ProposalStatus` exposes lifecycle state as a freely-mutable field, so any code with `&mut ProposalEntry` can jump an entry between arbitrary states (e.g. `Expired → Pooled`, or `Pooled → Promoted` skipping the documented promotion path). There is no transition validation at construction or mutation time. Consider (a) making the field `pub(crate)` with a typed setter like `fn transition(&mut self, to: ProposalStatus) -> Result<(), TransitionError>` that enforces `Pooled → {Promoted, Expired, Rejected}` and forbids reverse moves, or (b) provide a single constructor `ProposalEntry::new_pooled(...)` and seal status transitions through dedicated methods on the type.

comments.content: `derive::auto_applied_from_proposal` 是 pub 函数（doc 明确为「生产 apply 与回归测试共用」），但未在 mod.rs 顶层 re-export；同一模块的其余派生函数（derive_change_id / derive_layer / derive_mem_key / from_proposal / unique_change_id_for / DEFAULT_SCHEMA_VERSION）全部被 re-export。建议补上 re-export 以保持 API 对称；否则外部调用者要么走 `evolution::change::derive::auto_applied_from_proposal` 长路径，要么在 derive.rs 改回 pub(crate)，需要作者明确取舍。

`record::append` 在 re-export 处被改名为 `append_change`，而其余 IO/查询函数（find_by_id / find_children / find_roots / read_all）保持原名；模块内部读者按 `use record::append` 写，模块外部读者按 `append_change` 写，两套命名同时存在，建议要么统一在源里就叫 `append_change`，要么在 re-export 处也保留 `append`，避免外部实现细节 vs. 公开 API 的命名漂移。

三个子模块都是 `pub mod`，同时又把主要类型/函数在顶层 `pub use`——形成两条并行访问路径（例如 `evolution::change::ChangeRecord` 与 `evolution::change::record::ChangeRecord` 同物）。这扩大了公开 API 表面、增加了下游误用风险（绕过 mod.rs 的稳定性契约直接改用子模块路径）。建议把子模块改为 `pub(crate) mod` 或仅在子模块内部需要互访时保持 pub，但顶层仍通过 `pub use` 暴露稳定面。

comments.content: The exhaustive match silently maps semantically distinct statuses (Approved, Canary, Active, Shadowing, ShadowPassed, RolledBack) to `Pending`. These arms are unreachable from the current `status` derivation (only Pending / Rejected / Expired are produced), but the explicit `Pending` label makes them look like intentional mappings rather than placeholders. If a future refactor lets `status` take on one of these values (e.g., promoting an Expired entry through shadow stages), the wrong `approval_source` will be emitted without any compile-time signal — defeating the very purpose of the explicit-enumeration comment above. Replace the unreachable arms with `unreachable!(...)` (or document them clearly as placeholders pending a decision) so a future contributor must consciously pick a value.

When `entry.status == Expired` and `hard_constraint_compliance == false`, the override collapses the status to `Rejected` and (via the match below) sets `approval_source = SystemRejected`. Downstream consumers can no longer distinguish a naturally expired proposal from one that was hard-rejected, and a future "audit why this never went live" query loses the Expired provenance. Either preserve `Expired` (and map it to `SystemRejected`), or document this intentional collapse explicitly in the function doc and add a test pinning the behavior.

The field `parent_id: None` is hardcoded with the comment `// 根` (root), but the function signature gives no hint that only root entries are accepted. If `ProposalEntry` ever represents a refinement / child of an existing proposal, this function will silently emit a root record with no parent linkage — corrupting the ChangeRecord DAG. Either propagate a parent from `entry` / an explicit parameter, or move the invariant into the type system (a separate `RootProposalEntry` newtype) and document the contract here.
comments.existing_code: parent_id: None, // 根

comments.content: No test pins the behavior for `entry.status == Expired` combined with `hard_constraint_compliance == false`. Given the override on lines 30-34, this combination's resulting `(status, approval_source)` pair is the most likely place for an unintended refactor to silently change semantics. Add a test that asserts the chosen mapping (currently `Rejected` + `SystemRejected`) so any future change is intentional.

Implicit lock contract on `unique_change_id_for`: this function does not take any lock itself; it trusts the caller to hold `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` across the read-modify-rewrite window. All three current callers do (apply.rs:278, observe/shadow.rs:299, panel/commands.rs:289), so atomicity holds today, but the function gives no compile-time or runtime signal of that contract. A future fourth writer (e.g. a new background reconciler or a test helper) can silently violate it and produce the exact "two rows with the same change_id" failure mode the doc warns about. Consider (a) asserting `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK.try_lock().is_err()` (lock-held check), (b) documenting the contract in a `# Panics` / `# Errors` doc section, or (c) making the function take a `&MutexGuard` parameter to make the precondition type-checked.

O(n·k) collision scan in `unique_change_id_for`: each candidate triggers a fresh O(rows.len()) linear scan via `rows.iter().any(...)`, and the loop walks up to 9999 candidates, giving worst-case O(rows · 9999) per call. Build a `HashSet<&str>` of existing `change_id`s at function entry (or take one as a parameter from the caller, which already has the rows loaded) and check membership in O(1).

`auto_applied_from_proposal` does not explicitly call `strategy::gate_decision` before walking transitions; it relies on `status::transition(Rejected, Shadowing)` returning Err (via `is_terminal()` at status.rs:66) to bail out on non-compliant input. If anyone ever relaxes the terminal-state rule (e.g. an "un-reject" workflow that permits `Rejected → Pending`), the unconditional `cr.hard_constraint_compliance = true;` at the end silently overrides compliance to `true` and the entire auto-applied status walk succeeds on input that was never supposed to be auto-applied. Make the gate check explicit and return `Err` early — the explicit check also makes the function self-documenting and removes the coupling to status.rs internals.

`hard_constraint_compliance` is a one-shot construction snapshot: `from_proposal` calls `strategy::gate_decision(p)` once and stores the result as a `bool`, which is never recomputed even though the strategy rules may evolve (thresholds, category additions, policy changes). This preserves an immutable record of the gate decision at the moment of derivation (useful for audit/forensics), so it is fine *if* downstream code paths (apply, rollback, shadow) never re-read `gate_decision` and never trust the snapshot as a current compliance guarantee. Worth documenting this snapshot semantics in the field doc-comment and verifying that any "is this CR still compliant?" check calls `gate_decision` again rather than reading the stored bool.

The "theoretical unreachable" fallback at `unique_change_id_for` does not actually guarantee uniqueness: two calls inside the same wall-clock millisecond (or a clock that has not advanced — NTP slew, suspend/resume, monotonic vs. realtime drift) produce the same `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()` and thus the same candidate id. Even though the comment claims this branch is unreachable, it is still reached on every collision after 9999 attempts and must be a real uniqueness guarantee when it fires. Either (a) include a per-process counter / `AtomicU64` alongside the timestamp, (b) document that callers must serialize via `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` (which they already do), or (c) use a stronger source like `uuid::Uuid::new_v4()` so the fallback is genuinely unique regardless of timing.

comments.content: The hard constraint ② sandbox-bypass rule relies on every caller gating `Approved -> Active` on a skip-canary config, but neither `can_transition` nor `transition` accepts a config/feature-flag parameter. Callers who forget to gate this call will silently bypass the sandbox — the state machine has no way to reject it. Either (a) thread the skip-canary flag through `transition(from, to, skip_canary: bool)` and only allow `Approved -> Active` when true, or (b) move the policy check to a wrapper type so the matrix cannot be hit without the gate. Today the docstring is the only guard, which is exactly the kind of invariant that drifts.

comments.content: `Result<(), String>` collapses three semantically distinct failure modes (no-op, terminal-state lock, illegal topology) into opaque Chinese strings. Callers cannot pattern-match on cause; observability and downstream error mapping degrade at module boundaries; tests have to do fragile substring matching against Chinese wording (see tests below). Replace with a typed error enum (e.g. `pub enum TransitionError { NoOp(ChangeStatus), FromTerminal { from: ChangeStatus, to: ChangeStatus }, Illegal { from: ChangeStatus, to: ChangeStatus } }`) that derives `Debug` + `Display` (via `thiserror` or a manual impl). Tests then assert on variant identity.

When `from == to` and `from.is_terminal()` is true (e.g. `transition(Rejected, Rejected)`), the `from == to` branch returns first and produces the misleading '状态未变' message — when the actual violation is the terminal lock. Reorder so the terminal-state check runs first; terminal-to-terminal is semantically a terminal violation, not a no-op. Tests `transition_terminal_errors` and `transition_same_state_errors` do not exercise this overlap, which is why the bug hid.

Tests assert on Chinese-language substring matches against error strings (`e.contains("非法")`, `e.contains("未变")`, `e.contains("终态")`). Any wording tweak — translation, punctuation, or even a stray whitespace change — silently breaks these tests without surfacing a real regression, and the assertions couple test intent to phrasing. With a typed `TransitionError` enum (see prior comment), assertions can target variant identity (`matches!(err, TransitionError::Illegal { .. })`) which is both more robust and clearer about intent. Same fix benefits the `canary_to_approved_blocked` / `shadowing_to_active_blocked` style assertions that don't even look at the error.

The header docstring lists 'Active → Expired' and '任何非终态 → Expired (TTL 14 天)' as legal transitions, implying the state machine enforces a 14-day TTL. It does not — `can_transition` / `transition` validate only the topology, and no timestamp / deadline is ever consulted. TTL is purely a caller-side responsibility (scheduler reading `created_at_ms` and triggering an `Expired` transition). Reword the doc to clarify: the matrix permits the transition; a TTL scheduler (separate, not in this file) decides *when* to invoke it. Otherwise future readers will assume this file is the TTL source of truth and break invariants by, e.g., allowing premature `Expired` transitions.

Terminal-state authority is split across modules with no compile-time link: `transition` reads `ChangeStatus::is_terminal()` from `super::record`, while `can_transition` hard-codes the terminal set implicitly by having no outgoing arms for `Rejected` / `RolledBack` / `Expired`. Adding a new terminal variant (e.g. `Cancelled`) requires updating both — `is_terminal` in record.rs and the `matches!` matrix here — and there is no test that enforces agreement between the two encodings. Either move the `is_terminal` table into this module alongside the matrix so they live together, or add a `#[test] fn matrix_matches_is_terminal()` that cross-checks both encodings stay in sync.

The `debug_assert!` message string is passed as the only argument after the condition, so `{now_ms}` and `{window_start_ms}` are formatted as literal text rather than the actual values. To surface the offending numbers on panic, pass them as format args: `debug_assert!(now_ms >= window_start_ms, "metrics::compute: now_ms ({now_ms}) < window_start_ms ({window_start_ms})", now_ms, window_start_ms);` (and use `{}` placeholders).

`((now_ms - window_start_ms) as f64 / 86_400_000.0).max(1.0)` conflates two semantically distinct cases: it correctly guards against negative/zero windows, but it also silently inflates any legitimate window shorter than 1 day (e.g. a 12-hour or 6-hour window), biasing `candidate_generation_rate` downward. Guard only against `<= 0.0` and let short windows report their real duration.
comments.suggestion_code:
let raw_days = (now_ms - window_start_ms) as f64 / 86_400_000.0;
    let window_days = if raw_days > 0.0 { raw_days } else { 1.0 };
comments.existing_code: let window_days = ((now_ms - window_start_ms) as f64 / 86_400_000.0).max(1.0);

comments.content: The `if days >= 0.0` guard silently drops any record where `applied_at_ms > now_ms` (clock skew or re-apply race), with no logging or counter. This is inconsistent with the window-day handling and hides anomalies that callers should at least be able to observe. Either surface a separate `skipped_negative_survival_count` field, log a warning, or `debug_assert!` the invariant like the window check does.

`entry().or_insert()` keeps only the first `AppliedRecord` per `mem_key`, locking in a "first match wins" rule that is enforced by the `pollution_survival_duplicate_mem_key_uses_first` test. In a re-apply-after-rollback scenario the later `applied_at_ms` (the one that should reset the survival clock) is ignored, silently understating `pollution_survival_days`. Consider taking the *latest* `applied_at_ms` per `mem_key` (keep `max`) and updating the test, so the metric correctly reflects current pollution longevity.

`EmitReport::written` is misnamed and misleading: the field counts proposals added to the in-process dedup map, not audit rows actually persisted. When `APP_HANDLE.get()` is `None` (test path, or a real startup-ordering bug per the docstring at lines 44–58), `report.written` still reports `1` while nothing reached `bot.log`. The struct doc even says so explicitly: "处理过（计入 dedup 表）的 proposal 数；audit 是否实际写入取决于 AppHandle". Callers and dashboards interpreting `written` as "rows written to audit" will get the wrong number. Either rename the field to something like `dedup_inserted` and add a separate `audit_emitted` counter, or change semantics and only count when the audit path actually fires.

`format!("{:?}", p.origin)` writes a Rust `Debug`-formatted enum variant into `bot.log`, but the comment immediately above explicitly states the kv fields are frozen so `grep evolution.proposal bot.log` keeps parsing. `Debug` repr is not stable: a `#[derive(Debug)]` change, a field-order reordering, a variant rename, or even a compiler upgrade can silently change the emitted string (e.g. `ConsolidationReflection` → `ConsolidationReflection { ... }` if the variant gains a payload, or `ProposalOrigin::Foo` style if formatting flags change). Use a stable accessor such as `p.origin.as_str()` (matching the pattern used for `p.category.as_str()` and `p.impact.as_str()` a few lines above), or define an explicit `Display` impl.
comments.existing_code: "origin" => format!("{:?}", p.origin),

comments.content: Dedup-then-audit ordering has no failure surface. The dedup entry is committed *before* `audit_event!` runs (deliberately, to avoid serializing I/O under the lock — see lines 102–107). The comment calls the resulting "marked but not written" window "acceptable". But the function returns `EmitReport { written: 1, deduped: 0 }` either way, so a caller (or a downstream monitoring pipeline counting audit rows) has no way to tell that an audit row was lost. There is also no log line, counter, or metric for the lost-row case. If `audit_event!` panics, the proposal is now suppressed for 24 h with zero audit trail and no error escapes. At minimum: (a) wrap the audit write so a panic does not poison the mutex while a dedup row already exists (catch_unwind, or push the dedup write to *after* a successful audit, accepting the I/O-under-lock cost for the typical 0-row batch), and (b) emit a structured warning log (`tracing::warn!` / `log::warn!`) when the audit path is skipped so it is observable.

`register_app_handle` silently drops the second `AppHandle` on a duplicate call, leaving only an `eprintln`. The docstring (lines 44–58) acknowledges this is a startup-ordering error case, but `eprintln` is not a programmatic signal: it goes to stderr (often dropped in release builds, Tauri-bundled apps, or piped into a log file that no one watches), so a misconfigured second-setup hook or a test harness re-registering with a *different* runtime instance will bind the wrong handle for the entire process lifetime with no caller-visible error. Either return a `bool` / `Result<(), AppHandle<Wry>>` so the caller can react, or at least emit through the project's structured logging (`tracing::error!`) so the warning survives stderr redirection.

The dedup loop re-reads `p.proposal_id` once for `contains_key` and then clones it for `insert`, and `p` is moved into `to_emit` afterward. Two issues: (1) every iteration allocates a fresh `String` for `proposal_id` even when the proposal is deduped and dropped, since the clone happens unconditionally only inside the non-deduped branch (this is actually fine — but worth noting that the `to_emit.push(p)` move afterwards makes the clone mandatory in that branch, so the current code is correct); (2) the lock is held across the full `for p in proposals` loop plus the prior `retain`, so on a large batch with a large map, every `emit_proposals` call is O(batch × map) under one global lock. For the spec'd scale (proposals from one consolidate pass, likely single-digit) this is fine, but if batch size ever grows, partition by `proposal_id` first or use a `DashMap` / sharded mutex. Worth a `// TODO(scale):` if not addressing now.

`.expect(...)` on the spawn_blocking JoinHandle re-panics on the async worker if the blocking closure panics; `post_consolidation` returns `()` so the panic is unreportable. Depending on runtime config it either silently drops the failure (losing the only signal that consolidation-side work blew up) or aborts the worker (taking unrelated tasks down with it). Replace with a logged match on the `JoinError` and return — the caller cannot do better than record the failure, and propagating `()` with an `eprintln!` is strictly safer than a panic on the async worker.
comments.existing_code:
.await
    .expect("post_consolidation blocking 线程不应 panic")

comments.content: `gated.iter().any(|p| p.proposal_id == e.proposal_id)` is invoked for every entry in `new_entries` whenever `auto_allowed` is true — an O(n*m) nested scan on the notify hot path. Collect the gated `proposal_id`s into a `HashSet` once before the filter so the membership test is O(1) per entry.

The global `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` is held for the *entire* read_all → dedup → rewrite window inside `candidate::write_proposals` (which touches both `proposals.jsonl` and `changes.jsonl`). The comment correctly explains why the single-mutex design avoids dual-lock deadlocks, but the consequence is that every panel command (toggle/delete/keep_shadow/rollback) and every other concurrent consolidation blocks on disk. Under AV scans / network disks the critical section can stretch to seconds and freeze the UI thread that surfaces panel commands. Worth at minimum measuring worst-case rewrite latency, or scoping the lock per-file with an explicit lock-ordering protocol so unrelated writes can proceed in parallel.

Poisoned-mutex recovery via `e.into_inner()` per project `[mutex_poisoned]` convention lets execution resume after a prior holder panicked, but nothing in the recovery path verifies that the on-disk jsonl files were left in a valid state. If the panic happened mid-rewrite (e.g. inside `write_proposals` after `read_all` but before the final `copy`/rename), the candidate pool can be truncated or duplicated and the next call happily operates on the corrupt state — there is no integrity probe, no `read_jsonl` self-heal (which only fires on per-line JSON errors, not on missing trailing data), and no audit event emitted on recovery. At minimum, log to audit on recovery and run a `read_jsonl` round-trip to surface corruption, or fall through to the `.corrupt` backup dance `read_jsonl` already implements.

Silent data loss on corrupted attachments payload: `serde_json::from_str(&s).ok()` swallows the parse error and returns `None`, so callers cannot distinguish "no attachments" from "attachments JSON in DB is corrupt". If the TEXT column is ever malformed (migration from a different schema, manual SQL edit, disk corruption), the attachments silently disappear on every load with no log line, no event, no migration hook. Suggest logging via `inspect_err` (or similar) so corruption is at least surfaced to logs.
comments.existing_code: attachments: attachments.and_then(|s| serde_json::from_str(&s).ok()),

comments.content: Snapshot consistency depends entirely on `lock_db_write()`: `load_workflow` (existence + created_at) and `load_tasks_by_workflow` + `task_fingerprints` are read before `conn.transaction()` begins. The `debug_assert!(super::holding_db_write(), ...)` is stripped in release builds, so any future caller that calls this function without holding the write lock (or releases it before this function runs) can read a different task set than the one it then deletes from, leading to wrong keep/delete classifications. Either (a) move the reads inside the transaction (taking `conn` only via `&Transaction`), or (b) replace the debug_assert with a runtime guard so a misuse is loud.

Pervasive `map_err(|e| e.to_string())?` strips the rusqlite error type (which carries SQLSTATE / `ErrorCode` / primary key info) before it is wrapped into `CommandError::DbError(String)` or returned as `Result<_, String>`. When DB operations fail at a customer site, operators only see a flat string instead of e.g. `rusqlite::Error::SqliteFailure { code, message }`. Either (a) define a `From<rusqlite::Error> for CommandError` impl so the original error is preserved until the API boundary, or (b) keep `rusqlite::Error` and convert only at the boundary with `format!("{source:?}")` for diagnostics.

`partial_cmp` returns `None` for NaN, and `unwrap_or(Ordering::Equal)` silently treats NaN as equal — if any task's `order` value is ever NaN (e.g. corrupt DB row, frontend sending NaN), the sort will not flag it and the export will pick a deterministic but arbitrary order. Suggest rejecting NaN/Inf at write time (e.g. when CanvasPos is decoded), or at minimum surfacing a warning when NaN is encountered so the bad row is discoverable instead of silently normalized.

Tauri emit failures are silently dropped (`let _ = app_emit.emit(...)` / `emit_to(...)`): if the main window has been destroyed mid-save, the IPC channel is full, or the listener is gone, the broadcast no-ops while the DB commit has already succeeded. Downstream widgets/caches then hold stale state with no signal that a refresh is needed. The same pattern appears in `workflow_import` and `workflow_delete`. Suggest logging at minimum, or surfacing the error so callers (or a watcher) can decide whether to retry the broadcast.

The module-level contract advertises `derive_proposals` as a pure function: "输入相同 → 输出相同（proposal_id 稳定，dedup 前提）". In reality the helper calls `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()` internally and threads `now_ms` into `Evidence.created_at_ms`'s twin field `created_at_ms` on the proposal. So while `proposal_id` is stable, two calls with the same `ops`/`report`/`thresholds` will still produce proposals with strictly increasing `created_at_ms`, breaking the "纯函数" promise on its face and undermining any downstream check that compares whole-proposal equality for dedup. Two options: (a) document the contract precisely as "pure up to `created_at_ms`" and tighten the tests so they don't accidentally compare `created_at_ms`, or (b) take `now_ms: i64` as a parameter (mirror `derive_lesson_proposal`'s API) and let callers inject wall-clock or test fixtures.

`derive_proposals` reads the clock internally (`chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()`), but `derive_lesson_proposal` takes `now_ms: i64` from the caller. Two sibling public entry points in the same module therefore have two different time-injection strategies, which makes tests, replay, and any future Phase-2 evolution-counter logic awkward. Pick one: either both helpers take `now_ms` and `derive_proposals`/`derive_proposals_with` get a `now_ms: Option<i64>` (default `chrono::Utc::now()` when `None`) or both rely on the caller-supplied value. At minimum document the asymmetry where each function is declared.

The id-construction strategy differs across the three op branches: `Merge` and `Distill` `sort()` the `refs` before folding them into the secondary hash (canonical, set-like ids), but `Contradiction` folds unsorted `{keep}|{drop_id}`. The asymmetry is defensible — `keep` / `drop_id` carry semantic roles that are not interchangeable — but the file's inline comment only explains the "avoid digit-normalization collapse" motivation, not why this branch deliberately declines to canonicalize. A future maintainer copying the pattern to a fourth op variant could easily canonicalize keep+drop (treating them as a set) and start dropping dedup hits. Recommend adding an explicit "// keep and drop are not interchangeable: do not sort" note near the `{base_id}|{keep}|{drop_id}` call so the invariant is locally visible.

`derive_lesson_proposal` feeds the truncated lesson text straight into `proposal_id(category, &target, &text)` without the secondary `short_hash` disambiguation that the three op-derived branches go out of their way to add. The very comments on this file warn that `normalize_for_hash` collapses digit-only differences (UUID hex form), so two distinct lessons whose text differs only in digit positions (e.g. lesson mentions two memory ids `abc12…` vs `abc34…`) will share a `proposal_id` and silently dedup-collide even though they are semantically different rules. To stay consistent with the other three branches, follow them up with `let base_id = proposal_id(...); let id = short_hash(&format!("{base_id}|{}", some_disambiguator))` — for the lesson path the lesson text itself is the only input, so disambiguation is naturally weaker (dedup will collapse near-identical lessons, which may actually be desired). If that "collisions are intentional" reading is the intent, document it on the function; otherwise mirror the merge/distill pattern with an explicit extra input.

`suggestion.text` is built by `format!`-ing the raw `content` from the `ConsolidateOp` after a soft truncation. The corresponding test `derive_evidence_summary_does_not_leak_raw_paths` actually asserts that the raw `/Users/...` path *is* preserved in `suggestion.text` ("可保留原始 content（这是审计信号）"). That's a deliberate design choice, but it means PII / file paths / credentials supplied in memory content get materialized into the persisted proposal body, downstream of the only sanitization boundary in this module (the neutral fixed `evidence.summary` string). Risk: any future logging, telemetry, candidate-pool UI, or backup that serializes the full proposal will leak user-supplied secrets without any guardrail in this crate. Recommend either (a) documenting loudly at the function-level that `suggestion.text` is treated as sensitive user data and any caller must scrub before persisting/logging, or (b) introducing a small sanitization pass (e.g. redact `~/.ssh/...`, `password=...`, paths under `HOME`) before stuffing it into `Suggestion`. Option (b) plus an explicit "scrubbed at derive-time" comment is preferable because the burden is currently pushed silently onto every downstream consumer.

`evidence.occurrence_count: ids.len() as u32` silently truncates if the op ever carries more than `u32::MAX` ids. Realistically out of reach (4 billion-memory merges), but the file's "**不 panic** ... 异常 ids 全安全" contract says "all extreme input must not panic" — saturation to `u32::MAX` is a correctness bug, not a panic, and would distort the eventual cross-round counter anyway. Pick a saturating cast (`ids.len().min(u32::MAX as usize) as u32` or `u32::try_from(ids.len()).unwrap_or(u32::MAX)`) and add a tiny assertion in `truncate_chars` / `derive_does_not_panic_on_extreme_ids_count` that the result equals the true count for the value tested (currently 100, fine; document intent for larger ranges).

comments.content: Critical: `load_lesson_snapshots` acquires the global `DB_WRITE_LOCK` and holds it across three sequential DB operations (`open_db` + `ensure_table` + `load_all`). On top of being a write lock for a read path (which the in-file comment justifies by saying "store reads share the connection"), this serializes every other consumer of the DB while disk-bound I/O runs — for a "pure-function kernel" surface used on the decision panel, that's a broad blast radius. Recommend either downgrading to a read lock if one exists, scoping the guard so it covers only the actual `load_all` call (move `open_db`/`ensure_table` out of the critical section since the connection is still being set up), or replacing the global mutex with a connection pool.

append() opens the file with create+append and a single write_all of one JSON line, and has three correctness issues stacked together:
1. No inter-process file lock (no fs2/flock); concurrent writers (or a writer racing a reader) can interleave bytes and produce torn lines that break the JSONL audit log. The docstring defers to "candidate::entry::append" but no shared lock is enforced at this site.
2. write_all is not followed by sync_all(); a host crash between write and fsync can lose the most recent record and desynchronize evolution-changes.jsonl from evolution-applied.jsonl. An audit log of rollback decisions and hard-constraint compliance must fsync before returning Ok.
3. All errors are flattened into format!() strings (e.g. "序列化失败：{e}", "写入 ... 失败：{e}"), discarding the original io::Error / serde_json::Error source and any chained context. Callers cannot distinguish IO vs serialization failures or attach backtraces. Use thiserror/anyhow and propagate the original error so programmatic handling and observability are preserved.

The docstring "缺文件返空 vec" understates the contract. The tests in this same module show that the underlying crate::evolution::read_jsonl renames the file to a `.corrupt` backup and rewrites "good" lines when corruption is detected — but this wrapper exposes that destructive behavior as plain `read_all(...)?`. A read call mutating the underlying file has these footguns:
- Surprising side effect: callers reading the audit log do not expect the file on disk to be replaced under their feet, and any external backup job (or hand-edit) racing with the read can lose data.
- The file-level module doc says the backup is `.corrupt-<ts>` while the test grep in this same file uses `ends_with(".corrupt")` — these two contracts disagree (the sibling proposal/entry test uses `.contains(".corrupt-")` + `starts_with("...corrupt-")`, so the record.rs version is the outlier).
- For an audit ledger, silent "fix on read" can mask a more serious issue (e.g. half-written writes from a missing lock); recovery decisions should be explicit.
Recommend returning a `Result<Vec<ChangeRecord>, ReadError>` where `ReadError::Corrupted { backup: PathBuf }` surfaces the backup path so the caller chooses whether to repair, and reconcile the backup-name contract (doc + test + impl) in one place.

ChangeRecord carries several fields whose docs state derivation/invariant rules but provides no constructor or validator, so callers can persist internally-inconsistent records to the ledger:
- change_id is documented as `"chg-" + proposal_id` (构造时派生) but nothing enforces the prefix or that it matches `proposal_id` — append() in this same module will faithfully serialize any garbage.
- mem_key is documented as `"evo:<proposal_id>"` but nothing links it to `proposal_id` — a typo here will silently desynchronize evolution-changes.jsonl from evolution-applied.jsonl (the memoization layer's lookup key).
- human_approver is documented as "None = 还没批准 / 系统自动" but nothing enforces the implied link to `approval_source` (Some(_)=>HumanApproved; AutoApplied/auto paths=>None); the two ambiguous meanings of None ("not yet decided" vs "system auto-approved") are indistinguishable on read.
- parent_id is `Option<String>` with no existence or cycle check — `find_children` will happily traverse a cycle forever if one is present in the JSONL.
Consider newtype wrappers (ChangeId(String), ProposalId(String), MemKey(String)) plus a `ChangeRecord::try_new(...)` constructor that validates the three derived invariants above and returns `Result<_, ValidationError>`, so the JSONL cannot accumulate invalid rows even under schema drift.

`rolled_back_at: Option<i64>` and `rollback_reason: Option<String>` model a single logical event but are stored as two independent `Option`s. The type system allows (None, Some("why")), (Some(ms), None) and (None, None) in non-terminal transitions — all inconsistent states that JSONL will faithfully persist. The grep/test surface (and any UI/audit report) has no way to tell which pairing is the intended invariant, and any "set rolled_back_at" call must remember to set rollback_reason too.\nEncode the pair as a single `Option<Rollback { at_ms: i64, reason: String }>` field; this makes both-or-neither structurally impossible, removes the implicit invariant, and improves readability of the jsonl row (a single `rollback` key replaces two parallel optional keys).

EvalResult's metric fields are bare `f64` with no range/NaN validation. NaN, negatives, or values > 1.0 (for `task_success_rate`, `tool_call_efficiency`, `behavior_deviation`, `rollback_rate`) can be persisted to JSONL by append() and propagated downstream into dashboards, gating decisions, or auto-evaluation thresholds that assume well-defined rates. Because `eval_after` is deserialized straight from disk (`#[derive(Deserialize)]`), legacy or manually-edited rows containing garbage (NaN, ±inf, out-of-range negatives) will load straight into the system with no surfacing of the corruption.\nConsider bounding on construction (clamp to [0.0, 1.0] where applicable, reject NaN/inf) and on deserialization (a typed `BoundedF64` newtype, or post-validate in a `TryFrom` deserializer that returns a typed error rather than silently producing a NaN row in memory).

comments.content: Concurrency hazard: `shadow_apply_for_batch` is `pub async` but performs synchronous filesystem IO (`change::append_change` → `OpenOptions::create(true).append(true).open` + `writeln!` syscalls) inside the `for p in &gated` loop without `spawn_blocking`. The doc comment says "零生产调用方，仅测试", but the function is fully public with no `#[cfg(test)]` / `#[deprecated]` guard, so any future caller on the Tauri async runtime would block a tokio worker thread on real fs IO. Either gate the function to `#[cfg(test)]` (with the production entry as the only public surface) or move the loop body into `spawn_blocking` like `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app` does.

Shared global counter contract is split across two async entry points: this `shadow_apply_for_batch` and `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app` (the production entry) both `fetch_add` `TOTAL_WRITES`/`FAILED_WRITES` and each end-of-fn independently checks `if (failed / total) > 0.05` to emit `evolution.shadow_warning`. Since both paths share the same static atomics with no synchronization between them, every batch that observes an already-elevated historical rate will re-fire the warning (audit spam), and conversely if writes stop after a single failure with no further batch the `>5%` predicate is never re-evaluated so the "失败率 > 5% 告警" design promise is silently violated. Hoist the failure-rate check into a single helper that is also called from a periodic background task (so threshold crossings detected by either entry point surface exactly once), and remove the duplicate inline check from this fn.

Cross-counter snapshot is two separate `Relaxed` loads. `let total = TOTAL_WRITES.load(Relaxed);` and `let failed_count = FAILED_WRITES.load(Relaxed);` are not taken atomically as a pair, so between the two loads another writer's `fetch_add(1)` on either counter yields a rate `(failed / total)` that does not represent any actual moment in time. The audit payload `{failure_rate, failed, total}` will be reported with internally inconsistent fields. Read both counters in one critical section (e.g., wrap them in a single counter struct behind one `Mutex`, or use a `compare_exchange` loop to take a snapshot, or accept that consistency only holds at the latest counter-pair update and document it).

Public mutable fields on `AppShadowSink` (`pub changes_path: PathBuf`, `pub app: Option<&'a AppHandle>`) let any holder of `&mut AppShadowSink` redirect the shadow write target or inject a different `AppHandle` for audit emission, violating the production invariant that writes always go to `<data_dir>/evolution-changes.jsonl` and that audit events carry the same `AppHandle` as the rest of the Tauri runtime. Private fields with constructor-time injection (the existing `new` / `new_for_test` constructors already do this) preserve that contract.

Dedup check inside the store lock does an O(n) full-file read on every append: `change::read_all(&path)` re-parses the entire `evolution-changes.jsonl` (line 287) before each `append_change`. Under sustained proposal volume the cumulative cost across one batch is O(n·k) and the per-write `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` hold time grows linearly with the file, which serializes the three documented writers (shadow/panel/apply) on what is effectively a full re-read. Index non-terminal rows by `proposal_id` once on cold start (or maintain an in-memory `HashMap<String, ChangeStatus>` updated under the lock) so dedup is O(1) lookup, not O(n) parse.

Race vs. production path: `shadow_apply_for_batch` does *not* acquire `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` and *not* call `change::unique_change_id_for` (it appends raw `cr = change::from_proposal(p, now)`), while `shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app` does both. If this fn runs concurrently with the production entry on the same `evolution-changes.jsonl`, two writers can race on the same `chg-<pid>` row id (panel/rollback lookup by `change_id` will then collide) and the production `read_all` dedup can observe half-written lines. Either restrict this fn to `#[cfg(test)]` (and add an `assert!(cfg!(test))` inside if `pub` is required), or have it delegate to the production dedup+lock path so its writes participate in the same write-order contract.

`shadow_apply_for_batch_with_app` reads `bot-config.json` from disk on every call via `crate::evolution::activation::load_state_from_file(&config_path)`, and `is_enabled` reads `bot-config.json` again separately when called from `apply.rs`. Hot path: each shadow batch trigger pays two file reads + two JSON parses for config that changes only on user toggle. Cache the parsed `ShadowConfig` and `ActivationState` (behind a `OnceLock`/`RwLock` with file-mtime invalidation, or a Tauri-managed config event) so non-test code does not hit disk per batch.

Module-level `use` statements are split around the `gate_approved` definition: lines 24–25 import, then lines 31–32 import again after the fn. Although `gate_approved` uses fully-qualified paths so this compiles, mixing `use` and fn definitions at module scope hurts readability and breaks the convention that all imports live at the top of the module. Move both `use` blocks to the top of the file.

Test flake: multiple tests use `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_nanos_opt().unwrap_or(0)` to seed the temp-dir name; under heavy contention (CI parallel runs, fast clock) the `.unwrap_or(0)` collapses to `0` and the tests then share the same `std::env::temp_dir()` prefix, racing on the same `evolution-changes.jsonl` path. Use `std::process::id()` plus a per-test atomic counter, or a `tempfile::tempdir()` (already used in `changes_jsonl_appends_survive_concurrent_writers`) for the path, so collisions are impossible.

comments.content: Public API returns `Result<(), String>` and flattens `io::Error` / `serde_json::Error` via `format!` at the boundary. Original error types and `source()` chains are lost, so the settings-page caller (or any future programmatic consumer) cannot distinguish "JSON parse failed" from "IO read failed" from "serialize failed" without string-matching on Chinese substrings. Consider a domain error enum (e.g. `ConfigWriteError::{Parse, Io, Serialize, NonObjectRoot}` wrapping the original `io::Error`/`serde_json::Error` with `#[source]`) — or at minimum `Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>` — so callers can branch on kind and preserve the underlying chain for diagnostics.

Mutex poison is silently recovered via `e.into_inner()` after only an `eprintln!`. If a prior holder panicked mid-RMW (e.g. an unexpected panic inside the JSON path or `atomic_write`), the lock state is reset without surfacing the corruption signal. The argument that "atomic_write is atomic so file is never partial" only covers the on-disk state — it doesn't cover the in-memory `v` mutation, and a panicking thread could leave `v` in an inconsistent borrow state that the recovered guard then operates on alongside the next caller. Safer to (a) return `Err` on poison so the caller can refuse the write, or (b) document the invariant that nothing in this critical section can panic and at minimum upgrade the `eprintln!` to a metric/log record that monitoring can alert on.

Test couples to a Chinese error substring — if the production message is reworded (even for clarity), this test fails for reasons unrelated to the behavior under test. Brittle. Test the *kind* of failure instead: e.g. assert that the file content is unchanged after the rejected call (which the next `assert_eq!` already does), or define a typed error variant and `match` on it.

Hardcoded `/tmp/` paths are inconsistent with the other tests that use `std::env::temp_dir()`. The crate is part of a Tauri app (cross-platform); `/tmp/...` is a Linux convention and is at best a quirk on macOS/Windows. Use `std::env::temp_dir().join("no-such-thr-xyz.json")` (or `tempfile` crate) for portability and consistency with the rest of the module.

Temp-dir cleanup relies on `let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(p.parent().unwrap());` running at the end of each test. If any earlier `assert_eq!` panics, cleanup is skipped and the temp dir leaks (and on a busy CI host the nanosecond-based dir name plus `unwrap_or(0)` fallback can collide, multiplying the leak). Introduce a small RAII guard (e.g. `struct TmpDir(PathBuf); impl Drop { ... }`) so the cleanup runs on panic too, and add uniqueness (pid + an atomic counter) to the dir name.

Audit/observability gap for `ApplyOutcome::AlreadyPresent`: the arm is empty, so neither `apply::append_applied_record` nor `crate::audit_event!("evolution.human_applied", ...)` runs for this toggle. Control then falls through to 段③ where the CR is transitioned to Active with `approval_source = HumanApproved`. Downstream readers that key off `applied.jsonl` (notably `evolution_metrics` via `crate::eval::metrics::read_applied`, and any future evidence/dedup logic) cannot see that this CR became Active via a human toggle — only the auto-apply track will leave traces in `applied.jsonl`. At minimum emit an `evolution.human_confirmed_existing` audit event here so the human-vs-auto provenance is recoverable from the audit log even when no fresh apply happened.

comments.content: `precompute_human_apply_embedding` runs `candidate::read_all` on the entire `evolution-proposals.jsonl` file outside any lock, only to (a) locate one entry and (b) inspect `layer`. After this returns, `toggle_inner` 段① calls `load_proposals(app)` again and reads the same file inside the store lock — so every policy-layer toggle ON does ≥2 full-file reads and every non-policy toggle ON still pays the cost of two file reads for zero embedding work. Worse, because the outer read is unlocked, `entry.suggestion_text` read here can be a stale line (concurrent RMW between the read and 段①), causing `embed_text` to embed an old version while `apply::apply_one` will later persist the fresh version — the lesson row will store an embedding that doesn't match its content, which can break `embed_failed` fallbacks and conflict-detection recall. Restructure so the embedding is done in 段② (outside `EVOLUTION_STORE_LOCK` but using the freshly-cloned `entry` from 段①, no second file read), and short-circuit non-Policy layers without touching the file at all.

Time-source inconsistency in `evolution_keep_shadow`: this command uses `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()` directly, while the rest of the panel's persisted timestamps route through `crate::memory::now_ms()` (e.g., `toggle_inner` 段② `apply::append_applied_record(&applied_path(app), p, crate::memory::now_ms())?`, `human_apply_one`'s `apply::apply_one(..., crate::memory::now_ms())`, and `entry.expires_at_ms = candidate::compute_expires_at(now_ms)` in this same function which receives the wrong-style time). If `memory::now_ms` exists to provide a clock-injection / test-mock seam (commonly the reason centralizing `now_ms`), bypassing it here prevents integration tests from deterministically exercising TTL resets and shadows being kept across restart boundaries. Use `crate::memory::now_ms()` for consistency.

Same time-source inconsistency as in `evolution_keep_shadow`: `rolled_back_at` should be set via `crate::memory::now_ms()` to keep audit/test seams aligned with the rest of the panel. As-is this column will diverge from `created_at_ms`-style timestamps elsewhere under any clock-injection test harness, making rollback-timeline assertions flaky.

Doc says "其余（含缺字段）按 Auto" but the function returns `Option<Self>` and yields `None` for unknown input — it does NOT default to Auto itself. The "missing field" case is not even this function's job (it only parses strings). Every caller must coalesce `None -> Auto`, which is an easy foot-gun. Either tighten the wording (e.g. "其余返回 `None`，由调用方决定是否回落 Auto") or change the signature to return `Self` with Auto as the explicit fallback so the contract is enforced at the type level.

`importance_for` collapses both `Medium` and `Low` to 3, so the stored `mem_items.importance` cannot distinguish medium-impact from low-impact memory hints. This is preserved as "apply_one 迁移前内联映射原样", but it silently destroys information the upstream `gate_decision` just spent a branch to differentiate (Low gets rejected, Medium gets approved — yet both, when approved, share the same importance). Consider giving Medium its own value (e.g. `Medium => 3`) so the 1..=5 contract actually carries ordering, or document explicitly that importance is intentionally bucketed.

All four fields are `pub`, which prevents enforcing the documented "构造后不可变" invariant at the type level. Callers can freely build arbitrary/inconsistent snapshots or mutate an already-built one via `&mut`. The "snapshot per cycle, immutable thereafter" guarantee is only enforced at the use site, not by the type. Consider making fields `pub(crate)` (or private with a constructor that validates invariants — e.g. `now_ms >= 0`) so the immutability is structural rather than conventional.

`reason: &'static str` plus hard-coded Chinese literals baked into `gate_decision` make this fine for today's audit/test use but it cannot carry dynamic/contextual messages (e.g. "rejected because `evidence.occurrence_count=0`") without an API break. If you anticipate per-proposal reasoning fields (current evidence summary, occurrence count, etc.), consider `String` (or `Cow<'static, str>`) now to avoid the future break; if not, this is acceptable.

The three booleans encode a tiny, interrelated state space with documented precedence and contradiction rules (`all_auto_apply` ⇒ `shadow_only`). Per the type/API design checklist, this should be modeled with an enum so invalid/contradictory combinations become unrepresentable. For example, collapse the apply/shadow axis into something like `enum ApplyMode { Auto, ShadowOnly, Manual }` and keep `disable_notification: bool` as the only remaining primitive; that removes the need for `should_auto_apply` vs `should_shadow_only` to exist as separate derived booleans and removes the post-load normalization branch entirely.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq, Eq, Default)]
pub struct KillSwitch {
    #[serde(default)]
    pub all_auto_apply: bool,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub shadow_only: bool,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub disable_notification: bool,
}

comments.content: `should_auto_apply` returns `!all_auto_apply && !shadow_only` while `should_shadow_only` returns `shadow_only || all_auto_apply`; by De Morgan they are exact complements (`should_auto_apply == !should_shadow_only`). Encoding the same precedence rule twice invites drift: any future tweak to one predicate (or to the normalization step) can silently make them disagree and break the documented priority chain. Collapse to a single source of truth — derive one from the other, or (preferred) derive both from a single enum discriminant so the priority is enforced by the type rather than by hand-written boolean algebra in two places.

`load_from_file` returns `Result<KillSwitch, String>` and converts every failure (IO error, JSON parse error, schema error) into a formatted Chinese string via `format!`. This throws away the underlying `io::Error` / `serde_json::Error` chains, so callers cannot programmatically distinguish `NotFound` vs `InvalidJson` vs `MissingSchemaField`, and cannot preserve the source error for diagnostics. Use a typed error enum (or `thiserror`) that wraps the original error with `#[source]` and add `#[non_exhaustive]` so the schema-distinct error kinds are matchable while still allowing future variants.

The normalization only repairs the `all_auto_apply=true + shadow_only=false` contradiction at load time, but every field is `pub` on the returned struct, so any caller (apply.rs, tests, future code) can flip `all_auto_apply` back to `false` and reintroduce exactly the contradiction this branch just fixed. Either make the fields private with validated constructors/setters, or, better, encode the constraint in the type so the contradictory state is unrepresentable to begin with. Today the load-time fix is effectively a suggestion that callers can quietly undo.

Library/config code writes a diagnostic directly to stderr via `eprintln!`. This bypasses whatever logging/tracing the host application configures, cannot be silenced or redirected by tests, and hard-codes stderr as the channel for a non-error normalization notice. Route this through a `log` / `tracing` macro (e.g. `log::warn!(...)` with feature-gated logging) so the embedder controls sink and verbosity.

`kill_switch.clone()` deep-clones a `serde_json::Value` sub-tree just to hand it to `from_value`, even though `kill_switch` is only needed as the source for that one deserialization call. Cheap for a tiny config block, but it is an unnecessary allocation on the load path and a misleading API (the clone suggests the borrowed value is reused afterwards when it is not). Restructure to either `let ks_owned = evo.get("kill_switch").ok_or_else(...)?.clone(); let mut k: KillSwitch = serde_json::from_value(ks_owned) ...;`, or take the value out of `v` with `["kill_switch"].take()` once `v` is `mut`, removing the clone entirely.

comments.content: The Evidence doc explicitly forbids storing "原始堆栈 / 文件路径 / 用户输入" (raw stack traces, file paths, user input) in `summary` and "原始路径 / 对话内容" in `related_refs`, but the type system does not enforce this — both fields are plain `String` / `Vec<String>`. Any caller (e.g. `derive::derive_proposals` in another module) can silently violate the contract and leak sensitive data into the audit ledger. Consider a typed newtype like `pub struct EvidenceSummary(String)` with a validating constructor that rejects paths/control chars, and a `RelatedRef` enum (`TraceId`, `ToolName`, `MemoryId`) for `related_refs`, so the privacy contract is enforced structurally rather than by convention.

The MVP rule silently treats `SkillHint` as reversible when impact is `Medium`/`Low`. SkillDsl mutation can rename/rewrite skill DSLs whose rollback semantics are non-obvious and not justified in the doc — activation and shadow paths will both trust this default. Either add an explicit branch for `SkillHint` (and document the rollback story), or call out in the doc that "other categories are considered reversible" is an intentional MVP placeholder pending a per-category audit. Right now a reviewer reading just the function body sees two `if` returns and a bare `true` with no explanation of the default.

`related_refs` is documented as containing `trace_id / tool_name / memory id` but typed as a flat `Vec<String>`, so downstream consumers must string-parse to recover the kind and the audit consumer cannot tell which kind a ref is. Model it as a small enum (with `serde(tag = "kind", rename_all = "snake_case")` to keep the audit JSON readable) so the contract is structural and grep-stable, matching the discipline the rest of this module applies to `ProposalTarget`.
