comments.content: `ProposalTarget::tag()` interpolates the user-supplied name into `"kind:name"` without sanitizing `|`, but `proposal_id` uses `|` as the field separator: `format!("{}|{}|{}", category.as_str(), target.tag(), normalized)`. A `tool_name` like `"run_python|crash"` would produce two tags sharing a separator, and after FNV-1a collapsing two distinct `(category, target, summary)` triples could collide on the same `proposal_id`, silently breaking dedup. Either reject `|` (and other separator-like chars) in `ProposalTarget` construction, or pick a separator that normalize cannot emit and verify it cannot appear in `as_str()` / `tag()` outputs (e.g. unit-test both). The test `target_tag_format_is_stable` should be extended to assert no tag contains `|`.

`short_hash` emits 16 hex chars = 64 bits, so birthday-collision probability reaches ~50% around ~4 billion distinct proposals. The file's design assumes this is an audit-dedup ledger, not a security primitive, but with weeks of automated consolidation the dedup guarantee quietly degrades. Either surface this bound explicitly in the `proposal_id` docstring (e.g. "collision probable at ~4B distinct proposals; not suitable for adversarial dedup") or bump to 128-bit (32 hex chars) for a cheap, decades-of-headroom fix. The non-crypto warning is already there for FNV-1a itself, but the 64-bit output width deserves its own caveat.

Read-modify-write on the DB without a transaction. `db_load` → mutate snapshot → `db_upsert` is a classic lost-update window: two concurrent `mark_subtask_done` calls (or a confirmation overlapping with a manual edit) both load the same `updated_at`, both compute the same `expected_updated_at`, and the second upsert silently overwrites the first — one of the two `s.done = true` mutations is lost with no error. The `expected_updated_at` baseline is set, but unless `db_upsert` is verified to enforce an OCC check on that field (and to surface a typed error on mismatch so this function can retry or fail loudly), the comment "RMW 基线 = 快照 updated_at" is wishful — there's no actual compare-and-swap here. Either wrap the load/mutate/upsert in a transaction with row-level locking, or have `db_upsert` reject (and return an error the caller can map to a retry) when `expected_updated_at` no longer matches the row's current `updated_at`.

Identical `unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!(...); e.into_inner() })` block is copy-pasted across `has_pending_for`, `park`, and `take_pending_for`. Three concerns: (1) silent recovery from a poisoned mutex — a panic inside one of these critical sections (or any callback that runs with the guard held) may have left the `pending_map` in a logically torn state, and `into_inner()` papers over it; (2) the duplication makes it easy to diverge (different log message, different recovery policy) the next time someone touches one site; (3) the error message hard-codes the module path, so renaming the file silently produces misleading diagnostics. Extract to a single private fn `lock_pending(app) -> MutexGuard<...>` and decide explicitly whether to propagate the poison (return a `LockResult`) or recover with a single, named policy.

The reentrancy guard is held alive via Drop semantics on a field that is marked `#[allow(dead_code)]` and the comment claims it is "纯存活性持有…从不读取". That comment is already wrong — `resume()` destructures `PendingExec` to bind `exec_guard` and forwards it back into `run_step` — so the field *is* read. The real invariant is more fragile than the comment lets on: any of the following silently re-enables concurrent execution of the same card during the confirmation wait: (a) refactoring `run_step` to take `&mut self` instead of moving `PendingExec`, (b) destructuring without naming `exec_guard`, (c) replacing `PendingExec` with a smaller wrapper or moving the guard into an `Option`, (d) adding a `Drop` impl that touches other fields before the guard drops. Drop the `#[allow(dead_code)]`, add a compile-time guard (e.g. `const _: fn() = || { fn assert_send<T: Send>(_: T) {} let _ = assert_send; };` plus a doc test that destructures and re-uses the guard), and rewrite the doc comment to state the actual invariant in terms of *callers* rather than the field's "reads".

Check-then-act race between `has_pending_for` (reads the session slot) and the `park` performed later inside `run_step` (writes the same slot). Two concurrent `start()` calls for *different* task IDs in the *same* session — which is exactly the multi-task-in-one-chat scenario the per-session slot exists to support — can both observe the slot as empty, both proceed, and the second `park` silently overwrites the first. The `ExecGuard` only protects per-task-ID, not per-session, so it does not mitigate this race. Then the user's next "继续" reply resumes only the second task; the first task's pending entry, its bot-assigned flag, and its mid-flight model call are all dropped without any audit. Fix by performing the "if present, clear" and the eventual insert under one critical section — e.g. have `start()` call a single `replace_pending_for(session_id, new_entry)` that returns the displaced `PendingExec` so its cleanup runs deterministically.

`pending_exec_holds_exec_guard` reads the source file as a string and asserts the substring `exec_guard: ExecGuard` appears within the first 800 chars after `struct PendingExec`. This is brittle on three axes: (1) any attribute, doc-comment line break, or whitespace change before the field declaration breaks the test for no behavioral reason — false positives are common; (2) the test only checks that the substring exists, not that the field is *actually used* to keep the guard alive (e.g. a renamed field of the same type passes, a field that is dropped early in the flow also passes); (3) the test is in this same file, so any renaming of `PendingExec` itself (e.g. `pub(crate) struct PendingExec2`) silently makes the `text.find(...)` return Some and the substring still matches, masking structural drift. Encode the invariant in code that the compiler can check — for example, keep a `#[allow(dead_code)] const _ASSERT_GUARD_HELD: fn() = || { fn needs<T>(_: &T) where T: Sized {} let p: PendingExec = todo!(); needs(&p.exec_guard); };` so removing or renaming the field is a compile error.

Unnecessary clone in hot recursion path. `next` is already a `&Subtask` borrowed from `subs.iter().find(...)`, so `next.id` is a `String` field on the borrowed struct — `&next.id` already coerces to `&str` and `run_step` accepts `&str`. The explicit `.clone()` allocates a new `String` on every transition between subtasks. Drop it: `&next.id`.

`DefaultHasher` is explicitly documented in the stdlib as "not specified, and so it and its hashes should not be relied upon over releases" — different Rust versions (or different stdlib implementations) can produce different hash values for the same input, so the doc comment above that promises "保证同一执行重放时 id 相同" is not actually guaranteed by this implementation. Audit dedup that relies on the id will silently split records after a toolchain bump. If cross-build stability matters, use a stable non-cryptographic hash (`fnv`, `xxhash-rust`, `seahash`) or, better, a real cryptographic hash (`blake3`, `sha2`) whose output is independently verifiable.

Even if `DefaultHasher` were stable across versions, the `trace_id` is also not reproducible across retries/replays of the same execution: `ended_at_ms` is freshly sampled from the wall clock here and then fed into `compute_trace_id` below, so any retried run gets a different `ended_at_ms` and therefore a different id, silently breaking the dedup guarantee promised by the doc comment. Bind the trace to the actual completion time captured by the loop (passed in via `TraceContext`) rather than re-sampling the wall clock at emit time, or hash only `(session_id, started_at_ms)` and document replay-determinism only within a single execution.

`duration_ms` is correctly clamped via `saturating_sub`, but the `ended_at_ms` value written into `ExecutionTrace` and emitted to audit is the raw wall-clock reading with no monotonicity guarantee — a backward clock jump (NTP rollback, manual time change) will persist traces where `ended_at_ms < started_at_ms`, violating the implicit `ended >= started` invariant downstream consumers of audit data may rely on. Clamp the stored value as well (e.g. `ended_at_ms.max(ctx.started_at_ms)`) so the on-disk record is internally consistent; pairing that with a "clock_anomaly" flag makes rollback events observable instead of silent.

`unwrap_or_else(|_| "unknown")` silently swallows any `serde_json::to_string` failure as the literal string `"unknown"`. Because `TraceOutcome` derives `Serialize` and the tests `trace_outcome_serializes_with_snake_case_tag` / `outcome_serde_json_form_locked_for_emit` lock the JSON shape, a real failure here would only occur if those tests drifted from the production type, in which case silently writing `"unknown"` corrupts the audit record without surfacing anywhere. Propagate the error to the caller, or at minimum `eprintln!` the error and the `trace_id` so the failure is observable alongside the trace it failed on.

cleanup_on_exit_with 漏停多个长生命周期后台任务：`bot_scheduler::start_scheduler`、`trace_sink::init`、`due_notify::start_due_notifier`、`memory::consolidate::start_consolidation_scheduler`、`migration::spawn_polling`（以及 `tauri::async_runtime::spawn` 的 models.dev 同步、`mcp::reload_from_config`）都在 setup() 中启动并在 App 存活期内持续轮询 / 持 DB 连接。`cleanup_on_exit_with` 只 stop 了 exec / api / skill / py + mark_exiting，2s drain 期间这些 poller 仍可能在 DB 中写 audit、锁文件、刷 mpsc buffer，与 `kill_py()` 后面的 `audit::write_event` 形成写后写竞态，甚至在 AppHandle 已被销毁时 panic。建议给它们各自提供一个 stop / shutdown 句柄，并在 cleanup_on_exit_with 里在 `mark_exiting()` 之后立即按依赖逆序调用。

`wait_executions_drained` 在 `RunEvent::ExitRequested` 回调里以 50ms 步进 sleep 轮询 `active_execution_count`，最坏阻塞主线程 2s。RunEvent 是 Tauri 主线程上下文，sleep 会冻结 OS 退出握手（macOS Cmd+Q / Windows 托盘「退出」期间 UI 假死、动画不响应）。建议要么换成带超时的 condvar / channel、要么后台线程 drain 并在主线程只 await 标志位、要么直接放弃 drain 改为 fire-and-forget（已 mark_exiting 的执行实例自行收尾）。

`bring_main_to_front` 后台线程未与退出事件协调：spawn 的线程持有 `WebviewWindow` 克隆，sleep 80ms 后才把 `always_on_top` 置回。tray_quit（`app.exit(0)`）若在 80ms 内触发（极常见：双击托盘后立刻 Cmd+Q），主线程已进入 ExitRequested 流程并 `main.destroy()`，这条后台线程仍会 `set_always_on_top(false)` 操作已销毁窗口（目前 `let _ =` 吞掉错误，但线程本身跑到自然结束，无法与 cleanup 路径同步）。建议把 alwaysOnTop 句柄交给 cleanup_on_exit 一并处理，或改用更短的 GUI-线程原子操作（Windows SetWindowPos / macOS NSWindow ordering）。

bot 配置迁移失败仅走 `eprintln!`，未写入审计日志：`migrate_bot_config_schema`、`migrate_legacy_key`、`migrate_search_keys`、`migrate_mcp_server_secrets_locked` 任一失败都不会落 audit 行，但明文 apiKey / search key / MCP env 可能因此残留在 `bot-config.json` 落到磁盘。这是密钥残留场景，事后只查 audit log 无法定位失败；应改成 `audit::write_event(..., AuditLevel::Error, ...)`（并把错误串写入），同时把 `api_start` 自动恢复失败也升级为审计事件（避免「自动恢复」静默失效）。

`.expect("error while building tauri application")` 在生产 Tauri builder 链末尾 panic，注释说明「启动期 panic 可接受」。按项目规则：除非 panic 文档化了一个明确的编程不变量，否则生产/库路径应返回 typed error。此处 builder 失败既非用户输入非法、也非数据非法——它表示 `tauri::generate_context!()` 上下文损坏（编译期资产缺失）确实属于环境/配置不可恢复的 invariant，注释已写明，但 panic 会让崩溃栈回溯和 stderr 出现在用户面前（macOS 上是 dock 崩溃弹窗、Windows 上是 WER），建议改成「日志 + 进程退出码」而非 panic（`std::process::exit(1)` 之前先 audit Error 行），保持语义不变但避免 panic 抽象。

Mutex poisoning is silently swallowed via `lock().ok()?`. If `session.run(...)` ever panics (ONNX runtimes can on malformed inputs/OOM), the mutex becomes poisoned, then every subsequent `embed_text` call returns `None` for the lifetime of the process — with no log line, only an empty vector as evidence. Use `lock().unwrap_or_else(|p| { eprintln!("[memory] session mutex poisoned, recovering"); p.into_inner() })` to recover (or at minimum log when poisoning is detected).

`WMESSAGE_BGE_MODEL_DIR` is taken verbatim from the environment, joined straight into a `PathBuf`, and used without canonicalization or normalization. A relative path or symlink will resolve relative to the process CWD and may differ from the user's intent. More importantly, when the env var points to an unusable directory, the only diagnostic is the generic "模型目录缺失" message — it doesn't say the explicit override was set nor what path it expanded to, defeating the stated design goal of "显式降级并在日志里指出". Canonicalize the path and log the explicit override + failure reason at this site.

`embed_text` has at least 6 silent `ok()?` / `else { return None }` sites where error context is dropped on the floor. For a graceful-degradation embedding pipeline this is intentional, but at minimum the tensor-shape mismatch (`data.len() != seq * EMBED_DIM`) and the `try_extract_tensor` failure are model/output-contract errors that should be logged once so a future ONNX upgrade that changes output shapes is caught at startup instead of looking like "engine unavailable". Either funnel these into a single `eprintln!` inside a helper, or have `embed_text` return `Result<Vec<f32>, EmbedError>` for the in-process callers and only collapse to `None` at the public facade.

`attn.clone()` allocates a second `Vec<i64>` solely so the original `attn` can still be read for `mask_f`. Reorder: build `mask_f` (a `Vec<f32>`) from `attn` first, then move `attn` into the ORT tensor. Removes one allocation per call without changing behavior.

`Engine::tokenizer` is read concurrently from every `embed_text` caller with no synchronization at all — only the `session` Mutex serializes the run, not the encode/prep. Whether this is sound depends entirely on whether the bundled version of the `tokenizers` crate documents `Tokenizer` as `Sync` AND whether its `encode` path is re-entrant for read-only use. If you can't pin a version with an explicit safety guarantee, wrap the tokenizer in the same Mutex (or a `parking_lot::RwLock` if encode is read-only) so future crate upgrades don't silently introduce a data race.

The `Mutex` guard is held across `session.run(...)` and subsequent tensor extraction, fully serializing every embedder for the duration of the inference. This is documented as intentional, but combined with `with_intra_threads(2)` it means chat/IO threads calling `embed_text` block on a single global lock during ONNX forward — under bursty writes this is a hidden latency cliff. Consider a short-lived `Arc<Engine>` handed to a worker pool or at least releasing the lock before the output extraction (clone what you need from the run output).

`compile_rules` silently discards invalid regex via `Regex::new(p).ok()` and then drops whole rules with empty regex sets via `.filter(|r| !r.regexes.is_empty())`. There is no log, metric, return value, or caller signal: a single typo in a skill's `intents` frontmatter makes that intent silently unroutable forever, and the failure shows up far away as "the LLM never picks this skill". At minimum log each dropped pattern with skill name + raw pattern at WARN; ideally have `rebuild_routes` return a summary of skipped patterns so the calling rebuild pipeline can surface it.

The trim loop calls `block_chars` on every pop; each call walks every section header and every bullet line and recomputes `.chars().count()` over them. With `guard < 10_000` and ~10 sections × tens of bullets, the inner path is O(N²) in char counting on a function that runs every chat turn. Any `MemItem` whose `last_accessed_at_ms` / `updated_at_ms` lies in the future (clock skew, manual row inserts, replayed timestamps) makes `base > now_ms` and underflows in debug (panic) or wraps to a huge value in release mode — `.max(0.0)` runs too late to save it. Build a `HashSet<&str>` once per item (or cache the bag on `MemItem`) and bypass the `format!` path when the query has no keywords.

While this guard is held, every `mem_update` / `mem_delete` / `mem_import` / `mem_export` is serialized behind the panel search — a slow hybrid search effectively blocks all memory writes. The file's design comment acknowledges "DB_WRITE_LOCK + spawn_blocking 单写者" so this is intentional, but it is a real read-vs-write contention hotspot and worth either (a) splitting into a separate `DB_READ_LOCK` for reads, or (b) at least adding a TODO so future maintainers see it as a known bottleneck.

`q.and_then(embed::embed_text)` silently collapses a non-empty query down to `None` whenever the embed engine is unavailable (vs. `embed_text` legitimately succeeding and returning `Some`). The caller receives normal-looking search results with no signal that semantic matching was skipped — only `mem_stats` exposes `embed_ok` / `embed_error`. Consider returning a richer shape (e.g. `MemSearchReport { items, semantic: bool, embed_error: Option<String> }`) or, at minimum, logging a warning when the engine is down so this isn't invisible during incident triage.

TOCTOU between `fs::metadata(&path).len()` and the subsequent `fs::read_to_string(&path)` — a file that grows (or is replaced) between the two syscalls bypasses `MEM_IMPORT_MAX_FILE_BYTES`. Mitigations: (a) read into a bounded `BufReader` and stop accumulating once the cap is exceeded, returning a clean error; or (b) at minimum, swap `fs::metadata` for an `open` + `take(MEM_IMPORT_MAX_FILE_BYTES+1)` to make the cap a streaming property rather than a race-prone snapshot.

`parse_import` calls `serde_json::from_str(json)` with no depth / length cap, so a 50 MB JSON file whose values balloon (e.g. deeply nested tags, oversized `embedding` arrays beyond 512 floats, or pathological key repetition) can require far more than 50 MB of resident memory and OOM the worker. Consider rejecting items whose `embedding.len() != 512` (or whatever the engine expects), capping nesting depth, and bounding the total accumulated vector bytes during parsing — the file-size cap is necessary but not sufficient.

`prepare_import_items(&file.items, &|t| embed::embed_text(t))` runs sequentially on the blocking worker *before* the DB lock is taken. With `MEM_IMPORT_MAX_ITEMS = 50_000` and ONNX inference in the tens-of-ms range, this can stall the async runtime worker for minutes outside any cancellation/timeout hook — if the user closes the window or the app is shut down, all of that inference is discarded and the user must restart. Consider: (a) reporting per-batch progress to the UI, (b) bounding the pre-embed pass with an item-count cap (e.g. only pre-embed items without an existing embedding up to N, ask the UI to confirm the rest), or (c) moving embed work inside the per-item loop in `import_items` so the lock's natural contention provides some back-pressure / observability.

`ensure_json_path` is the *only* gate between caller-supplied paths and direct `std::fs` / `atomic_write` calls — it only does a lowercase `.ends_with(".json")` check. There is no canonicalization, no symlink resolution, no rejection of `..` segments, and no restriction to a base directory (e.g. dialog-returned paths). If the Tauri dialog is bypassed (deep-link, IPC replay, webview script injection), an attacker can target arbitrary host paths, including overwriting non-memory JSON files under permissive ACLs. Either: (a) drop the path argument and accept raw bytes from the dialog, or (b) canonicalize the path, verify the parent directory is one of a configured export-dir allowlist, and reject symlink chains.

In `stats_core` the per-column block reads `GROUP BY {col}, COUNT(*)`, which already returns one row per distinct value with the final count. The subsequent `*m.entry(k).or_default() += n` then iterates those rows and re-aggregates into a `BTreeMap` whose `+=` is functionally just assignment — `GROUP BY` guarantees the key occurs once per row. The whole `BTreeMap` round-trip is dead work and adds an O(N log N) sort + hashmap overhead on top of the SQL aggregation. Stream the `query_map` rows straight into the `Vec<(String, i64)>` and rely on `BTreeMap` (or `GROUP BY ... ORDER BY col`) only if ordered output is required.

`mem_export` and `mem_import` wrap their inner `String` error with `.map_err(CommandError::from)`, while `mem_list`/`mem_update`/`mem_delete` use `.map_err(CommandError::DbError)`. The `from(String)` path discards the variant specialization, so callers can't programmatically distinguish DB errors from filesystem/serialization failures. Pick one mapping (e.g. always `DbError`, or add `CommandError::IoError` / `CommandError::SerializationError`) and apply it consistently.

While today's IDs are alphanumeric, this couples the test to a non-escaping assumption and will silently produce malformed JSON if the ID format ever changes (e.g., to allow internal punctuation, slashes, or quotes). Both an `async fn` (binding impl Future<Output=()>) and a synchronous `fn` returning () bind successfully here, so converting post_consolidation back to a sync fn would NOT break this test — exactly the regression the doc comment warns about (sync blocking I/O on the tokio worker) would slip through. comments.content: Auto-mode `apply_adjudications` is not wrapped in an explicit DB transaction. Unlike the Confirm branch (`conn.transaction()`) and `mem_pending_approve` (also transactional), this code opens `&conn` and runs N independent insert/update statements on SQLite's autocommit path. A crash, panic, or `?`-propagated error mid-batch leaves partial adjudication applied (e.g., 3 of 5 facts committed), and the audit entries (`extract_insert_failed` / `extract_adjudicated`) only fire *after* `apply_adjudications` returns — so the user has no signal that some statements landed. Wrap the apply in `conn.transaction()` (mirroring the Confirm branch) so the whole batch commits or rolls back atomically.

`pending_insert` is **not** self-atomic: it does `SELECT COUNT(*)` → conditional `DELETE … LIMIT 1` → `INSERT` with no internal transaction. Today it is only safe because every caller wraps it in `conn.transaction()` (the Confirm branch in `run_extract_with` and `mem_pending_approve`). But this is a silent convention: any future caller that forgets the transaction wrapper (or a test that calls it on a bare connection) will violate `PENDING_CAP` under concurrency — two callers can both observe `count < PENDING_CAP` and both insert, or both DELETE the same oldest row. Either open the transaction inside this function when `conn` is not already in one (rusqlite exposes `conn.is_autocommit()`), or rename it / document the precondition loudly and make the function private to the two call sites that get it right.

`pending_delete` issues one `DELETE … WHERE id = ?1` per id while `store_lock` is held (called from `mem_pending_reject` for arbitrary-length `ids` and from `mem_pending_approve` inside its transaction). For N ids this is N round trips under a held in-process mutex and N separate SQLite write transactions. Collapse into a single `DELETE FROM mem_pending WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)` via `rusqlite::params_from_iter`, returning `Ok(conn.execute(...)?)` for the rows-affected count. Atomic, faster, and avoids holding the lock across many statements.

Fire-and-forget spawn in `maybe_extract_from_session` has no JoinHandle, no timeout, and no shutdown awareness. Errors are swallowed to `eprintln` + a single WARN audit; the function returns immediately so the caller can't observe failures. Combined with the design choice that `throttle_check_set` *occupies the window even on hard failure* (defending against LLM failure storms), a session that hits an environmental error (network, embedding model missing, DB locked) gets blackholed from re-extraction for 30 minutes. Additionally, if the app is shut down mid-extraction, the Auto-mode apply is **not transactional** (see separate finding), and any work the runtime has done is lost with no audit trail beyond the post-mortem `extract_failed` line. Consider: keep the JoinHandle (or use `tauri::async_runtime::spawn` with a structured task tracker), release the throttle window on infra errors (network/DB) but not on parse errors, and propagate shutdown so partial writes aren't committed silently.

`LAST_EXTRACT_MS` is a process-global `HashMap<String, i64>` that grows monotonically: `throttle_check_set` calls `map.insert(session_id.to_string(), now_ms)` but nothing ever evicts. In a long-running app with thousands of sessions over its lifetime (chats reopened, ad-hoc session ids, etc.), this leaks memory — every entry also pins the `String` for the session_id. Add a periodic GC sweep that drops entries older than (say) `2 * EXTRACT_MIN_INTERVAL_SECS`, or bound the map size with an LRU. As-is the map size is unbounded.

Dead `let _ =` on the Confirm branch: `let _ = crate::bot::read_memory_tuning(app);` is called and its result silently discarded. The comment above says "配置读取在锁外" but the value isn't used anywhere in the Confirm path (unlike the Auto path, which feeds `StoreParams::of(...)` into `apply_adjudications`). Either this is leftover from a refactor (and should be removed, since silently swallowing a config-load error hides real problems), or the result should be threaded through to `pending_insert` (e.g., as a `priority`/importance override). As-is it's misleading and a potential silent error source.

Docstring/code mismatch on `apply_adjudications` Update path. The docstring explicitly says: "目标已消失（裁决在锁外、落库前被删）→ 回退 New" (vanished target → fall back to New), but the implementation treats `Ok(0)` (the vanished case) as `counts.failed += 1`, identical to the `Err` arm. Either fix the docstring to match the deliberate design ("vanished 与存储故障同口径，均计 failed，不插入兜底"), or — arguably more correct — restore the original fallback to `apply_insert` so the user's information isn't silently lost when another process deletes the target row between adjudication and apply.

gather_candidates materializes the entire memory table on every tick via store::load_all, then filters and sorts in Rust. For large stores this is the dominant cost and grows linearly with memory size even though the result is bounded by CONSOLIDATE_BATCH_LIMIT. Push the predicate (updated_at_ms >= ? OR access_count >= ?) and the score-based ORDER BY ... LIMIT into SQL so the database returns only the batch.

`first_char_upper` uses `c.to_uppercase().collect::<String>()`, which is multi-character-aware and produces `"SS"` from `'ß'`, `"İ"` → `"İ"` (with combining dot), etc. The doc says "取名称首字符" (single character) and downstream UI treats `fallback_char` as a single glyph for the avatar tile; the comment "非字母/中文原样返回" is also misleading because Unicode letters in Latin/Greek/Cyrillic DO get uppercased. 16MB body cap is misleading: the per-chunk `buf.len() + chunk.len() > MAX_BODY` check runs *after* the `Bytes` chunk has already been materialised in memory by `bytes_stream()`. A single oversized chunk from the server (or a malicious/buggy proxy) is fully allocated before this guard rejects it, so the cap does not actually bound peak memory. Either check `Content-Length` up front and bail before the first read, take the body via `resp.bytes_with_limit(...)` / chunked reader with an internal ceiling, or use `take(MAX_BODY)` on the stream so the upstream is signalled to stop.

`SYNC_TIMEOUT` (30s) only bounds the request up to the response headers via `client.get(url).timeout(SYNC_TIMEOUT).send()`. Once headers are received, the body-stream `while let Some(chunk) = ...` loop has no per-read or total-read deadline: a slow trickle of bytes, a stalled TCP connection, or a server that never finishes the body can hang the sync indefinitely and pin the `lock_db_write()` guard once the body later resolves. Wrap the stream in `tokio::time::timeout` (or use `tokio_stream::StreamExt::timeout`) for the whole read phase, or apply a deadline-aware chunk read.

Cancellation safety: `spawn_blocking` here owns `crate::db::lock_db_write()` and the SQLite transaction. Dropping the outer future (caller timeout, app shutdown, manual-sync abort) drops the `JoinHandle`, but the blocking thread continues and can still commit the transaction and hold the write lock — silently updating the DB for a caller that believed the sync was cancelled, and starving every other writer in the meantime. Either propagate cancellation into the blocking task (e.g. abort on a shared token), or structure the work so a cancelled future cannot leave a half-applied state — for instance, perform the write under a short-lived lock and abort+rollback if `is_cancelled` flips.

comments.content: The "公开路径稳定" list is misleading: only `migration::spawn_polling` is actually re-exported at the top level via `pub use run::spawn_polling;`. The other items (`migration::now_ms`, `migration::filename_matches`, `migration::resolve_archive_dir`, `migration::validate_rules`, `migration::load_rules`, `migration::journal_replay_pending`) are NOT top-level paths — callers must use `migration::ops::now_ms`, `migration::ops::filename_matches`, `migration::rules::validate_rules`, etc. Either add matching `pub use` re-exports or rewrite the list to use the full submodule-qualified form so the "稳定路径" contract actually matches what lib.rs and other modules can write.

All seven submodules are declared `pub mod`, which exposes the entire internal surface (including `db_write_lock`, `MAX_MOVE_REMOVE_FAILURES`, `decide_src_missing`, `SrcMissingAction`, `journal_pending_inner`, `expand_year_placeholder`, etc.) to every downstream consumer. The module-level doc only lists a handful of items as "公开路径稳定", but the actual visibility is much broader than the contract advertises. If integration tests in `tests/` don't need this, prefer `pub(crate) mod` for the non-command submodules and re-export only the documented public surface — this prevents accidental coupling to internal helpers like `journal_*_inner` / `db_write_lock` from outside the migration module.

The `journal_writes_serialize_on_db_write_lock` test claims to verify "全程无 busy 失败" (no busy-timeout fallback), but the assertion `waited >= Duration::from_millis(100)` cannot actually distinguish proper `db_write_lock` blocking from a busy_timeout retry loop — both paths would block until the holder's 200ms sleep elapses, producing ~150ms elapsed time either way. To strictly prove no busy-timeout fallback, either (a) extend the holder's sleep to longer than rusqlite's typical busy_timeout (e.g., 3+ seconds) and assert `waited >= 3s`, or (b) instrument the journal code path to expose whether the lock was acquired immediately vs. after a retry. As written, the test only proves "the call waits", not "the call serializes on the documented lock".

The second assertion `PathBuf::from(&expanded).is_absolute() || expanded.contains('/')` is vacuously true: every template in the iteration (`"工资/{year}"`, `"归档/{year}/Q4"`, `"{year}/发票"`) already contains `'/'` in the input, and `expand_year_placeholder` only replaces `{year}`, so the output also contains `'/'`. The left disjunct `is_absolute()` is false for all three (they're relative templates). The assertion adds zero verification. Either replace with a meaningful check (e.g., the substituted year equals the current year, or that the result is a valid relative path component) or drop the redundant line — keeping vacuous assertions erodes the test suite's signal-to-noise ratio.

The accompanying comment acknowledges this (`// 不能在这里调 recover_move_db，因为需要 AppHandle + 完整 task 表`), but the test name is then actively misleading: future readers will assume replay detection is covered. Rename to something like `journal_state_preserved_after_simulated_move_crash` to match what it actually

The hardcoded upper bound `for _round in 1..8` (7 iterations max) implicitly assumes `MAX_MOVE_REMOVE_FAILURES <= 7`. The assertion `assert_eq!(copies, MAX_MOVE_REMOVE_FAILURES as usize, ...)` will fail whenever MAX exceeds 7, because the loop would terminate via iteration exhaustion rather than via the `break` on `move_remove_permanently_failed`. This couples a test-side loop bound to a production-side constant without any compile-time or runtime link. Use `for _round in 0..=MAX_MOVE_REMOVE_FAILURES + 1` (or a `while`-loop bounded by the same constant) so the test adapts if `MAX_MOVE_REMOVE_FAILURES` is ever retuned upward; otherwise the next bump to that constant will silently turn this regression-guard test into a flaky/dead test.

The module-level doc explicitly states 'Widget/未标记 = 挂件上报' — i.e. a payload with an absent `source` field should be treated as Widget. However, this enum derives `Deserialize` with no `#[serde(default)]` and no fallback/`Other` variant, so a JSON `tasks-updated` event missing the `source` field will fail to deserialize instead of defaulting to `Widget`, breaking the documented protocol contract. Either add `#[serde(default)]` (with `Default = Widget` — but that requires a `Default` impl too) or introduce an `Untagged`/`Other` variant and map it to Widget at the consumer boundary.

`as_str(self)` takes `self` by value. For a `Copy` enum this is functionally equivalent to `&self`, but `&self` is the conventional signature for an accessor/getter and avoids implying any move semantics. Consider `pub fn as_str(self) -> &'static str` → `pub fn as_str(&self) -> &'static str` for consistency with idiomatic Rust accessors.

comments.content: `move_entry` checks `src.is_dir()` only after `fs::rename` has already failed, and then uses that snapshot to choose between `fs::copy`/`fs::remove_file` and `copy_dir_recursive`/`fs::remove_dir_all`. Between the `is_dir()` call and the subsequent I/O, a concurrent rename/replace can change src's type, so the helper may invoke a file-only routine on what is now a directory (or vice versa), producing confusing errors and potentially corrupting state. Re-stat src right before each operation, or capture both `is_dir()` and `is_file()` and assert one of them, e.g. `if src.is_dir() != src.is_file()`.

`copy_dir_recursive` never validates that the staging sibling `<dst>.copying` does not already exist, and never cleans it up if the final `fs::rename(staging, dst)` fails. Two failure modes:
1. Stale `.copying` left over from a prior crash: `fs::create_dir_all(&staging)` is idempotent and `fs::copy` overwrites, so the recursive copy silently mixes stale files with new ones, and the final `rename` then atomically commits the corrupted result to `dst`.
2. Rename failure (target held open on Windows, ACL change, etc.): staging is leaked on disk for the rest of the run.

Before step 3, fail if `staging.symlink_metadata().is_ok()` and after step 5 run `let _ = fs::remove_dir_all(&staging);` on rename failure (or, better, do the staging inside the same RAII guard pattern). On startup, also consider sweeping stale `<name>.copying` siblings in the archive parent.

`claim_dst_name`'s `if next == candidate { return None; }` branch is documented as "theoretically unreachable", but the function returns the same `None` whether the 99-iteration cap was hit due to genuine exhaustion or due to live-lock. Callers cannot tell "no name available, give up" from "all 99 candidates got pre-empted under contention, retry may succeed", and may incorrectly report a hard error or skip the file. Distinguish the two cases — e.g. introduce a separate `Result<PathBuf, ClaimError>` with `Exhausted` vs `LiveLocked` variants, or at minimum return a different sentinel — and let the caller retry/back off for the live-lock variant.

N+1 SELECT per pending memory notification: for each id in `payload.ids` an individual `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mem_pending WHERE id = ?` is issued, giving M*K round-trips per call. Also non-atomic: a `mem_pending` row can be consumed between the COUNT check and the surrounding UPDATE, making the trim/resolution decisions racy. Batch with `WHERE id IN (rarray(?))` (or use `json_each`/temp table) and wrap the read+update in a single transaction so the snapshot stays consistent.

Error swallowing on journal state transitions: `journal_committed_inner(&conn, entry.id).ok()` and `journal_cleared_inner(&conn, entry.id).ok()` discard DB errors. If a state-update fails (e.g. DB locked, disk full), the row stays `pending` and replays on every startup — and the recovery function then sees the same split-brain condition again, but its pre-checks (src.exists()/dst.exists()) may now be inconsistent because user state has moved on. For permanent cases this is benign, for transient cases it turns one hiccup into an unbounded retry loop that can repeatedly clobber user state. At minimum thread the error through `errors` (already counted) and propagate when transient, or commit/clear inside the same transaction as the upsert so they cannot drift. The trim `let _ = conn.execute(...)` has the same problem — a silent maintenance failure lets the journal table grow unbounded.

Per-entry full-table `db_load` defeats the `file_path_untouched` check on two axes. First, `db_load` returns `Vec<super::Task>` and the recovery does an in-memory `find` by id — with N tasks and M pending entries startup work is O(N*M) (and the equivalent in `db_upsert` round-trips). Second, the `expected_src` comparison runs against a freshly loaded snapshot, opening a TOCTOU window between `db_load` and `db_upsert`: a concurrent user rebind (or another writer) can change `file_path` between the two awaits, reintroducing the very "old journal overwrites new binding" class of bug this guard exists to prevent. Replace both with a targeted SQL guard executed atomically with the write, e.g. `UPDATE tasks SET file_path=?1, updated_at=?2, expected_updated_at=tasks.updated_at WHERE id=?3 AND file_path=?4` and check `conn.changes()` to decide whether to commit/clear the journal row.

Permanent-vs-transient classification is a literal substring match (`e.contains("不存在")`) against a user-facing error string. This is brittle in three ways: (a) it is currently coupled to a single `format!("task {task_id} 不存在")` site, so any future wording change silently flips recovery semantics; (b) any transient error message that happens to mention "不存在" (a localized IO error, a SQL "column does not exist", etc.) gets misclassified as permanent and the pending row is dropped; (c) the inverse — a genuine "任务不存在" wrongly classified as transient — turns the bug into an unbounded retry loop on every startup. Use a typed error variant (or at minimum a stable error-kind tag) that the recover functions return, and let the caller decide based on the type rather than parsing free-form text.

Abnormal-state branches drop diagnostic information. The doc-comment promises 'clear 行 + 记错误' for the move case and the equivalent for delete, but the catch-all `_ =>` arms just call `journal_cleared_inner(...).ok();` with no `log_line`, no error classification, and no debug capture. Conditions like 'move already rolled back but dst vanished', 'src still present after a delete attempt that should have removed it', and 'move with both src and dst present' are exactly the split-brain states that users will report later — and right now they vanish silently from the journal, making future diagnosis ('why is my file gone / duplicated?') impossible. Emit a structured log entry (error level) before clearing, or move those rows to a separate `failed_replay` audit table so the evidence survives the cleanup.

Two serial `tauri::async_runtime::block_on` calls per pending entry inside the replay loop. Even ignoring the O(N*M) `db_load` flagged above, each pending entry today pays two async round-trips (db_load + db_upsert) sequenced through `block_on` from the polling `std::thread`. If M pending entries accumulate (a flaky upgrade, a hung DB), startup time grows linearly and the polling thread stays busy holding the SQLite connection for the entire duration. Load the task map once into a `HashMap<String, Task>` at the top of `journal_replay_pending`, batch repairs with a single `db_upsert` (the API already takes `Vec<Task>`), and defer the work to a tokio task on app startup rather than blocking the polling thread.

`notif_resolve` writes whatever `status` string the caller passes; only the `notifications_resolve` Tauri command rejects values outside `done`/`dismissed`. Today `notif_sync_memory` and `notif_resolve_artifact` only forward known constants, but nothing in this function prevents a future internal caller (or refactor) from persisting `STATUS_PENDING`, an empty string, or an arbitrary token into a terminal-state column — which would then never be cleaned up by `notifications_clear_done` and would confuse the navigation badge. Validate inside `notif_resolve` itself (or change the parameter to a small enum / `&'static str` whitelist) so the invariant lives at the data layer, not at one caller.

`notifications_resolve` / `notifications_clear_done` always broadcast `notifications-changed`, even when 0 rows were updated (id not found, already non-pending, or nothing to delete). Each broadcast forces the frontend to refetch the list and the pending-count badge; on rapid double-clicks or stale clients this becomes noticeable UI churn for no state change. Return the affected-row count from the blocking task and only call `emit_changed` when `n > 0`.

Corrupted `payload` JSON is silently coerced to `Value::Null` (`unwrap_or(Value::Null)`) in `notif_sync_memory` and likewise in `notif_resolve_artifact`. A damaged memory_proposal then has `payload.get("ids") == None`, so the loop `continue`s and the row stays `pending` forever (the same applies to artifact_bind with a bad `taskId` — it never matches). Combined with the `unwrap_or_else`+`eprintln` fallbacks in `row_to_view` (which set `created_at` to `0`), schema/IO corruption becomes invisible: the navigation badge keeps a stuck entry, and `notifications_clear_done` never cleans it up. Treat damaged rows as a diagnosable signal — at minimum mark them `dismissed` with a sentinel payload and log a structured warning so the operator can see and clear them.

comments.content: Security/correctness gap: `parse_rules_csv` returns parsed rules without ever invoking `validate_rules`, so the import path trusts callers to validate. Any consumer (front-end command handler, future test, scripted batch import) that forgets the post-parse `validate_rules(&rules)` call can persist rules with `..` paths, bad actions, empty keywords, or absolute-path archive dirs into the JSON file. Either call `validate_rules` here before returning, or document the validate-after-parse contract at the function's signature (e.g., in a doc comment + a `# Panics`-style `/// # Contract` note) and make every caller enforceable through a single entry point. As written, the comment block immediately above lists the very invariants that should be enforced here.

Windows path-traversal bypass: `is_absolute() || has_root()` does not catch Windows drive-relative forms like `C:foo` or `C:..\foo` — they have no root, are not absolute, and `reject_parent_dir_components` only looks at the resolved component string. When later joined against the desktop directory, such paths resolve relative to the CWD of the listed drive (often `%USERPROFILE%` or `C:\Windows`), escaping the configured base. Add a Windows-specific check, e.g. also reject when `r.archive_dir` contains a `:` after the first character or when `Path::components()` yields a `Prefix` component. Defense-in-depth should at least ensure `path.components().any(|c| matches!(c, std::path::Component::Prefix(_)))` returns false.

Unbounded CSV input: the for-loop pushes one `MigrationRule` (with owned `String` fields, freshly-generated UUID, and `Vec<String>` keywords) per record with no row cap, byte cap, or progress/cancellation hook. The csv crate reads the entire input into memory before the first iteration yields, so a malicious or accidentally large CSV forwarded through Tauri IPC can exhaust memory before any per-row validation runs. Cap the maximum row count (and/or total byte length checked up front via `text.len()`) and return a structured `DomainRule` error when exceeded, e.g. `const MAX_RULES: usize = 10_000;` enforced inside the loop.

comments.content: Validation contract mismatch for delete actions: `validate_rules` accepts delete rules with any relative (non-absolute, non-`..`) archive dir (the test `validate_rules_delete_action_archive_dir_boundaries` explicitly asserts `delete` + `"归档/旧文件"` is OK), but `parse_rules_csv` rejects the same input as a stray column. Either `validate_rules` should also enforce empty-archive-dir for delete (preferred — collapses to one rule source) or `parse_rules_csv` should drop the empty enforcement and let `validate_rules` decide. Keeping both produces path-divergent behavior between manual JSON edits and CSV import.

`save_rules_to` collapses every error via `.to_string()`, dropping the original `io::Error` / `serde_json::Error` kind, and the message contains the full absolute filesystem path. Two issues at once: (1) front-end surfacing will leak the user's installation directory (often includes their OS username on macOS/Linux, e.g. `/Users/alice/Library/Application Support/...`) — trim to a basename or relative path before returning; (2) programmatic callers can't pattern-match on the cause — propagate `CommandError::IoError`/`Serialization` with both the structured cause and a human-readable detail, mirroring the structure used in `load_rules_from`. See checklist item on error conversion: errors should not be reduced to strings at boundaries.

Two assertions on the same content use inconsistent length metrics: `content.len() <= 800` (byte length) vs `c2.chars().count() <= 800` (character length). The first will fail when the content contains multi-byte UTF-8 characters (e.g. CJK) past the limit even if the char count is within 800, while the second allows up to ~800 chars regardless of byte size. Use one metric consistently (prefer `chars().count()` since the surrounding code deals with CJK) and pick the metric that matches the production truncation rule.

The `mk` closure hardcodes `id: "x".into()` for every item it builds. If `hybrid_score` / `hybrid_search` (or any downstream consumer used by future tests) ever starts deduping, indexing, or joining on `id` inside a single call, this placeholder will silently mask the bug because every item shares the same id. Prefer a per-item id (e.g. a monotonic counter in the closure) so id-based behaviour is exercised correctly even when items are batched.

comments.content: Strict `assert_eq!(..., 0.0)` on `f32` is intentionally a hard regression guard, but it will also fire on harmless 1-ULP floating-point drift in the guard logic. Consider widening to `assert!(score.abs() < 1e-6)` to keep the regression value while tolerating normal f32 quantization, unless the exact 0.0 is itself part of the API contract.

Tolerance `1e-9` absolute on a value of magnitude 1.0 in `f32` is at the edge of representable precision (≈7 decimal digits). If the renormalization path accumulates in any order other than the assumed `(0.20+0.15+0.10)/0.45`, the result can be `1.0 ± 1e-7` and this test fails on otherwise-correct code. Relax to `1e-6` (or a relative epsilon) unless exact 1.0 is contractually required.

The `use crate::memory::MemoryTuning;` import is placed mid-file rather than at the top of the module. While legal, it splits the import block in two, makes future additions easy to miss, and forces readers to scan the whole file to know what's in scope. Move it to the top-level `use` block.

The anti-hijacking coverage has a gap in the mid-cosine band: `dedup_hint_branch_mid_cosine` shows evo/user pairs in `[0.75, 0.92)` take the hint branch and produce `InsertOutcome::Inserted` + a hint, but no test asserts that the *lesson-vs-user* variant of that branch refuses to co-locate the lesson with the user key. If the anti-hijack guard is currently scoped only to the high-cosine merge path, a regression that lets an evo lesson slip through the hint branch with an `Inserted` outcome pointing at the user's key would not be caught.

comments.content: Stage 1 emits `due` to the UI and then appends the same `due` into `changed`. The unified tail block at the end of the function runs `db_upsert(changed)` again and calls `emit_upserts(app, &changed)`. Result: every archived-due task is upserted twice and emitted twice to the frontend in the same migration run. The comment "阶段一的 due 已包含在 changed 中，重复 upsert 幂等无害" only covers DB idempotence — frontend emission is not idempotent, so downstream listeners/stores will see duplicate update events (and possible list re-render churn). Drop `emit_upserts(app, &due)` here and let the final emit broadcast all `changed`, or skip `due` when pushing into `changed` and only re-emit non-archive items.

`journal_committed(..., id).ok()` discards every error from the final journal-commit loop. If commit fails (lock contention, disk full, schema drift), the journal stays pending forever and the next run will re-execute the same unbind logic via `decide_src_missing`, paying for an extra `db_upsert` and producing a misleading "解除绑定" log entry for a task that was already unbound. Combined with point 1, persistent failures here are silent. At minimum log via `log_line` like the rest of the function does, and consider a consecutive-failure counter to surface stuck journals.

The comment claims the TOCTOU is addressed at this point, but the only post-resolve verification is `verify_archive_dir_created` earlier; the window between `claim_dst_name` returning `Some(dst)` and `move_entry(&src, &dst)` is unguarded. A concurrent run, an external process, or another task with the same `name` can create/replace `dst` in that interval, causing `move_entry` to either silently overwrite (Unix `rename`) or fail without indicating which case occurred. Either re-stat `dst` immediately before `move_entry` (and bail if it now exists), or persist the journal *after* a successful move using a separate "moved_uncommitted" flag so the recovery path always reconciles to the on-disk truth.

Inside `spawn_polling`'s std::thread, `run_migration_inner` calls `tauri::async_runtime::block_on` for `db_load`, then once per task batch in the move/delete loop, plus the final unified upsert — every call clones the entire batch (`due.clone()`, `changed.clone()`, `app.clone()`, `nt.clone()`). Each `block_on` constructs (or re-uses-but-still-blocks) a runtime on the polling thread, and O(N) full-payload clones ship across the async boundary per run. Consider a long-lived `tauri::async_runtime::Runtime` (or single-threaded tokio runtime) owned by `spawn_polling` so the thread isn't building/tearing down a driver each call, and `move` the batches into the async fn rather than cloning. The `app.clone()` per call is also avoidable if `db_upsert` ever takes `&AppHandle`.

comments.content: The repeated `let line = format!(...); report.log.push(line.clone()); log_line(app, &line);` pattern (here and ~20 other call sites) allocates an extra `String` per migration log line. Reorder to `log_line(app, &line); report.log.push(line);` — `log_line` only needs a `&str` borrow, so the buffer can then be moved into `report.log`. Saves one allocation per emitted event, which is meaningful for an archive run of N tasks.

`PromptSlot`'s derived `Ord` ties prompt composition order to enum variant declaration order. Inserting a new variant mid-enum silently reorders every assembled system prompt with no compile-time signal — only the module-level doc comment warns against it. Anyone adding a slot (e.g. between `SkillBody` and `Recovery`) could ship a regression that just reorders sections of every prompt. Consider either (a) an explicit `priority: u8` field on `PromptSlot` with `Ord` derived from that, or (b) a build-time `const _: () = assert!(matches!(PromptSlot::Plan as u8, 5));` style check, or (c) a unit test that asserts the variant→ordinal mapping so a mid-enum insertion breaks CI rather than silently reorders output.

Empty strings are stored in `parts` and only filtered at `build` time. For the typical one-shot chat prompt this is fine, but it means `push(Plan, "")` (which the test `skips_empty_slots` does) still costs an allocation and a Vec slot. Consider skipping empty content in `push` itself (or document explicitly that empty segments are retained by design, e.g. to preserve position). Currently it's an undocumented side effect.

`out` is created via `String::new()` and grown via repeated `push_str`; with N non-empty segments this incurs O(log N) reallocations as the buffer doubles. Since `parts` is fully known at this point, pre-sizing with `String::with_capacity(parts.iter().map(|(_, c)| c.len() + is_empty_offset).sum())` (or a conservative upper bound) avoids those reallocations and is essentially the only thing in this function's hot path. Minor, but cheap to fix.

Both `Default` (derived) and `new()` are provided, but they are functionally identical (`parts: Vec::new()`). This is harmless but slightly redundant — Rust callers can rely on `Default::default()`. If `new()` is kept for readability it should be `#[must_use]` (it currently isn't, unlike `build`). Consider deleting `new()` and relying on `Default`, or at minimum annotating `new()` `#[must_use]` to match `build`'s convention.

Network-path blocklist is incomplete: only http://, https://, and data: are rejected. UNC paths (e.g. \\server\share\img.png on Windows) and file:// URIs slip through, so resolve_with_perm could end up streaming bytes from a network share into the OCR engine — directly violating the documented '识别绝不上传外网' privacy red line. Add explicit denials for 'file:', 'ftp:', '\\\\' (UNC) and '\\\\?\\' before falling through to resolve_with_perm.

Engine Mutex is global, held through the entire blocking ONNX inference, and OnceLock cannot retry. Any single panic during session.run() poisons the Mutex, after which lock().map_err() returns Err on every subsequent OCR call for the lifetime of the process — the only fix is restarting the app. Consider wrapping the Mutex with a panic-safe reload (e.g., catch_unwind around the inference and drop/reload the poisoned Session via a Mutex<Option<Engine>>) so one bad image doesn't permanently brick OCR.

prob_to_boxes uses an explicit Vec as the DFS stack with no upper bound. For a single huge connected component (e.g., a near-full-image probability blob from an adversarial/noisy/dirty lens image), the stack can balloon to O(region_size) entries — easily millions for a 960×960 det input — spiking memory and risking OOM. Bound the stack size (e.g., convert to a true iterative BFS with a preallocated deque and break the loop when the stack exceeds a sane cap, treating the cap-hit case as "ignore the rest of this component" or as an Err).

rec output semantics are assumed, not validated. shape.len() == 3 is checked and logged on mismatch, but the axis order is never asserted (channels=3 must be at axis 1; classes at axis 2; time at axis 1 for rec, classes at axis 2). A swapped or re-exported ONNX (e.g., NCHW vs CHW vs NHWC, or class axis first) would pass the shape check, feed garbage into the argmax loop, and produce silently corrupted text — no typed error surfaced to the caller. Add explicit asserts on shape[1]==3, shape[2]==keys.len()+2 (or similar) before consuming the tensor, and surface a real Err on mismatch instead of eprintln+continue.

CTC decoder silently drops any class index that isn't in [1, keys.len()+1]. Cross-extension avatar cleanup is NOT atomic with the JSON save. In the cross-extension case (e.g. live PNG → upload JPG): the previous avatar file is deleted by the read_dir block BEFORE save_data runs. If save_data then fails (disk full, permission denied, audit append failure inside atomic_write, etc.), the in-memory entry.avatar was never persisted (save failed), so profile.json on disk still references the now-deleted old file. Result: permanent dangling reference; the next profile_get silently shows no avatar and there is no record that the user's original was lost. Only the same-extension path is protected (entry.path() == dest skips deletion). Fix: defer cross-extension cleanup until AFTER `std::fs::rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)?` succeeds; track the old file path captured from `old_avatar` and rename/remove it as the last step (ideally also tolerate prior failures by leaving the cross-extension file in place until success).

Severity: critical — silent user-data loss.

TOCTOU between avatar size validation and copy. `std::fs::metadata(&src)?.len() <= MAX_AVATAR_BYTES` is checked OUTSIDE PROFILE_WRITE_LOCK, but the actual `std::fs::copy(&src, &dest_tmp)` runs INSIDE the lock after directory creation. An attacker (or a process racing on a writable shared path) can grow the source file between the two reads, causing the 5 MB cap to be bypassed — the copy then lands a multi-MB or unbounded avatar in profile/, which the read path in entry_view will then base64-broadcast over IPC. Move the size check (re-stat right before copy) inside the lock, or stat the temp file after copy and bail out + cleanup on overflow.

If `save_data` succeeds but the subsequent `std::fs::rename(&dest_tmp, &dest)?` fails, the new avatar bytes remain stranded in `avatar-<kind>.<ext>.tmp` and no cleanup path is invoked — the `?` simply returns the IoError. Repeated failures (e.g. AV scanner holding the dest open, perms on profile/) will accumulate orphan `.tmp` files in profile_dir and the disk profile.json will reference the OLD file while a stale new file sits alongside. Also, the in-memory `data` returned to the caller has the NEW filename but the on-disk file is the OLD one — caller-visible view diverges from truth until next successful write. Wrap the rename in a cleanup-on-failure helper that removes dest_tmp on Err, and consider reading meta on dest after rename to detect the rename target's disappearance.

comments.content: Truncation guard is too permissive to do its job. `chars().count() >= 30` only catches catastrophic truncation (a prompt accidentally reduced to a single line). A real failure mode is partial copy-paste truncation — e.g. a 3000-char prompt reduced to 200 chars by an editor mishap — which would still pass. Either tighten the lower bound to something closer to the actual prompt lengths (and assert it in a per-prompt `const MIN_LEN`), or — better — record the byte length of each prompt at the time it is added and assert `current_len >= recorded_len - DRIFT_BUDGET`, so accidental shortening trips the test even if legitimate additions later lengthen the prompt.

Behavioral coverage gap: `ADJUDICATE_PROMPT`, `EXTRACT_PROMPT`, `REFLECTION_SYSTEM_PROMPT`, `SUBAGENT_BASE`, the three `PROFILE_*`, `RESULT_SCHEMA_HINT`, `CONSOLIDATE_PROMPT`, and `STEPWISE_ADDENDUM` only receive the generic ≥30-char / non-empty checks. Each of these encodes domain contracts (e.g. extract's JSON schema, consolidate's dedup rules, reflection's stop conditions, subagent profile boundaries, the stepwise precedence already partially asserted here). Silent semantic regressions in any of them will ship undetected. Promote one anchor assertion per high-risk prompt next to its definition in its submodule — same pattern as `system_prompt_keeps_core_rules_and_safety_redlines` — so the contract lives where the string does.

Implicit coupling between the prompt text and runtime call sites is asserted but never enforced. The test docstring notes that `link_file_to_task` / `complete_task` are coupled to dispatch / `bot_slash` and that `STEPWISE_ADDENDUM` is appended after `EXECUTE_SYSTEM_PROMPT` so its phrasing wins on conflict — but nothing here verifies those orderings. If a future caller rearranges the concatenation or renames a tool, this test will still pass while the prompt contract silently diverges from the call site. Either (a) introduce a single `pub(crate) fn build_execute_prompt() -> &'static str` in `execute.rs` that performs the concatenation in code (so the order is the type-checked contract) and has the prompt constants individually assertable, or (b) add a test that reproduces the actual concatenation sequence and asserts the result still contains both segments in order. Same applies to the anchored tool names: a `const fn declared_tools() -> &'static [&'static str]` returned by the same place that owns the tool registry would let this test cross-check against the real tool surface rather than copy-pasting strings.

Mutex guard spans multiple blocking I/O calls. The `BOT_LOG_LOCK` guard `_g` lives until the end of the function, so the lock is held while `rotate_log_if_large` scans/renames files, while `open_log_append` opens the file, and while `writeln!` flushes. File I/O can block, so concurrent audit writers (and any other consumer of this global lock) all serialize behind potentially slow disk operations. Consider scoping the guard to only the critical section (e.g., around `open_log_append`/`writeln!`), or moving rotation outside the lock and using a `BufWriter` kept on a thread-local / once-cell basis.

Silently continues on poisoned mutex. `e.into_inner()` reuses a guard from a poisoned `Mutex`; if the panicking holder was mid-rotation or mid-write, the protected file may be in an inconsistent state (partial rotation, truncated tail), yet subsequent audit lines still get written as if everything is fine. Either treat poison as a hard error (propagate via `Result` / `expect` with documentation) or do an explicit consistency check before continuing; do not silently recover.

Write errors are silently discarded via `let _ = writeln!(...)`. For an audit/forensics log, a dropped line is a silent gap in the trail — full disk, broken pipe, mid-write rotation failure, or permission changes all go unnoticed. The branch that fails to `open_log_append` is also discarded by `if let Ok(...)`. At minimum log the failures; ideally propagate via `Result` so the caller (or a metrics counter) can react.

comments.content: Cache fill is racy under contention. The 'check-cache, release-lock, detect, reacquire, double-check' pattern in `cached_python` and `cached_dotnet` only deduplicates the cache *write* — every concurrent caller that observes an empty cache independently spawns the full 3 s-per-candidate probe sequence (up to 4 candidates × 3 s = 12 s of wasted process spawns under contention). Consider holding a `parking_lot::Mutex`/`tokio::sync::Mutex` and serializing detection, or use a once-cell style initializer (e.g. `OnceCell`/`LazyLock`) so only one probe ever runs.

Busy-wait polling blocks the calling thread. `probe_version_ok_with` (and the sibling `probe_output_with_timeout`) loop with `try_wait` + `thread::sleep(20 ms)` up to a 3 s timeout. `py_env_check_blocking` calls the version probe and then the `-c` lib probe back-to-back, so worst case a single detection call blocks the caller for ~6 s — and because `detect_python` is `pub`, any caller that uses it from a UI / async task pays this cost. Either replace the polling with a `wait_timeout` (not stable on stable Rust today — use `child.wait()` plus `recv_timeout` on a spawned blocking helper, or platform APIs like `WaitForSingleObject` on Windows / `poll` on Unix) or document very clearly that these helpers must not be called from the GUI or async reactor threads.

Silently recovering from poisoned mutexes hides real bugs. Every lock acquisition across `cached_python`, `cached_dotnet`, and `invalidate_python_cache` uses `unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!(...); e.into_inner() })`. A poisoned `Mutex` means a previous holder panicked while holding the lock, which by Rust's contract means the protected state can be in any intermediate form. Continuing to read/write `Option<Option<String>>` here is harmless, but the pattern is copy-pasted as if it were universally safe; if this convention ever spreads to a lock guarding richer state it will silently corrupt data. Either panic on poison (the default) or add a documented invariant that the protected type is panic-safe.

Atomic ordering is stronger than needed for a metric. `PY_PROBE_COUNT` is a monotonic counter used purely for diagnostics; nothing else synchronizes through it. `Ordering::SeqCst` on every `fetch_add` adds a full memory fence on every cache miss for no synchronization benefit. Use `Ordering::Relaxed`.
