When the inner re-check flips skip=true — most notably the `t.tags.as_ref().is_some_and(|v| !v.is_empty())` case where a concurrent writer already set the tags — the closure returns `Ok(t)` with the unchanged task. The code below that unconditionally emits `tasks-changed` and `tasks-updated` with `[row]` in `upserts`, writes a success `Info` audit under the `task_autotag` label, and returns `Ok(row.tags)`. Receivers will treat the unchanged row as a fresh update (which can clobber fresher local state on the main window), and the audit log will credit `task_autotag` for tags it never wrote (often attributing another writer's tags to itself). Change the closure return to a tagged result (e.g. `Result<(crate::db::Task, /*wrote_tags*/ bool), String>`) and only broadcast/audit on the `wrote_tags == true` branch.

Hardcoded `MutationOrigin::Main` misattributes the source. `task_autotag` is fired fire-and-forget from any frontend observer (module doc: "前端观测...后 fire-and-forget 调用"); the command has no window/origin parameter, so we genuinely don't know whether `main` or a `widget` triggered this round. Forcing `source: "main"` causes the main window to treat widget-driven autotag writes as its own, defeating the very purpose of `MutationOrigin` (compile-time-locked conflict resolution per `docs/ARCH-REFACTOR-PLAN.md`). It can also feed echo loops in the receiving merge logic. Either (a) extend the command signature with an explicit `origin: MutationOrigin` argument and have the caller pass it, or (b) add a dedicated `MutationOrigin::Bot` (or `System`) variant for bot-driven mutations and use that here.

The "下次不会重试" comment contradicts the guard code, so the empty-tags path can re-invoke the LLM indefinitely. When the model returns `{"tags":[]}` the function returns `Ok(Some(vec![]))` without writing to the DB, so `task.tags` stays `None` (or `Some(vec![])`), and the very next archive transition re-evaluates `t.tags.as_ref().is_some_and(|v| !v.is_empty())` — which is `false` for both `None` and `Some(vec![])` — so the guard does not skip and the LLM is invoked again. For tasks the model keeps judging "no suitable tag" this is a slow cost leak (each re-archive transition = one LLM call). Persist an empty-tag sentinel (e.g. `{"tags": []}`) so the guard can treat "already-autotag-decided-empty" as skippable, or strengthen the guard to e.g. `t.autotag_attempted_at.is_some()` with a sibling column. Either way, make the comment true.

Both `spawn_blocking` closures return `Result<_, String>` and the outer code converts via `CommandError::from(String)` (prelude: `Err(e) => return Err(crate::error::CommandError::from(e))`; lock path: `.map_err(crate::error::CommandError::from)?`), discarding the typed errors `crate::db::open_db` / `load_task` / `apply_task_patch` actually produced (and that `apply_task_patch` already `.to_string()`'d once before reaching here). The audit log only ever sees a flat string, and programmatic error matching on `CommandError` variants is lost. Either thread `CommandError`/`Box<dyn Error>` through the closure return type, or define a small enum that classifies db errors and propagate that — at minimum change `apply_task_patch(...).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?` to keep the error structured before the lossy conversion.

LLM call has no per-attempt timeout and the retry fires immediately with no backoff. A slow/hung `summarize_messages_with_model` will block the Tauri command indefinitely; a transiently failing downstream (rate limit, 5xx) is hit twice in quick succession, which can compound throttling instead of giving the provider time to recover. Wrap each call with `tokio::time::timeout` (or pass an explicit deadline into `summarize_messages_with_model`) and insert a small backoff (e.g. `tokio::time::sleep` with jitter) before the second attempt; also consider cancelling on `attempts >= 2` so the degraded audit reflects a bounded wait, not a runaway one.

`load_review_model` (DB read) is invoked on every retry iteration. If the setting changes between the two attempts the retry can use a different model than the first attempt, breaking the audit story (`attempts=2` then implies a self-consistent retry). Hoist the read above the `loop` so both attempts use one snapshot and the per-call cost is paid once.

The `_attached_ok` flag returned by `build_attachment_blocks` is silently dropped. Partial/failed attachment reads are invisible to both the caller and the audit log, so the model can be asked clarifying questions against truncated or missing context with no signal that the input was incomplete — exactly the kind of “clarification is enhancement, not gate” failure that should at minimum be audited. Either thread the flag through (return it on `ClarifyResult` for telemetry) or write a `WARN` audit event when any attachment failed to load.

Only the attachment *count* (≤10) is bounded; the per-attachment byte size is not, and the concatenation into `user_content` (and again into the retry `user_content`) has no total cap. This is both a memory/DoS concern and a cost/amplification concern (the LLM provider is billed per token; an attacker-controlled attachment list can drive prompt size arbitrarily high). Enforce a per-attachment byte cap and a total prompt-byte budget here, parallel to the goal length check above.

`chars_truncate` silently drops overflow with no ellipsis and no `truncated: bool` flag, yet `validate_clarify` applies it to every visible string (`question`, `why`, each option, `default`). The frontend therefore cannot tell whether the user is seeing the model’s full sentence or a clipped fragment, and a question like “投放哪个平台？📺 vs 📱” can become meaningless junk without any diagnostic. Either append `…` on truncation, or surface a per-field `truncated` flag on `ClarifyQuestion` so the UI can mark the field.

`kill_tree` does `child.id() as i32` without the `pid > i32::MAX` guard that `is_live_group_leader` explicitly defends against (the wrapped `-1` would target PGID 1 = init and `kill -9 -- -N` for any wrapped value silently hits an unrelated live process group). The two functions are asymmetric: `is_live_group_leader` defends but `kill_tree` doesn't, so a future refactor or a caller passing an externally-sourced PID through `kill_tree` becomes unsafe. Recommend the same `if pid > i32::MAX as u32 { return; }` early-return (or fall back to `child.kill()` + `child.wait()` without a group signal) so the two helpers stay aligned.

Panic safety: there is no RAII guard that actually kills the spawned child on unwind. `ChildRegGuard::register` only adds the PID to `PY_CHILDREN` and removes it on `Drop`; if any code between `cmd.spawn()` (≈ line 756) and the explicit `cleanup_after_fail` / `kill_tree` panics (e.g. a reader thread panic surfacing through `join_reader_threads`, an `unwrap` inside `drain_output`, or any future edit), the child is left running: the PID is yanked out of the set on unwind so `kill_all_py_children` won't find it either, and on Unix nothing else reaps it. Recommend wrapping the spawned `Child` in a `scopeguard`-style cleanup guard (kill on Drop unless explicitly `disarm()`-ed at the explicit cleanup sites) so all panic paths between `spawn` and `cleanup_after_fail` still terminate the child.

Silent setrlimit failure inside `pre_exec` contradicts the S20 contract that lives everywhere else in this file. The cached probe classifies each resource as `Available` only when the upper-bound value succeeded; inside `pre_exec` the two `libc::setrlimit` calls throw away their return values. So if the probe said `Available` but the in-child call now fails (env mutation between probe and spawn, kernel change, EINTR race, etc.), the limit is silently not applied and no audit line is emitted — the run looks healthy in the audit log. The surrounding comment ("探测可用后此处再失败 ... 仍 best-effort 静默") documents this, but the rest of S20 is built around "宁可误判不可用留痕". Consider at minimum logging via `audit` on failure (e.g. capturing errno via `std::io::Error::last_os_error()` and pushing through an `Arc<Mutex<Vec<String>>>` carried into the closure), or returning `Err(PreExecFail)` so the spawn fails loudly instead of a process that thinks it has no memory cap.

`EXITING` is documented as "set once at shutdown, polled in gate paths and tests", but every load/store uses `Ordering::SeqCst`. SeqCst is the most expensive ordering and is unnecessary here — the synchronization that matters is (a) `mark_exiting()` happens-before any subsequent `py_gate_acquire_inner` reject, which only needs `Release` on store + `Acquire` on load, and (b) `reset_exiting_for_test` ordering doesn't matter (it is test-only and there are no concurrent readers using it). Replacing `SeqCst` with `Release` on stores and `Acquire` on loads expresses the actual contract and removes a memory-barrier instruction on the hot acquire path that runs every 200ms during backpressure.

Question budget is debited before the DB insert is attempted: `asks_left.store(left - 1, ...)` runs unconditionally (when `left > 0`), and only afterwards does the code spawn-block on `notif_insert`. If `notif_insert` returns `Ok(false)` (id collision) or `Err(_)` (write failure), the budget is permanently consumed without any question ever being recorded or any audit/emit_changed happening — the next call sees the leaked decrement and silently falls into the 'budget exhausted' warn branch. Debit only after a successful insert, or re-credit the counter on failure (use `fetch_update` / a `match` around the insert and roll the atom back on the failure paths).

The comment correctly states the waiter must precede audit/emit/OS notification, but it is registered *after* `notif_insert` has already produced a `pending` row in `notifications`. The comment in the response command treats "通知不存在" as the only idempotent path; nothing handles the case where the response command fires in the gap between insert and waiter registration — the responder will resolve the notification, persist the answer into brief + audit, find no waiter, and silently drop the wakeup, while this async function then times out and falls back to the assumption. The result is a permanent inconsistency (archive shows the real answer; engine ran on the fallback). Either register the waiter before inserting the notification, or have `workflow_question_respond` re-check the `question_waiters` map briefly after resolving to absorb the racy answer.

Every shared-state lock on `ask_contexts` and `question_waiters` (here in `engine_ask_user`, also in `register_ask_context`, `unregister_ask_context`, and the responder) recovers from poisoning with `unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!("[mutex_poisoned] ..."); e.into_inner() })`. Silently continuing past a poisoned mutex means whatever invariant the panicking thread broke — e.g. a partially-updated `AskRegistration`, or a waiter map left in a torn state — is hidden from later operations and the corruption can propagate. Either panic explicitly on poisoning, or move the recovery to a single helper and document the invariant that makes recovery safe; do not spread this pattern across every call site.

The system notification result is dropped with `let _ = ...show()` and no audit or log line records the outcome. Combined with the 24h `ASK_TIMEOUT_SECS` and the 500ms stop polling, a silent failure here (denied permission, platform notification service down, builder error) means the user is never alerted and the engine still blocks for the full timeout window — a quiet stall with no diagnostic trail. At minimum route the `Result` to `audit::write_event` (warn level on `Err`) so the missed-delivery case is observable, the same way `notif_insert` failures are audited just above.

`invalidate_workflow_questions` issues `SELECT id, payload FROM notifications WHERE kind=? AND status='pending'` and then JSON-parses every row in Rust to filter by `workflowId`. For workspaces with many concurrent runs this is O(total_pending_questions) on every run teardown, plus a JSON parse per row. Push the predicate into SQL (e.g. `WHERE kind=? AND status='pending' AND json_extract(payload, '$.workflowId') = ?`) and parameterise both bindings so the work stays in SQLite and is bound by the size of one workflow's pending queue.

`ACTION_ANSWER` only validates emptiness and then writes the raw `answer` text straight into both `brief` (twice, at the card and global layers) and the audit JSON payload — there is no upper bound on the answer's length. A user can paste an arbitrarily large string into the response card and the file will accept it; both `brief_insert` and `wa_insert` then store the full blob, and the engine later passes `brief_text` back as the tool result. `parse_ask_args` enforces `question ≤200 / why ≤100 / options ≤4×40 / assumption ≤200` on the ask side; mirror the same caps on the answer here (or document and validate a separate answer cap) so a single oversized response cannot bloat DB rows or produce a multi-MB tool result.

TOCTOU race between `set_apply_policy` (writes bot-config.json) and `auto_apply_allowed` (reads bot-config.json). Because both go through the live shared deps directory and there is no in-process cache, the three-attempt retry loop is a documented workaround, not a fix: a sibling test process (e.g. llm_integration U15) can interleave a write/delete of bot-config.json between the write and the read inside any single iteration, so the final `gated_ok` assertion can pass by luck. Deterministic verification requires either an in-memory seam the library can take in tests, or a cross-process file lock around `policy` reads/writes in this test.

`cleanup` swallows every file/DB error (`let _ = ...`), which directly contradicts the module-level invariant that no residue may survive into the next run. If `remove_file` fails because the file is read-only, a sandboxed permission, or held by another process, the next `u20-gov` run inherits stale `proposal_id`s and the segment-0/segment-7 hardcoded ids collide with leftover rows. At minimum, log failures (`eprintln!`) so the residual is attributable; better, propagate or count and fail the test.

The trailing inline `cleanup(...)` plus the `GovGuard::drop` cleanup are an idempotent double-pass, but the FS branch (`fs::remove_file`) is not coordinated across processes and runs unlocked. A sibling test binary can repopulate proposals.jsonl between the two passes, so the second pass may delete `another` test's freshly written entries or leave this test's pid-prefixed entries intact. Holding `DB_WRITE_LOCK` only covers the SQLite branch; consider a process-shared FS lock, or verify after each cleanup that the expected file is empty before dropping the guard.

`GovGuard::drop` performs unchecked FS writes and calls `db_write_lock()` which can panic on poisoned mutexes. If the drop fires while another panic is in flight (the intended purpose of the guard), a panic inside `cleanup`/`restore_cfg` causes a double-panic and aborts the test process before any diagnostic is captured. Wrap the cleanup in a panic-swallowing helper, or precompute idempotent side effects outside the drop path so the drop stays infallible.

Dead hook plumbing undermines the test's stated intent. `hook_for_run` is cloned into the runner closure but immediately discarded via `let _ = hook;` — the success path calls `run_model_loop_core` directly, so `TraceCapture` is never populated on this code path. The test still passes only because `run_task_in_chat_with` writes its own `exec_traces` row (independent of the hook's LoopTrace stats). Two options to make the assertion honest: (a) drop the dead plumbing entirely and rename the test to reflect that it only asserts the lifecycle row, or (b) actually drive a code path that fills the hook so the assertion covers LoopTrace aggregation as the docstring claims.

Time-bounded polling for background writer side effects is the most flake-prone assertion in this file. The 5 s window (100 × 50 ms) is generous, but the writer task is opaque (no synchronization channel, no `await` barrier), so on contended CI the loop can expire with both `span_ok` and `change_ok` false even though the writes are merely delayed. Consider: (1) using a oneshot/`Notify` from `trace_sink::init` so the test can deterministically wait for flush, or (2) exposing a `trace_sink::flush()` test-only barrier and awaiting it before the count query. At minimum, add a diagnostic in the final `assert!` failure (print the latest observed counts) so flakes are debuggable rather than opaque.

Documented production-side divergence: failure-path `exec_traces.session_id` is a runtime-generated id that does not match the caller's `session_id`. The cleanup comment explicitly calls this out ("trace 行落的是运行期生成的会话 id...按 '-' 清不到") and the test papers over it by dual-deleting on session_id AND task_id. The comment also says deps-library pollution by `et-* failed` rows was observed in practice. This is a real upstream contract bug worth tracking independently: `run_task_in_chat_with` should either (a) propagate the caller's session_id onto the failure trace row so downstream consumers can correlate, or (b) document the runtime-generated id as the canonical failure-path session_id and expose it on `TaskChatRun` even when the runner returns `Err`.

`SERIAL` mutex is deliberately held across the entire test body, which forces strict serialization for all three tests against the shared deps DB. This kills nextest parallelism for any test binary that includes this file and concentrates all cleanup pressure on one DB connection per test process. The comment justifies the choice ("整个用例独占共享 deps 库") and the tokio Mutex avoids `await_holding_lock`, but worth confirming with the test harness: (1) nextest's `-j` setting is not being relied upon for speed here, (2) no other integration test binary in this crate opens the same `data_dir` concurrently (e.g. `task_chat_exec`), and (3) the flag-file (`bot-enabled.flag`) deliberately not being cleaned does not break `task_chat_exec`'s assumption. If any of those invariants are wrong, the serialization here will mask a real shared-state bug elsewhere.

`Box::leak(Box::new(tauri::test::mock_app()))` is called once per test invocation (in `setup_task` for the first two tests, and inline in the third). Each call permanently leaks a `Tauri<MockRuntime>` plus its internals for the remainder of the process. Required pattern for 'static handle, but worth noting: if this test file ever grows to dozens of tests via `setup_task`, the per-test leak compounds. Also, the third test (`trace_sink_writes_spans_and_file_changes`) calls `mock_app()` separately instead of reusing `setup_task`, so the helper could be extended with an `init_handle()` variant that lets all three tests share the leak.

The assertion that `127.0.0.1:1` always yields immediate ECONNREFUSED is OS- and firewall-dependent. On hosts that silently filter or drop packets on low ports, `probe_connection` will block until the OS connect timeout (no explicit `Client` timeout is configured here), turning a "fast failure" into a slow stall that can also affect CI wall-clock time. Either build the client with `Client::builder().timeout(...)` (a few seconds is enough for a refused-connect case) or pick an unreachable target whose behavior is fully deterministic in your test environment.

Every probe in this file uses `reqwest::Client::new()`, which configures no timeout at all. If a future change makes `probe_connection` connect successfully but the server never replies (e.g. a hung mock or a regression in a real vendor), the test will stall until the OS read timeout, masking the bug as a slow CI run instead of a failed assertion. Hoist a single `reqwest::Client::builder().timeout(...).connect_timeout(...).build()` into a helper (e.g. `fn test_client() -> reqwest::Client`) and reuse it in every test for a hard upper bound.
comments.suggestion_code: let r = probe_connection(&test_client(), &server.base_url, "openai", "k").await;
comments.existing_code: let r = probe_connection(&reqwest::Client::new(), &server.base_url, "openai", "k").await;

comments.content: `paths.iter().all(|p| p.contains("GET /v1/models"))` is looser than the regression it claims to guard. A malformed path like `GET /v1/models/v1/models` (probe double-prepending `/v1/models`) or `GET /v1/models/` would silently pass even though they are not the canonical probe path, so a real suffix-stripping bug could ship undetected. Pin the path more strictly — e.g. exact equality with `"GET /v1/models"`, or `p == "GET /v1/models"` after first capturing each probe's URL — so the assertion actually rejects any path other than the documented one.

The `MockLlmServer` records only paths (and possibly bodies), not headers, so this integration suite gives zero signal if `apply_anthropic_auth` (or its openai counterpart) silently drops / corrupts the `Authorization` header — the test only verifies that the *URL* is correct. The comment defers this to a unit test "in bot_anthropic module", but if that test ever drifts or is removed, real-vendor auth regressions will surface only in production. Add a thin extension to `MockLlmServer` that captures request headers and assert `req.headers["Authorization"]` (or equivalent) here, so an auth wiring regression fails at the integration layer rather than in the field.

comments.content: `include!("mock_llm.rs")` inlines the helper file as raw tokens at parse time and bypasses Cargo's normal module resolution. This means top-level `cfg`/`cfg_attr` attributes, non-item statements, or `use` declarations inside `mock_llm.rs` are re-parsed in the surrounding test crate's context, which can quietly change semantics and produce confusing errors that point at this file rather than the helper. Prefer `#[path = "mock_llm.rs"] mod mock_llm;` (or move the helper to `tests/common/mod.rs` and `mod common;`) so the helper is parsed and resolved as a normal module with its own scope.
comments.suggestion_code:
#[path = "mock_llm.rs"]
mod mock_llm_re_export;

comments.content: O(n²) stale-content check: `store::load_all(&conn)` is invoked once per corpus item solely to assert no row still holds the old content. With 10 corpus items and a shared test DB this is 10 full table scans where a single load + HashSet<String> (or a targeted `SELECT id WHERE content = ?1` query) would be O(n) total. As corpus grows or the shared DB accumulates more rows, this check becomes the dominant cost of the test.

Raw JSON string interpolation of corpus text into mock LLM reply bodies. `format!(r#"[{{"content":"{new}",...}}]"#)` injects user-visible text straight into a JSON string literal with no escaping; the comment claims "mock 侧负责包 envelope 与转义", but the value is already serialized here. Current corpus is ASCII/Chinese without `"` or `\`, so it works today, but any future utterance containing a quote/backslash/backtick will produce invalid JSON and silently derail both the extract and adjudication stages (the test will then fail at the `request_count` assertion with a confusing message). Either JSON-escape at the boundary (e.g. `serde_json::json!([{"content": new, ...}])` or `json!`) or add a comment guaranteeing the corpus is quote-free and validate it.

`Box::leak` in `mock_handle` leaks a `tauri::test::mock_app()` for the process lifetime to get a stable `AppHandle`. This is the standard tauri-test workaround, but it's an unbounded leak at the API boundary of a helper shared across tests — if more tests adopt this helper the leak compounds and the contract is undocumented. Either guard it with `OnceLock<AppHandle<MockRuntime>>` (one leak per process instead of per call) or add a doc comment stating the leak is intentional and per-process.

On Rust 2024 edition `std::env::set_var` is `unsafe fn` and must be wrapped in an `unsafe { ... }` block (or annotated via `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn`). Calling it in safe code is a compile error, and even on older editions the call is racy because another thread can read the environment concurrently. Use a `static` initializer guarded by `OnceLock` for the test fixture, or move the path into a function parameter that the embed engine accepts, instead of mutating process-wide environment state from a test.
comments.existing_code: std::env::set_var(embed::MODEL_DIR_ENV, "/nonexistent-wm-bge-model-dir");

comments.content: The doc comment asserts the test runs in an independent binary so the embed engine's `OnceLock` failure is cached locally, but there is no runtime guard: if cargo test ever bundles this file with other integration tests, the cached failure will leak and downstream tests in the same binary can no longer exercise the healthy embed path. Either explicitly start a subprocess (`std::process::Command::new(std::env::current_exe()?)`), use a build-script `[[test]]` `harness = false` directive to ensure isolation, or factor the embed engine to accept a path override so the `OnceLock` can be re-armed between tests.

comments.content: The bogus `WMESSAGE_BGE_MODEL_DIR` is set for the whole process but never restored (no `set_var` to the previous value, no `remove_var` after the test). Any doc-tests, examples, benchmarks, or subprocesses spawned from this binary inherit the invalid path and silently fall back to keyword mode. Capture the prior value (or `Option<String>`) at the start of the test and restore it in a `Drop` guard / explicit teardown step.

The assertions couple the test to incidental formatting details of `format_memory_block`: exact prefix `## 记忆`, exact substring `口味：不吃辣`, and exact section heading `### 近期摘要`. Any legitimate tweak to the renderer (whitespace, punctuation, ordering of pinned vs. summary sections, fallback header wording) breaks this test even though the degraded pipeline is still correct. Prefer asserting on semantic invariants (presence of the preference item's content, presence of at least one fallback section, non-empty block) and reserve exact-format checks for a separate, smaller snapshot test that explicitly tracks the format.

Cleanup helpers discard DB errors via `.ok()`. `delete_by_content` and `store::delete_by_key_tag` both silently swallow their `Result`; if the schema drifts (e.g. `mem_items` renamed) or a partial delete leaves residue, the test will silently mis-count the `updated >= 9` bucket without any diagnostic. At minimum, log on `Err` (`eprintln!("[cleanup] {key}: {e:?}")`) so silent data drift between runs is observable rather than masquerading as a clean state.

Per-iteration allocations in the `llm` closure construction. Inside the for-loop body, `server.base_url.clone()` and `client.clone()` feed a fresh `move |...| async move { ... }` closure each iteration; the closure then clones both again to move into the inner `async move` block (necessary for the `async move` capture). Result: 2 client clones + 2 base_url clones per iteration. The outer `client` and `base_url` could be hoisted before the loop and the closure built once, with only the `msgs` payload varying per iteration, reducing allocations and clarifying that `llm` is a reusable adapter rather than per-iteration state.

`mock_handle()` leaks a fresh `tauri::test::mock_app` (plus its associated runtime state) on every call via `Box::leak`, then clones the AppHandle out. The inline comment already acknowledges that "多轮用例下泄漏随调用次数增长". Today the leak is bounded (a handful of calls per `cargo test`), but any future caller that grabs a handle inside a per-iteration closure will compound it silently. Prefer a single shared instance via `std::sync::OnceLock` (or `std::sync::LazyLock`) so the test process leaks one mock app globally rather than one per call.

Synchronous filesystem I/O (`std::fs::write`) runs on the tokio worker thread inside a `#[tokio::test]`. Under `cargo nextest` parallelism this stalls the runtime worker while the write commits and can cascade into pool starvation. Move the write into `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| std::fs::write(...))`, switch the test attribute to `#[test]` (these memory-gate scenarios do no real `.await` work), or use `tokio::fs` for native async I/O.

Synchronous SQLite operations (`db::open_db`, `lock_db_write`, `upsert_tasks`) execute on the tokio worker thread inside `#[tokio::test]`. The mutex guard `let _g = lock_db_write();` plus the synchronous upsert can block other concurrently running test futures on the same worker, especially since the shared `target/debug/deps/wmessage.db` is contended by U15 and T1 sections. Wrap the block in `tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| { ... })`, or move the seed/RMW setup out of `#[tokio::test]` into a synchronous helper, leaving only the actual `run_model_loop_core` async call on the executor.

Synchronous filesystem setup (`std::env::temp_dir`, `std::fs::create_dir_all`, `std::fs::write`) runs on the tokio worker thread inside `#[tokio::test]`. Same concern as the other sync-I/O sites above. Additionally the directory name is derived from `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap()` which silently panics on a clock earlier than the epoch with no actionable message. Consider `tempfile::tempdir()` (auto-cleanup RAII) which also addresses the cleanup-on-panic issue flagged separately.

The `std::fs::remove_dir_all(&dir).ok();` is the final statement of the function — it runs only after every preceding assertion has succeeded. If any of the body-shape or position assertions between this dir's creation and this line panic, the unique temp directory under the OS temp dir leaks permanently and accumulates with each iteration of the test during development. Replace this manual cleanup with a RAII guard (`let _dir = tempfile::tempdir()?;` from `tempfile`, or a custom Drop type) so cleanup runs on every exit path including panics.

comments.content: JSON string escaping is incomplete: only `\\` and `"` are replaced. comments.content: `req_count` and `consumed` are incremented before validating the request is well-formed. If the read loop exits on EOF/timeout/parse failure without a complete header, this code still consumes the next pre-pushed `MockBehavior` and pushes an empty/garbage entry into `bodies`/`paths`. Subsequent tests reading `request_count` / `request_bodies` will silently misalign with the behaviors queue.

`parse_content_length` scans `text.lines()` over the *entire* buffer — including the request body — so a JSON body containing a literal `Content-Length: N` substring will be misread as a header line. Iterate only up to the `\\r\\n\\r\\n` boundary, or fold header parsing into the same `find_body_start`-aware helper. Also guard against absurd `Content-Length` values that would cause unbounded reads (`HttpError(413, ...)` or a sane cap like 1 MiB).

The listener loop processes one connection at a time on a single thread (`for stream in listener.incoming()`). Although the docstring calls this out, it means any caller-side parallelization is silently serialized by the mock — masking real race conditions, ordering bugs, or cancellation issues in the production chat-loop code under test. If parallel test scenarios are ever needed, spawn a worker thread per connection (or use a small `thread::available_parallelism`-sized pool).

`build_http_response` uses `unreachable!()` for `FragmentedTextReply` based on the invariant that the listener loop pre-filters it before calling the builder. Adding a new `MockBehavior` variant requires updating *both* match arms, and a missed update makes the server thread panic at runtime with no diagnostic. Either (a) move all variant dispatch into `build_http_response` and remove the duplicated `match &behavior` in the listener, or (b) add an explicit "handled elsewhere" log + early `return` at the listener boundary so the invariant is enforceable.

comments.content: The HTTP parser trusts whatever Content-Length the client sends and loops until either that many bytes arrive or the stream hits EOF/error. A buggy or hostile client sending an enormous `Content-Length` can pin the worker thread (and the entire mock, since it's single-threaded) for the full 5s read timeout per request, exhausting test resources. Cap `Content-Length` (e.g., 1 MiB) or fail fast on suspicious values and return `413`.

Per-file truncation does not reconcile `total_used`. comments.content: `panic!()` inside `async move {}` closure for the mock executor: if `run_skill_scheduler_core` (or a regression introducing `catch_unwind`) swallows the panic, `scheduler_e2e_paused_run_returns_await_user` would silently pass with `DslOutcome::AwaitUser` even though the executor was actually invoked. Either invoke a direct counter (e.g. `Arc<AtomicUsize>` incremented before the panic to assert 0 calls) and remove the panic, or document that the scheduler core must not catch executor panics.

`RoutesResetGuard` is constructed AFTER the mutation it is meant to undo (`intent_router::rebuild_routes(...)` runs first, then `let _routes_guard = RoutesResetGuard;`). If `intent_rules_from_dirs` or `rebuild_routes` panics, the guard never gets installed and the global routing table stays seeded with fixture rules for any later test in the same cargo-test process. Invert: bind the guard first, then perform the mutation, so the Drop always pairs with the side effect.

`mock_handle()` permanently leaks one `tauri::App` per scheduler test (≥4 leaks per test binary run), and each scheduler test does `test_hook_insert_skill_run` then `test_hook_remove_skill_run` at the end with no RAII cleanup: if any assertion between them panics, the run remains attached to the leaked mock App's state and the temp DB file persists on disk across runs (only `std::env::temp_dir()` cleanup will eventually sweep it). Compare with `RoutesResetGuard` — add a small guard struct (e.g. `struct InsertedRunGuard<'a>(&'a tauri::AppHandle, &'a str);` with `Drop`) and a `temp_db_path` guard so cleanup is exception-safe and the per-test memory churn is documented.

`bot_log_path()` constructs and drops a fresh `tauri::test::mock_app()` on every call, and `bot_log_tail_since()` reads the entire bot.log and decodes it as UTF-8 every time, just to substring-match a small set of needles. With a long-lived test process the shared log accumulates and each scheduler case re-reads the full appended tail. Cache the path (or compute once via a `OnceLock<PathBuf>`), and stream the tail with a `BufReader`/line scan rather than loading + lossy-decoding the whole file.

TOCTOU race between registry check and insert: the `runs()` mutex is acquired and released by the `contains_key` check, then `load_workflow_tasks(...).await` runs without the lock, and only afterward is the lock re-acquired to `insert(...)`. Two concurrent `workflow_run` invocations for the same `workflow_id` can both pass the existence check before either registers, spawning two parallel `run_controller` instances with disjoint `cancel` flags, audit timestamps and DB writes (the second `insert` silently overwrites the first `RunHandle`). Consolidate the check-and-insert into a single locked critical section (e.g. reserve the `Entry` while still holding the lock, dropping the reservation on early failures) so that concurrent invocations deterministically see each other.

`OutcomeFallback::drop` hardcodes `cancelled: false`, so when the spawned future is dropped (panic, runtime shutdown, or normal early-return paths that forget to set `sent = true`) the controller classifies the outcome as a regular failure. In the main loop this falls into the `should_retry` branch and can spawn a duplicate execution, double-charge the acceptance rework budget, and double-write the structured result. Either propagate the cancellation state explicitly (e.g. add a `DropReason`/`Panicked` outcome variant and stop the controller from retrying on it), or set `fallback.sent = true` at every exit point and reserve the Drop path for genuinely unrecoverable panics — never feed Drop-fired outcomes into the retry logic.

`attempts.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| { ...; e.into_inner() })` silently recovers from a poisoned mutex. `attempts` drives the acceptance rework counter — losing the corruption can desync the rework budget from the actual number of attempts, causing the same node to be reworked twice (or not at all) and breaking the evidence chain that downstream audit logs depend on. A poisoned mutex always indicates a previous panic while holding the lock; surface the error (e.g. return a `CommandError`/`Result` from the surrounding helper) or at minimum emit an `AuditLevel::Error` and refuse to mutate, never `into_inner()` on a counter that feeds control flow.

`DB_WRITE_LOCK.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| { ...; e.into_inner() })` silently recovers from a poisoned DB writer. Holding the global DB write lock around `workflow_set_report`, a panic under the lock would mean the previous transaction left the SQLite connection in an unknown state; clearing the lock via `into_inner()` and proceeding can persist a partial/garbled workflow report and cascade into the next `open_db`. Convert to a `Result` so the surrounding `persist_and_emit_report` can log and skip the write rather than continuing in a poisoned state.

`runner_is_running` returns `false` on lock failure. When the registry mutex is poisoned the UI believes no workflow is running, which (combined with the TOCTOU above) makes a second `workflow_run` attempt much more likely to actually register. At minimum log the failure and return an error to the caller; prefer surfacing the inconsistency rather than silently masking it as "idle".

Preallocate the maps at `tasks.len()` and run Kahn's algorithm in place over the existing `indegree` (decrementing to 0 the same way the controller does, but on the original structure) — the clone-and-discard is wasteful on long workflows and on retry it doubles the per-call allocation cost.

Cycle detection re-clones `indegree` and `ready` solely to mutate a scratch copy; the original maps already carry the live state needed by the consumer. comments.content: `duplicate_trigger_rejected_by_exec_guard` correctness depends on a tight ordering: `entered_tx.send(())` must happen strictly *after* `run_task_in_chat_with` has acquired the per-task ExecGuard. Today this is fine because the runner is invoked synchronously after guard acquisition, but the test pins no contract on that ordering — a future refactor that defers guard acquisition, switches to `tokio::spawn` internally, or moves the runner call before the guard, will turn the "正在执行中" assertion into a flaky race that occasionally succeeds (and the `panic!("并发触发应被拒绝")` will then flake). Consider asserting the invariant directly — e.g., have the spawned runner block *before* `entered_tx.send` on a check that the guard is held (via `bot::exec_guard::*` introspection) — so the test fails loudly if acquisition order changes. Also, `release_tx.send(())` happens unconditionally before `first.await`; if the spawned task panics before reaching `release_rx.await`, the runner returns Err, the spawn JoinError's `expect()` panics, and the cleanup path is skipped entirely.

Any regression in (a) tool argument parsing ("taskId" -> SqlArg), (b) audit emission, (c) the conversation-tool-result JSON shape used by the second LLM turn, or (d) the `complete_task` handler itself will keep passing this high-signal test green. `cleanup()` does best-effort DELETEs and silently `.ok()`s them. The inline comment correctly explains why `bot-enabled.flag` is intentionally retained, but the same blind `.ok()` is applied to row deletes against a DB that is *shared across tests and binaries*. comments.content: `readlink -f` is not POSIX. On older BSDs (and some embedded `coreutils`-stripped environments) the `-f` flag is missing or behaves differently, so `readlink -f "$0"` would fall through and `dirname` would land in the wrong directory before any of the later guards run. Since the shebang is already bash, prefer `realpath` if available, or fall back to a POSIX-safe chain: try `readlink -f`, then `realpath`, then `cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."`. Also worth noting: on macOS the BSD `readlink` does support `-f`, but the script's portability story isn't documented anywhere.

SCRIPT_PATH="$0"
if command -v realpath >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    SCRIPT_PATH="$(realpath "$0")"
elif readlink -f "$0" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    SCRIPT_PATH="$(readlink -f "$0")"
fi
cd "$(dirname "$SCRIPT_PATH")/.."

 1. `?:*` 实际匹配「任意单字符 + 冒号 + 任意」，并不仅限 Windows 盘符——合法的 `release-1:beta` / `tag:x86` / CI job 名带冒号都会被拒；若想收紧可改成 `?:[\\/]*`（盘符后必须接分隔符）。
 2. `*..*` 拒绝任意包含两连续点的字符串，因此 `file..backup` 这类合法文件名也被误判为路径注入；可改成更精确的路径段级匹配：`case "${OUT_ROOT}/" in *"/../"*|*"./.."*) ... ;; esac`。
 3. `'\\'*` 在 bash 单引号里是两个反斜杠字面量 + `*`，匹配 UNC 前缀 `\\server\...`，目前 OK；但行首注释把它写成「UNC \\ 开头」（只画了一个反斜杠）容易误导继任者，建议把注释里的 `\\` 改成 `\\\\` 或单引号显示，避免下次有人改写 pattern 时把单反斜杠当转义。
本用法（默认目录仅 `wmessage-portable-<日期>`）影响可忽略，但作为安全边界文档化值得补一句。

comments.content: `set -euo pipefail` 配合这里的 `find ... | wc -l | tr -d ' '` 流水线：若 `tr` 不在 PATH（极少见但 minimal 容器有遇到过）、或 `wc` 实现异常，整条流水线会被 pipefail 判定为失败并连带 exit 1——但 COUNT 仅用于日志，没有真值校验，意义不大；同时 `tr -d ' '` 只剥空格、剥不掉 macOS 罕见情况下的 tab 填充（BSD wc 实际通常用空格，所以这条只是理论风险）。综合两点建议改用更便携且更易读的实现：`COUNT=$(find "$OUT_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f | wc -l | awk '{print $1}')` —— awk 直接取第一个空白分隔字段，比 `tr` 更稳。
comments.existing_code: COUNT=$(find "$OUT_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f | wc -l | tr -d ' ')

comments.content: The `\b` word boundary anchors in the BAD_LINES regex are a GNU grep extension and are NOT recognized by BSD grep on macOS (which this script explicitly targets — see the `~/.cargo/bin` PATH handling). On macOS, `\b` is typically matched as a literal `b` (or silently dropped), so patterns like `\bP[012]-[0-9]+\b` will either fail to match anything (false negatives — forbidden ticket markers slip through) or match the literal letter `b`. Combined with the trailing `|| true`, a broken regex on macOS would make the entire security gate fail-open with no error output. Use POSIX-portable boundaries like `(^|[^A-Za-z0-9])…($|[^A-Za-z0-9])`, or require/document GNU grep, or use `awk` for the scan.

The vitest "fast gate" fallback runs the ENTIRE test suite whenever NEED_TS is true from a config-only change (tsconfig.json / vite.config.ts / package.json) but no `src/` file changed. This directly contradicts the stated "<30s warm / <10s fast" goals — a full vitest run can take many minutes, blocking the commit for no benefit when the diff didn't touch any test or source file. Either skip vitest entirely when only configs changed, or pass an explicit `HEAD`/ref so `--changed` always has a baseline.

comments.content: Untracked-file scanning has no size cap, no binary detection, and no protection against `cat` failure. `cat "$f"` reads the entire file into the shell variable `NEW_LINES`; large or binary files (e.g., a stray log/asset dragged into the repo, a FIFO) can OOM the shell or produce garbled regex input. Under `set -e`, a permission-denied or special-file failure aborts the script mid-scan with a confusing message rather than a clean skip. Add a size guard (e.g., skip files > 1 MiB), binary detection (`file`/`grep -qI`), and `cat … 2>/dev/null || true`.
comments.suggestion_code:
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    if [[ -f "$f" ]] && [[ -r "$f" ]]; then
        sz=$(wc -c < "$f" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
        if (( sz < 1048576 )) && ! grep -qI . "$f" 2>/dev/null; then
            NEW_LINES="$NEW_LINES
$(cat "$f" 2>/dev/null || true)"
        fi
    fi
done < <(git ls-files -z --others --exclude-standard -- '*.rs' '*.ts' '*.tsx' 2>/dev/null)

comments.content: Several git invocations use `2>/dev/null || true`, which conflates "no changes" (expected) with genuine repository failures (not a git repo, corrupt `.git`, permission errors, missing `git` binary). If the script is invoked from a non-repo directory or with a broken `.git`, it silently proceeds with empty/wrong `CHANGED` and `DIFF_SRC`, and the 工单号防线 can be entirely bypassed (empty input → no BAD_LINES → passes). Add an explicit `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` guard at the top, and only suppress stderr on the "empty diff" branch, not on the whole call.

fi
if git diff --cached --name-only 2>/dev/null | grep -q .; then
    CHANGED=$(git diff --cached --name-only)
else
    CHANGED=$(git diff --name-only 2>/dev/null || true)
fi

This file does NOT enforce the stated "warn not deny" policy — readers may incorrectly assume that tweaking this file controls lint severity. Consider either (a) moving the policy statement to a CONTRIBUTING/DEVLOG file and keeping the config purely numeric, or (b) adding the relevant `#![warn(clippy::too_many_lines)]` / `#![allow(...)]` wiring (or `[lints]` entries) somewhere clearly cross-referenced from this file.

comments.content:
`dueChipOf` reports overdue in whole days via `Math.floor`, so a due time that was only hours ago (e.g. yesterday 23:59 with `now` at today 01:00, ~1h ago) is shown as "逾期 1 天". Either include hours when within ~24h, or accept and document the day-rounded semantics. As written, "overdue" granularity is coarser than the actual elapsed time inside the same calendar day.

```ts
const overdueDays = Math.max(1, -dayOffset); // loses sub-day resolution
```

`done` and `ok` are both optional booleans on the same struct, leaving partial states semantically ambiguous: `done=true & ok=undefined` (success or failure?), `done=false & ok=true` (impossible per the contract, but the type allows it), and a missing `result` while `done=true` are all representable but not defined. Consider a discriminated union keyed on status (`pending | ok | failed`) so the relationship between `done`, `ok`, `result`, and `ms` is enforced by the type system rather than by every consumer re-deriving the convention.

Many optional fields on `Msg` (`streaming`, `thinking`, `tools`, `fileChanges`, `skillFailure`, `actionSessionId`) are loosely correlated but the type does not encode their mutual exclusion. Several combinations are clearly nonsensical in practice (e.g. `streaming=true` with a populated `skillFailure`, or both `tools` and `actionSessionId` set on the same turn), yet the current shape silently allows them. A discriminated/tagged representation (e.g. `{ phase: 'streaming', ... } | { phase: 'complete', ... }`) would make invalid combinations unrepresentable and reduce the chance of inconsistent message objects from the backend.

`ChatModelEntry` is an intentional local re-declaration of `SettingsPage/types.ts:ModelEntry` (per the JSDoc) because ChatPanel does not import across directories. There is no compile-time link between the two, meaning a field added/renamed on the settings side will silently drift here. Mitigation: either expose `ModelEntry` from a shared module (and remove the copy), or add a structural-equivalence test that imports both modules and asserts key shape — at minimum, add a CODEOWNERS / review checklist reminder so any change to one is mirrored to the other.

The JSDoc states `SkillFailure` is **session-memory only** and is dropped on refresh/restart; persistence would require changes in `src-tauri/`. Any consumer that serializes `Msg` (IndexedDB, telemetry, export-to-file, log dump) must strip this field — otherwise either the half-finished context leaks to disk or, if a future DB column is added, the session-only intent becomes ambiguous. Suggest documenting the strip requirement next to `Msg` itself, or modeling it as a sibling non-serialized field rather than a property of the persistent `Msg` shape.

ApprovalSource includes "pending", which is semantically wrong for a source enum. "pending" is a status, not an approval source — it duplicates the meaning of ChangeStatus === "pending" and will likely cause label/switch fallthroughs to render nonsense like "Approval source: pending". Confirm with backend whether this tag exists in the real Rust enum; if it does, this is a backend schema bug being faithfully mirrored and should be fixed at the source rather than duplicated here.

comments.content: Refs declared after the useEffect that mutates them. `committedRef`/`cancelledRef` are only safe to reference inside the effect because React runs effect callbacks after the function body completes (avoiding TDZ), but the order is fragile and confusing — group all `useRef` calls (including `prevEditing`) before the effect.

`committedRef.current = true` is never cleared on its own — only the next `onBlur` clears it. If the consumer's `onCommit` is invoked (Enter) but `editing` stays true (validation rejection, async save, parent bug), the flag stays set until the next edit-enter and the next blur is silently swallowed, losing the user's edit. The hook assumes `onCommit` always ends edit mode but has no signal when it doesn't. Either clear the flag after the unmount-blur window (e.g. via a microtask/useEffect) or document/enforce the contract loudly.

`cancel()` resets `draft` to the current `value` prop, not the value that was visible when editing started. If the parent updates `value` during the edit (e.g. another tab/window saved), Escape restores to a different value than what the user originally saw — breaking the "cancel = revert to original" expectation. Snapshot the value at edit-enter into a ref alongside the draft.

`onBlur` commits unconditionally, but `onKeyDown` correctly skips Enter while `e.nativeEvent.isComposing`. If the input loses focus mid-IME-composition (e.g. user clicks away while composing), `onBlur` commits the partial composition as the new value. Defer commit when `e.nativeEvent.isComposing` (BlurEvent also exposes `isComposing` on nativeEvent).

`widgetDragActive` is an exported `let` global mutated outside React. Components reading it during render won't re-render when it changes; only event handlers see the latest value, which is fragile and a classic source of "drag-finished-but-still-collapsed" bugs. There is also no `try/finally` reset, so an exception inside any drag handler leaves the flag stuck `true` forever and the widget stops collapsing at all. Consider replacing with a tiny event emitter / React context / Zustand store that consumers subscribe to, and always clear the flag in a `finally` block at call sites.

`screenSize` silently catches every Tauri failure (genuine API errors, no-monitor on headless builds, web-mode where the Tauri shim throws, etc.) and returns a hardcoded 1920×1080 with no log. Downstream callers — including `anchorFromRect`'s screen-width argument — will then compute snap positions against fictional dimensions, producing silently wrong widget placement. At minimum log the failure, and defensively guard against `m.scaleFactor` being `0` or non-finite (would yield `Infinity`) before dividing.

`loadAnchor` only verifies that x/y are finite numbers — there is no bounds check, in contrast to `loadSize` which defends against bad values with `PANEL_W_MIN/MAX` and `PANEL_H_MIN/MAX`. An anchor persisted on a previously-attached larger monitor, or one tampered with in `localStorage` (e.g. `x = -99999`), is happily accepted and then fed into `anchorFromRect`, where it drives snap-edge detection. Add a sane range cap (or compare against the live monitor width via `screenSize()`) and return `null` when out of range so the caller can fall back to a default layout.

`setTaskH` / `getTaskH` are lossy and asymmetric: the writer accepts any number (including negatives and absurd values) and serializes it raw into the CSS variable, while the reader silently clamps the read with `Math.max(0, v)`. A caller doing `setTaskH(-10); getTaskH();` gets back `0`, not `-10`, so the round-trip is lossy in a non-obvious way. The accompanying comment specifically says `0` is a legitimate state but warns not to treat it as invalid — yet nothing prevents writing negative values that will read back as `0`. Clamp on write too (or document the lossy contract and have the getter return the raw value).

`draftFromDecompose` does a direct `nodes[d].localId` lookup, which throws `TypeError` if the AI payload (or any upstream stage before this call) returns a negative or out-of-range index — the docstring promises the server guarantees `< i`, but there is no defensive bounds check here. comments.content: Case-sensitivity hazard between filesystem-derived `LOBE_ICONS` keys and lowercased lookups. The keys here are taken verbatim from the asset filename (`path.split('/').pop()!.replace(/\.svg$/, '')`), but every consumer of `resolveLobeIcon` ultimately lowercases the slug (via `normalizeVendorName`'s `.toLowerCase()`), and `slugIcon` does not lowercase its argument before lookup. If any SVG in `src/assets/providers/lobe/` is shipped with uppercase letters (e.g. `OpenAI.svg`), it gets stored under `"OpenAI"` while callers query `"openai"` and silently miss — falling through to the text-fallback when the asset actually exists. Lowercase the key at insertion time (e.g. `LOBE_ICONS[basename.toLowerCase()] = url;`) or normalize keys via `.toLowerCase()` at insertion to make the invariant explicit, rather than relying on the sync script's filename convention.

`PROVIDER_ALIASES` is a hand-maintained map with no runtime or build-time validation that each mapped slug actually resolves to an asset. Any alias whose target slug (e.g. `"agnesai"`, `"opencode"`, `"wafer"`, `"kilocode"`) has no corresponding `-color`/monochrome SVG under `src/assets/providers/lobe/` will silently return `null` and rely on the ProviderLogo text fallback, making alias drift invisible. Consider emitting a one-time warning at module load when `slugIcon(target)` returns `null` for every alias target (or running the same check inside `scripts/sync-lobe-icons.mjs`) so that broken aliases surface immediately rather than as missing logos in production.

comments.content: The `import.meta.glob` result is asserted with `as Record<string, string>`, discarding Vite's generated module-shape types. The `query: "?url"` + `import: "default"` shape is actually `{ default: string }` per module; the cast hides that and would silently mask a future query change (e.g. dropping `?url` would yield `{ default: string /* SVG source */ }` and store asset sources, not URLs, without compile error). Use Vite's `GlobEnv`/`ImportGlobString` types or the documented `import.meta.glob<{ default: string }>(...)` overload so a query/import change produces a real type error.

`path.split("/").pop()!` uses a non-null assertion that bypasses the safety guarantee; while glob results do always have at least one segment in practice, this also assumes paths use forward slashes. Under `import.meta.glob` Vite returns POSIX-style paths in all environments, so the split is portable, but a safer pattern (`path.replace(/^.*\//, "")` or a small helper) avoids both the `!` and the assumption. Minor, just removes a small code-smell.

comments.content: Type-hole: `loadGraphFilters` only checks `status.todo/doing/done` and `includeOrphans` for shape, then casts `f.status as GraphFilters["status"]`. If the `GraphFilters['status']` type requires any additional fields (or if `GraphFilters` has other top-level required fields), partial JSON like `{status:{todo:true,doing:true,done:true}, includeOrphans:true}` will pass validation and propagate a partially-typed object to callers. Tighten the shape check to be exhaustive against the actual type definition, or explicitly narrow the return type to `Partial<GraphFilters>` / `GraphFilters | null` after explicit per-field validation.

Unguarded `JSON.stringify` in `saveGraphFilters`: if `GraphFilters` ever contains a non-serializable value (circular ref, `Function`, `Symbol`, `BigInt`, `undefined` in a non-array context), `JSON.stringify` will throw uncaught, while every other `write()` call in this file is wrapped in try/catch. Either wrap the stringify in try/catch and drop the partial write, or assert/document that `GraphFilters` is always JSON-safe.

Single-writer invariant for `sizeMode` (and the other keys) is asserted in the header comment ("图谱图例与设置页共用，永远同值") but enforced only by convention. If any other module (e.g. the G7-SIZEMODE legend implementation) writes `wm.graph.sizeMode` directly to `localStorage`, drift will occur with no read-side reconciliation. Consider documenting this in code (e.g. a `@remarks` note on the setter) or add a small dev-time assert / console.warn if the on-disk value is mutated outside this module.

Asymmetric `setGraphRememberFilters`: turning the flag off deletes the stored filters, but turning it on does not seed them — callers enabling the flag will get `loadGraphFilters() === null` until the user re-applies filters. The current behavior is internally consistent (the header comment calls this "语义诚实"), but the contract is non-obvious; consider a JSDoc note on `setGraphRememberFilters` to make the asymmetry explicit for future maintainers.

The 2-digit zero-pad helper `pad` is duplicated three times: this module-scope declaration, an identical re-declaration as a shadowing local inside `scheduleToDatetime` (which silently hides this one), and a renamed `pad2` inside `isValidDateTimeLocal`. Consolidate to a single module-scope helper — the local declarations are pure duplication and create a drift risk if the format ever changes (e.g. switching to a 4-digit year padding elsewhere).

comments.content: `h` and `m` are destructured but never range-checked. A corrupted persisted schedule such as `"weekly:1:25:99"` will render as a user-visible malformed timestamp (`每周一 25:99`) instead of being treated as bad data. Apply the same per-field integer-and-bounds checks used in `isValidDateTimeLocal` (`Number.isInteger`, `0..23`, `0..59`) and return `s` raw when violated, mirroring the existing `Number(d)` weekday handling.

Inconsistent validation contract between the `weekly` and `monthly` branches of `formatSchedule`: `weekly` performs an explicit `parts.length < 3` guard before destructuring, but `monthly` has no length guard and only validates the day-of-month. Truncation should fail the same way in both branches, and both should additionally bounds-check `h` / `m` (see the related comment on the `weekly` branch) so corrupted schedule strings uniformly fall back to the raw input instead of rendering partial / malformed times.

Only the weekday `target` is validated; `Number(h)` / `Number(m)` flow into `new Date(y, m, d, NaN, NaN)` and the invalid result is rescued only by the inner `fmt`'s `isNaN` fallback. This couples two functions' error handling and obscures intent (compared with the `monthly` branch a few lines down, which validates explicitly). Validate `h` / `m` in this branch as well — same `Number.isInteger` + `0..23` / `0..59` checks used elsewhere — and return `fallback()` directly when invalid, so the contract is local and obvious instead of relying on a downstream NaN guard.

Strict equality violation: `e == null` uses loose equality. Per project rules, `==` / `!=` is prohibited; replace with `e === null || e === undefined` (or hoist a `const isNil = e === null || e === undefined` helper if you want the nullish idiom without the rule violation). The current form also makes a strict-mode audit/linter flag this line.

Silent cross-language code drift risk: `hintForCode` is typed `(code: string) => string|null` with `default: null`, so a new Rust `CommandErrorCode` added without a TS case falls through to message-only and TypeScript cannot flag it. The top-of-file comment claims `errorHandler.test.ts` + `tests-audit/audit_error_codes.py` guard this, but those defenses are external to this file and not enforced at compile time. Tighten by typing the parameter as `CommandErrorCode` and adding an exhaustiveness check (e.g. `const _exhaustive: never = code;`), so an unhandled case fails to compile.

Permissive duck-typed guard: `isCommandError` accepts any object shaped `{code:string, message:string, recoverable:boolean}` regardless of provenance or whether `code` is a known `CommandErrorCode`. A non-Tauri source producing such a shape — a network payload, a test mock, or a hostile event detail on `window` — will be routed through the structured-error branch (with full hint lookup and a retry prompt), which is a misclassification / confused-deputy risk. At minimum validate `code` against `ALL_COMMAND_ERROR_CODES` (or reject unknown codes by treating them as non-CommandError).

Hardcoded timeout value in user-facing copy couples UI text to a backend constant: the CONFIRM_TIMEOUT hint hardcodes "60 秒" while the actual deadline lives in Rust `src-tauri/src/error.rs`. If the backend timeout changes, the UI will lie, and the existing drift defenses (enum-name audit, hint-coverage test) won't catch display-text drift. Either source the value from Rust alongside the error payload, or at minimum add a comment flagging the coupling so future edits know to keep both in sync.

comments.content:
Module-level `let` cache is shared mutable state across the whole app with no synchronization. Two race-prone scenarios:
1. **Startup race**: any consumer that calls `applyArchiveRule` before `loadArchiveDaysFromConfig()` resolves will use the default 7. The comment asks callers to await, but the function gives no way to enforce this — the moment a UI hook renders the task list before init completes, the wrong threshold is applied.
2. **Re-entrant loads**: if `loadArchiveDaysFromConfig` is invoked concurrently (e.g. via the `bot-config-changed` event mentioned in the header comment plus an initial boot load), both promise chains race against `archiveDays` writes; readers may observe a stale value mid-resolution.
Consider `await`-ing the load before any consumer can render, or move the threshold into a getter that reads from a config store (event emitter / context) rather than a bare mutable variable.

comments.content:
`applyArchiveRule` has two correctness issues for legacy `done` tasks lacking `completedAt`:

1. **Semantic corruption**: `completedAt ?? now` backfills with the *function call's* current time, not the real completion time. After this result is persisted, the task is recorded as "completed moments ago", wiping any surviving historical signal of when it actually finished. On the next call, `now - completedAt` counts from the first backfill rather than truth.

2. **Per-call object churn**: because `now = Date.now()` is recomputed on every invocation, `t.completedAt === completedAt` is *always* false for legacy tasks (the stored value is from a previous call's `now`). The trailing `t.completedAt === completedAt ? t : { ...t, completedAt }` therefore emits a fresh object reference for every legacy task on every call, defeating downstream `React.memo`/`useMemo` reference-equality checks and triggering unnecessary re-renders / store dispatches.

Either drop the backfill entirely (treat missing `completedAt` as "do not archive") or stamp it once and persist it separately so subsequent reads reuse the original reference.

Silent error swallow: a failed `bot_get_config` invoke only emits `console.error`, leaving `archiveDays` at whatever value it had previously. Real-world impact — user updates the threshold in Settings, a subsequent boot/IPC failure prevents the new value from being loaded, and the user silently sees the *old* threshold in effect with no UI signal that their setting was not applied. The catch block should either (a) surface a user-facing error so the user can retry, or (b) at minimum record the failure so a stale-cache banner can be shown in the settings page. Right now "保持现值" is indistinguishable from "successfully loaded the same value".

approveMemoryProposals is typed Promise<unknown> while its sibling rejectMemoryProposals returns Promise<number>. Both call mem_pending_* commands that very likely return the same shape (e.g. count of accepted/rejected items). The Promise<unknown> is inconsistent with the rest of the module and forces callers to either cast or ignore the return value, losing the type contract that the reject wrapper provides.

payload is declared as Record<string, unknown> for every kind, but each kind (memory_proposal / evolution_proposal / artifact_bind / workflow_question) almost certainly has a distinct shape. A discriminated union keyed on `kind` would let TypeScript enforce per-kind payload contracts at compile time and prevent UI/runtime shape mismatches when reading notification.payload.

NOTIFICATIONS_CHANGED_EVENT is declared and documented as the cross-module refresh contract ("列表与导航角标据此刷新"), but this file neither emits it nor listens to it. There's no enforcement point in this module, so a typo or rename here will silently break every subscriber. Consider re-exporting from a single source of truth or adding a small wrapper (emitNotificationChanged / onNotificationsChanged) so the constant isn't passed around as a raw string.

comments.content: Bare `catch {}` silently discards the error object. As the explicit IPC boundary to the Rust meta module, every transport failure (command unregistered, Rust panic, schema drift, timeout) becomes invisible — no console output, no telemetry. The header comment justifies returning `null` for graceful degradation, but swallowing the error means regressions in the meta module go undiagnosed. Suggest at least `console.warn("meta_list_providers failed", err)` (or capture and surface via a separate channel) before returning null, and extracting a shared helper so the three identical wrappers stay consistent.

Same `try/invoke/catch{return null}` wrapper as fetchProviders, with two compounding issues: (1) the empty catch hides the underlying cause, and (2) the `null` sentinel conflates distinct failure modes — "meta module unavailable" vs "sync timeout" vs "Rust panic" vs "payload parse error" — so the settings page cannot surface a meaningful hint even when one is available. Recommend a shared `safeInvoke<T>(cmd, args?)` helper that logs once and centralises the policy; call sites then become a one-liner.

Third copy of the same wrapper. Worth noting: the Rust `MetaSyncResult` already carries `{ok:false, error:string}` for *logical* failures, so anything that reaches this catch is a *transport-level* error (IPC unavailable, command not registered, panic) — the very class of errors the user-facing `ok:false` branch will never report. Those are precisely the failures worth logging. Centralising into the shared `safeInvoke` helper proposed above would fix all three sites in one place.

All four wrappers just `return invoke<T>(...)` raw, so callers receive un-normalized Tauri/IPC rejections with no consistent shape, no user-friendly message, and no distinction between "not found" (which is conveyed as `null` on `traceDetail` only) and "IPC failure" (thrown). For a client-facing API that drives UI, consider a thin error-normalization layer (or at least documented rejection shape) so the UI can render a stable error string and so that "no such trace" is not silently conflated with a transport failure.

`traceListByTask` is typed `Promise<TraceRow[]>` with no null guard, but `traceDetail` is typed `Promise<TraceDetail | null>` for the "not found" case. The list endpoint can likewise return `null`/undefined from a malformed Rust payload (e.g. `Option<Vec<_>>` serialized as `null` in some failure paths). Downstream UI code commonly does `.map`/`.length` on the result without a null check and would throw a `TypeError`. Either narrow to `TraceRow[] | null` for symmetry, or assert/validate the shape at the boundary.

Every sibling API is named with the `trace_` prefix (traceListByTask -> `trace_list`, traceDetail -> `trace_detail`, traceExport -> `trace_export`), but `fileRollback` operates on a `changeId` rather than a trace and breaks both the function-name and IPC-command prefix convention. This hurts discoverability and may cause callers to look for a non-existent `trace_rollback`. Rename for consistency, e.g. `traceRollbackFile(changeId)` -> `trace_rollback_file`, or document the deliberate divergence.

`origin` is the discriminator for how a trace was produced (run_task_in_chat / scheduler / workflow / batch per the header comment) but is left as an unconstrained `string`. Every other enum-like field in this file (`status`, `kind`) is properly typed as a string literal union. Mirror that here, e.g. `origin: "run_task_in_chat" | "scheduler" | "workflow" | "batch"`, so call sites get exhaustive checks and typos surface at compile time.

Multiple optional fields combine `?:` with `| null` (e.g. `taskId?: string | null`, `errorClass?: string | null`, `toolCallId?: string | null`, `beforeRef?: string | null`, `beforeSha?: string | null`, `afterSha?: string | null`). This is redundant: Rust's `Option<T>` serializes to either `null` or a missing key depending on the serializer config, so pick one convention and stick with it project-wide (`string | null` if Rust always emits the key, or `string?` if it omits it). Currently every consumer must check both, doubling the null-handling surface.

`limit = 20` is a hardcoded magic number default buried in the function signature. Page-size policy belongs in a shared constant (or module-level `DEFAULT_TRACE_PAGE_SIZE`) so other list views don't silently diverge, and so the cap semantics (20 items per page) are documented in one place rather than inferred from a default parameter.

Silent catch swallows all errors without any logging. The comment justifies the behavior for the documented "plugin unavailable" case (web/headless test missing mock), but in production an unexpected failure of `ask` (e.g. Tauri IPC bridge error, malformed plugin response) will be completely invisible. Consider at least a `console.warn` (or a project-standard logger) so unexpected failures show up in dev/maintainer telemetry, while still defaulting to the safe `false` rejection.

Failure-mode conflation: both "user clicked Cancel" and "dialog threw/errored" resolve to `false`. Callers of `confirm()` cannot distinguish a deliberate rejection from a hidden infrastructure failure. For destructive actions (delete model, clear keys, rotate token, etc.) a thrown/thrown error silently rejects it without an indicator, which may mislead users into thinking their action was canceled when the dialog never actually appeared. Consider returning a tagged result or at least surfacing the error path so the UI can react (e.g. show a toast on failure vs. silently abort on cancel).

Overly broad `catch` (no binding, no narrowing) accepts any thrown value. While safe-by-default (returns `false`), it will also mask programmer errors like passing a malformed `options` shape. Consider narrowing with `catch (err)` and filtering known/expected failure modes from truly unexpected ones, so genuine bugs aren't silently absorbed in production.

The protocol literal strings are duplicated across BACKEND_PERSISTED_SOURCES and KNOWN_SOURCES (5 of 6 strings are repeated). The header comment requires this file to stay in sync with `src-tauri/src/mutation.rs MutationOrigin`, so adding a new source variant must update BOTH sets in lock-step — a missed update silently misroutes persistence (e.g. a new "backend-persisted" variant treated as widget-style or vice versa). Consider declaring a single `as const` tuple as the protocol source-of-truth and deriving both sets from it (e.g. `const SOURCES = ["main","widget","bot","api","migration","initial-load"] as const;` then `KNOWN_SOURCES = new Set(SOURCES)` and `BACKEND_PERSISTED_SOURCES = new Set(SOURCES.filter(s => s !== "widget"))`), so each string is typed exactly once.

`source: string | undefined` accepts any string, even though the documented protocol is a closed set mirrored from the Rust enum. A typo at a call site (e.g. `"widgte"`) silently falls through to the widget-style persistence branch and won't be caught at compile time. Tighten the parameter to a union of the protocol literals (or `(typeof PROTOCOL_SOURCES)[number] | undefined`) so TypeScript surfaces typo'd source strings and the closed-set intent is explicit.

`isBackendPersisted` returns `false` for any value outside the closed protocol (typos, future variants, undefined), which quietly routes them to the main-window persistence branch. The doc comment describes the closed set as the protocol but doesn't explicitly specify the fallthrough behavior; if a new variant is added on the Rust side and forgotten here, the main window will start writing duplicate state instead of failing loudly. Consider either (a) an explicit assertion (`invariant(s === undefined || KNOWN_SOURCES.has(s))`) so drift surfaces in dev, or (b) documenting the "unknown == widget-style persistence" decision in this file's comment so the silent fallthrough is intentional and reviewable.

Stale-handler capture across re-renders: the `eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` silences the missing dep, so `handler` is captured only on the first effect run. If the caller passes a non-stable callback (e.g., one closing over component state), every subsequent event keeps invoking the original closure with stale state. The docstring asks callers to pass only stable setState-shaped callbacks but there is no runtime guard. Consider either adding `handler` to the deps (with an internal ref so the listener identity stays stable while the latest handler runs) or a dev-mode warning when the handler reference changes between renders.

  }, [event, handler]);

comments.content: `unlistenSafe` swallows every unregister error silently (`.catch(() => {})`). The comment says this is intentional ("卸载路径上失败无行动点，静默"), but it makes the very hazard the comment describes (unlisten_js_script throwing under register/unregister races) completely invisible at runtime — there is no log, no metric, no debug breadcrumb to detect leaked listeners. At minimum, log at `debug`/verbose level or expose a hook so callers can plug in telemetry.

Async-only error handling: `.catch` only fires for a rejected Promise. If `listen()` ever throws synchronously (e.g., argument validation, plugin not initialized, Tauri API missing in a non-Tauri/test environment) the error bypasses the catch and surfaces as an uncaught exception, contradicting the docstring's "catch 防 unhandled rejection" guarantee. Wrap the call or attach a `.then(..., onError)` second argument so synchronous throws are also funneled into the same handler.

No null/undefined guard on payload: `handler: (payload: T) => void` assumes `Tauri` always delivers a payload. Tauri events can fire without a payload (`undefined`) or with an unexpected shape, and this hook does no runtime narrowing — the caller's handler will dereference an undefined value with no upstream protection. Either document the contract (T must allow `undefined`) or guard at the call site: `if (e.payload !== undefined) handler(e.payload as T)`.

comments.content: Hardcoded event-name channel: this hook is intended as a generic Tauri-event wrapper, but it makes no effort to validate or namespace the `event` string. Callers passing user-controlled strings (e.g., from a URL or IPC bridge) could subscribe to arbitrary internal channels. Add a parameter shape check or namespace prefix requirement at the hook boundary so caller mistakes are caught at dev time.

No input validation in setWorkflowSettings despite documented constraints. The JSDoc states `askBudget` must be 1–5 (default 3) and `reviewModel` is a model-library entry id or '' for 'follow global'; the wrapper forwards any value (negative numbers, NaN from `Number("")`, runaway budgets) straight to the backend. UI bugs here can silently corrupt persisted settings. Add explicit validation (or at minimum a `Number.isInteger` + range check + a non-empty/empty-string allow-list for `reviewModel`) before forwarding.

`path` in exportWorkflowAudit is an arbitrary filesystem path forwarded verbatim to a Rust command that writes the audit JSON. While a file-picker dialog is the normal source, any caller sourcing it from free-form input or concatenation risks writing outside the intended directory. The wrapper performs no sanitization, canonicalization, or extension check; consider either (a) accepting a directory + filename and joining on the backend with bounds enforcement, or (b) at minimum asserting the path ends with `.json` and rejecting relative paths with `..` segments here.

`clearAllWorkflowAudit` is a destructive, unscoped operation that wipes the entire audit table across all workflows in a single IPC call; the wrapper exposes no confirmation, soft-delete, or scope filter (e.g. `workflowId`). This makes accidental data loss a one-keystroke-away bug at any call site. Either accept a required `workflowId` argument so scoping is enforced, or rename to make the global blast radius obvious (e.g. `clearAllWorkflowAudit` is fine, but require an explicit `{ confirm: true }` token).

Every export here is a thin pass-through to `invoke` and re-throws whatever the backend rejects as-is. For destructive/export operations specifically (clearAll, export) this means a single string error from Rust surfaces to UI as a raw unhandled rejection with no contract. Consider wrapping IPC rejections in a small `WorkflowAuditError` (or at least documenting the expected failure modes per command) so callers and tests have a stable shape to handle.

`payload: Record<string, unknown> | null` plus a flat `kind: string` forces every consumer to cast on read and re-narrow the shape ad hoc. With a closed set of audit kinds, prefer a discriminated union keyed on `kind` (e.g. `kind: "node_failed"; payload: { errorCode: string; ... }`) so that adding a new kind on the Rust side is a TypeScript exhaustiveness check, not a silent runtime hole.

JSDoc claims "返回 null 表示无新增" but the implementation never returns null — its return type is `{ files: TaskFile[]; truncated: boolean }` and the only `return` statement always returns an object. This stale documentation contradicts the signature and will mislead callers expecting a nullable return (and is also the source of the inconsistency with the comment "返回 null 表示无新增" — it appears to be leftover from an earlier API design). Either drop the "返回 null" clause or make the function actually return `| null`.
