comments.content: Project rules require `async/await` with proper error handling, but `openTarget` uses two `.catch()` promise chains that duplicate the error path and make control flow harder to follow. Refactor to a single `async` function with `try/catch` so all three branches (URL, path, fallback) share one error-reporting site and so future additions (e.g. timeout, retry, telemetry) can be inserted in one place.

`handleCommandError` is being called with a plain object literal `{ code, message, recoverable }` rather than an `Error` instance. If the helper checks `instanceof Error`, inspects `error.stack`, or reads `error.cause` for diagnostic chains, this synthetic object will bypass those paths silently and may lose stack trace context. Either construct a real `Error` (`new Error(msg, { cause: { code, recoverable } })`) and attach `code`/`recoverable` as custom properties, or pass an `Error`-shaped object that the helper explicitly accepts (and update its type signature accordingly). Also note the message embeds the raw `target` verbatim — confirm `handleCommandError` escapes it for any UI/toast surface to avoid reflecting potentially attacker-controlled text.

`normalizeUrl` happily returns `mailto:` and `tel:` URIs as-is, and `openTarget` then forwards them to `openUrl` from `@tauri-apps/plugin-opener`. That plugin typically only opens http(s) and OS-registered URL schemes; on many platforms `mailto:`/`tel:` either fail with a generic error or open an unrelated default handler, leaving the user with a confusing toast instead of the mail/phone app. Either narrow `normalizeUrl` to return `null` for these schemes and let the caller decide, or branch in `openTarget` to use a different opener (e.g. an OS `open` command via Rust, or a dedicated plugin). Also `BARE_DOMAIN_RE` accepts IDs/hostnames that are not valid TLDs (`foo.invalid`, `bar.local`) — adding a small allow-list or a public-suffix check would reduce false positives.

comments.content: Error-observability asymmetry: `loadTasksFromDb` only `console.error`s, while `loadWorkspaceFromDb` routes the same kind of failure through `handleCommandError(..., { silent: true })`. This breaks the file's own stated doctrine ("失败不再静默吞错") and means task-load failures have different telemetry than workspace-load failures. Either call `handleCommandError(e, "db_load", { silent: true })` here too, or drop the call in the workspace version so both paths share one policy.

`diffTaskRows` `createdAt` expression is fragile: `t.createdAt ?? (p ? undefined : now)` evaluates to `undefined` whenever an existing task (`p` truthy) arrives with `createdAt` missing. The comment leans on "后端 UPDATE 不覆盖该列" for safety, but that only holds if the Rust handler treats `None`/`undefined` as "skip column" — if the upsert serializes `createdAt: undefined` to `NULL`, every mutated-then-diffed existing row loses its original creation timestamp silently. Recommend defaulting to `p.createdAt ?? now` instead, so the prior value is always carried forward regardless of caller discipline.

`assignInsertOrder` integer-reset branch contradicts its own docstring ("只有被拖条目生成新对象"). When `hi - lo <= 1e-9`, the fallback returns `arr.map((t, i) => (t.order === i ? t : { ...t, order: i }))`, which reassigns `order` (and rebuilds the object) for every out-of-sequence item — not just the dragged one. Beyond breaking React reference equality on non-dragged rows, this silently rewrites baselines for in-flight concurrent writers holding `expectedUpdatedAt` snapshots that reference the old orders, causing their next upsert to be rejected and their updates lost. Limit the rewrite to the active row only, or recompute baselines-preserving orders (e.g., spaced integers with a known step) instead of forcing a dense index reassignment.

`loadPeople`, `exportTasksToFile`, `importTasksFromFile`, `exportWorkspaceToFile`, `importWorkspaceFromFile` are raw `await invoke` with no try/catch and no logging — unlike upsert/delete which surface via `handleCommandError`. A failed import or export produces an unhandled promise rejection with zero diagnostic trail (no `console.error`, no structured handler call), violating the file's own "不静默吞错" doctrine for the user-facing I/O paths even though the docstring pushes responsibility to callers. At minimum add a `console.error("[<cmd>] failed", e)` (or a `handleCommandError(..., { silent: true })`) before re-throwing so failures are observable in dev tools.

The same observability gap exists on the workspace import/export pair: no try/catch, no `console.error`, no `handleCommandError` — failures become silent unhandled rejections. Apply the same fix as the task-side I/O pair (logging + silent handler) so the import/export surfaces are uniform.

If the write fails (quota exceeded, storage disabled in private mode, etc.) the UI shows a theme that silently reverts on the next reload, while in-memory state and persisted state diverge with no signal to callers. The system-change handler reads getSetting() twice — once for the guard and again as the onChange argument. A concurrent localStorage write (e.g. a storage event from another window landing in the same tick, or a racing click on cycleSetting/toggleTheme) can make the second read return a value different from the guard, so onChange may be invoked with 'light'/'dark' even though the guard only accepted 'system'. toggleTheme silently drops the 'system' preference: it resolves the current setting through effectiveTheme and always writes back a concrete 'light'/'dark'. A user who explicitly chose 'system' is pinned to a concrete mode the first time they hit the shortcut, with no way to recover the follow-system preference through this API. The JSDoc states this is intentional ("落到具体模式"), but it's a UX regression worth surfacing — consider a separate dedicated shortcut for cycling through all three states, or letting this one preserve 'system'.

cycleSetting is a non-atomic read-modify-write on localStorage. Between getSetting() and applySetting(next), a storage event from another window can mutate THEME_KEY, so the cycle reads stale state and persists a value that doesn't reflect the latest cross-window intent (the cycle can skip a state, or revert). At minimum, re-read after writing and re-apply if it changed; better, hold a local cache and write through it.

comments.content: Test fidelity regression risk: silently no-op'ing both methods means production scroll behavior — restore-on-data-load, focus-jumping on modal open, auto-scroll-to-bottom in `ChatPanel`, etc. — is never exercised. Tests will pass while the real app silently fails to scroll. This is the documented purpose of the helper, but the comment understates the trade-off: any test that *intends* to verify scroll behavior needs to call `vi.spyOn(Element.prototype, "scrollTo")` *after* the patch is installed, which works only because the patch sets `writable: true`. Document that explicitly, or replace the unconditional no-op with a `vi.fn()`-returning factory so callers can assert on call counts.

Both `scrollTo` and `scrollIntoView` are patched to the *same* anonymous `() => {}` reference, so a debugger or stack trace cannot tell which method was invoked, and any future `vi.spyOn(Element.prototype, "scrollTo")` after the patch lands will replace one shared function rather than distinguishing per-method. Minor: use `Object.defineProperty(Element.prototype, name, { ..., value: function (this: Element) { /* noop */ } })` — at minimum, naming the inner `function` lets stack traces identify the call site.

crypto.randomUUID shim is not collision-safe: `Math.random().toString(36).slice(2)` provides only ~8 base36 chars of entropy and `Date.now()` is identical across any tests that run within the same millisecond. Parallel test workers or two synchronous calls in the same tick will produce duplicate IDs. Any consumer that uses the result as a React `key`, as a Map key for dedup, or for `expect(id1).not.toBe(id2)` style assertions will flake. Use `crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(16))` + standard hex formatting, or at minimum combine with a per-test monotonic counter.

Existing code:
```js
  // eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any
  (globalThis.crypto as any).randomUUID = () =>
    `uuid-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2)}-${Date.now()}`;
```

comments.content: Coverage is configured as reporters only — no `coverage.thresholds`. Coverage reports are therefore informational and CI cannot fail on regressions in data-integrity-sensitive or security-sensitive modules. Add explicit thresholds (or at least `lines`/`statements` floors) so a dropped-in `@tauri-apps/api` mock or a removed assertion in a security-related test is caught at PR time instead of silently eroding the suite.

Write path lacks the `handleCommandError` call that `loadProfile` uses. If `invoke` rejects and the caller forgets to `.catch`, you get an unhandled promise rejection with no user-visible error, while a load failure is at least routed through the central handler. Either propagate via `handleCommandError` (matching `loadProfile`) or add explicit `.catch` for parity — and consider re-throwing or returning a structured error so the UX between read and write paths doesn't diverge.

Severity: high

`profile-changed` ignores `loadGen` and unconditionally writes `cache` + notifies, while the write path's `adoptProfile` deliberately suppresses when `gen` is stale. Two consequences: (1) the backend's echo of a local write causes a second `notify()` after the write's own, so subscribers re-render twice for one logical change; (2) if a broadcast arrives while an in-flight write/force load is still pending, the broadcast's payload can win cache and then be overwritten (or vice-versa) by an older/different response, producing intermediate snapshots that violate the "last writer wins" invariant. Apply the same `gen === loadGen` guard (or a monotonic seq check) to keep the broadcast and write paths consistent.

Severity: medium

On `listen` rejection, `listening` is reset to `false` and the next `loadProfile` call will immediately retry `listen()`. If the underlying failure is persistent (event bus saturated, backend down, etc.), every UI that calls `loadProfile` will re-attempt and `console.warn` indefinitely with no backoff or escalation. Add retry throttling (e.g., exponential backoff or a "give up after N attempts" flag) so a permanent failure surfaces clearly instead of spamming the log.

Severity: medium

`getProfileCache` and the `subs`/`cache` design hand out the same mutable module-scope `ProfileView` reference to every consumer, and `ProfileView`/`ProfileEntryView` are not `Readonly`. Any subscriber that mutates the returned object (e.g., `cache.user.name = ...` or `Object.assign`) silently corrupts the cache for all subsequent readers and every `notify()` cycle until the next load overwrites it. Either return a shallow clone (`{ ...cache, user: { ...cache.user, bot: { ...cache.bot } } }`) or mark `ProfileView` as `Readonly<...>` and freeze on write so the contract is enforced.

Severity: medium

The "last writer wins" intent of `adoptProfile` only holds when there is a *later* writer/loader that wins. If a write's `gen` becomes stale (because a concurrent write or force load bumped `loadGen` again) and no subsequent operation ever resolves successfully (e.g., the next force's invoke fails, or the user goes idle), the cache is left permanently stale: the write's caller got the fresh `v` back, but subscribers never see it and `profile-changed` may not arrive. Consider: (a) on a stale `gen`, still update the cache if the value is observably newer than what's there (compare some monotonic seq/id from the backend), or (b) ensure every successful write also kicks a tiny recovery load so the invariant is restored. At minimum, document this gap — right now it contradicts the "并发两次写时后写者赢" guarantee.

Severity: medium

Inline style on the root container violates the 'no inline styles' rule. The values are static constants, not dynamic, so they should live in a CSS class (e.g. in the imported `main.css` or a dedicated demo stylesheet).

Silent `.catch(() => {})` discards profile-load errors. The comment claims `profile.ts` records them via `handleCommandError`, but if that contract changes the UI will permanently fall back to the bot logo / initial with zero observability. Either propagate the error to the cache/subscription so subscribers can react, or at minimum re-throw so a global handler can log it.

Race between `loadProfile()` and `subscribeProfile`: the subscriber is registered after `loadProfile` is kicked off, but it reads from `getProfileCache()`. If a profile event fires before `loadProfile` resolves, the subscriber will `setP(getProfileCache())` with the stale cache, and the later `.then(v => setP(v))` will overwrite it — but if events fire repeatedly in that window, intermediate states can flicker. Make the subscriber the single source of truth (call `setP(getProfileCache())` in both branches) or guard the initial `loadProfile` result against subscriber overwrites.

Message body is rendered as a single text node, so embedded `\n` characters collapse to whitespace and multi-line user messages appear as one run-on line. If user bubbles are expected to support line breaks, render through a whitespace-preserving element (e.g., `
{text}
`) instead of a bare text node. Note: React still auto-escapes this output, so XSS is not a concern.

openTarget() is invoked unguarded in both the onClick and onKeyDown handlers. openTarget likely touches the OS shell / filesystem / browser launcher and can throw (ENOENT, EACCES, blocked popup, protocol handler missing, etc.). An unhandled rejection will be swallowed by React with no user feedback — the link looks clickable but does nothing. Wrap each call in try/catch and surface a user-visible error (toast / inline message).

For non-URL tokens this element is rendered as role="link" with no href, and only the Enter key is wired up. Two accessibility problems compound here: (1) ARIA explicitly discourages role="link" without href — screen readers and gestures treat it inconsistently; (2) for role="link" the spec'd key is Enter, but if you intentionally want a button-like activator you must also handle Space (and repeat on keydown for held keys). Either restore a non-navigating href (e.g. a javascript: void(0) is still bad; consider a real <button> styled like a link) or add Space handling and a proper aria-label.

e.preventDefault() runs unconditionally in onClick, which silently strips the browser's native Ctrl/Meta-click and middle-click "open in new tab/window" behavior — even for real https URLs where the user clearly expects a hyperlink. Detect modifier keys / button !== 0 and either skip preventDefault (so the native new-tab flow runs) or branch openTarget to honor the modifier (e.g. open in a background tab). At minimum, don't intercept middle-click.

The matchAll loop assumes every match strictly advances the cursor. If LINK_OR_PATH_RE (owned by another module and free to evolve) ever produces a zero-width match — e.g. an empty alternative, a lookahead without a consuming group, or a quantifier that can match zero chars at a boundary — then `idx === last` and `last = idx + token.length` never advances, hanging the renderer on that text input. comments.content: **`tasks-updated` handler lacks atomicity between DB writes and `tasksRef.current` update.** The handler awaits `upsertTasks(upserts)` (or backend-persisted path), then merges and computes `next`, then awaits `upsertTasks(ruleChanged)`, and only *after* that assigns `tasksRef.current = next` and calls `setTasks(next)`. If any mid-handler `await` throws (e.g. `upsertTasks(ruleChanged)`), the chain's outer `.catch((err) => console.error(...))` swallows the rejection and resolves the chain. The next mutate then runs against a stale `tasksRef.current`, while SQLite already holds rows the handler committed. This produces write-conflict symptoms and "lost" rule fixes. Wrap the DB-write + memory-commit region in try/catch, and on failure refetch from DB to align memory with ground truth before re-emitting `tasks-changed`.

**`deleteTaskRows` failure is swallowed, causing UI/DB divergence.** Both the `mutate` path and the `tasks-updated` `handle` path catch `deleteTaskRows` errors with `console.error` only, then proceed with `tasksRef.current = next; setTasks(next); emit("tasks-changed")`. The deleted rows disappear from local UI and other widgets honor the broadcast, but SQLite still retains them. On next reload the rows resurrect as if never deleted. The "下次 db_load 自愈回来" comment is misleading: this isn't healing, it's silent resurrection. Either retry deletes, refetch on failure (mirror the suggestion above), or surface a user-visible error so the user can retry.

**`applyRemoteRows` does not emit `tasks-changed`, breaking multi-window/multi-widget consistency.** `setTaskColumn` and `patchTask` invoke a backend command then merge the returned row into local state via `applyRemoteRows`. No `tasks-changed` broadcast is emitted. The design relies on the *backend* to emit, but for self-originated or reply-only backend writes other widgets may not refresh until the next unrelated event. Broadcast locally so peer instances align without depending on backend echo.

**`addTask` sets `editingId` before the new task exists in `tasks`.** `setEditingId(id)` runs synchronously, but the new task only enters `tasks` after the async `mutate` chain reaches `setTasks(next)`. Between these two updates, the board renders with `editingId` pointing to a task that doesn't yet exist in the visible list — depending on `TaskTimelinePage`'s lookup, this can flash an empty edit pane or a "no task to edit" state before the next render reconciles. Apply the optimistic insert synchronously (via a local array or a custom `mutateSync`) before setting `editingId`, so both updates land in the same render.

**`hardDeleteTask` is fire-and-forget with no user-visible failure feedback.** It goes through `mutateFire`, whose `.catch` only `console.error`s. Inside `mutate`, `deleteTaskRows` failures are swallowed (see issue 2), so the row is removed from the UI and `tasks-changed` is broadcast, but if SQLite delete never landed the row reappears on next reload — with no toast/dialog the user can't tell. `setTaskColumn` already routes failures through `handleCommandError` with retry; `hardDeleteTask` should do the same.

`onDeleteConfirm` clears `deleteTarget` synchronously *before* awaiting `runCmd`, and `DeleteConfirmDialog` is unmounted as soon as the state is null. Two problems: (1) on backend failure the dialog is already gone, the user loses the proposal/cascade context and has to hunt for the row to retry; (2) a double-click on the confirm button (or a fast re-mount) can fire two `evolution_delete_proposal` calls against the same id — `runCmd` does not lock per-id, only globally via `busy` (which is set by the same `runCmd` so it self-guards the second call, but only because the first invocation set it synchronously; if React batches oddly the second invocation can still slip through before `busy` becomes true). `refresh()` wraps three sequential invokes in a single `try/catch`. This is an unusual pattern that hurts readability and prevents extracting the chip into a small named helper (e.g. `renderChip(current, now)`) or a tiny render function. Consider hoisting it to a function above the component or inlining the conditional rendering directly.

Rotation index `idx` is never reset when `due` content/ordering changes (e.g. the parent passes a new `now`, a task just crossed into the due-soon window, or one dropped out). Because `useEffect` only depends on `due.length` and `paused`, the ticker keeps walking from the previous index, so the most-urgent task may not surface until a full cycle elapses, and a task no longer in `dueSoonTasks` could be displayed if `safeIdx` happens to land on it during the gap. Race condition / no request de-duplication: clicking retry (or any re-mount of `load`) starts a new fetch without aborting the previous one. If two fetches are in flight, a slow failing response can resolve after a fast successful one, calling `setData(null); setError(...)` and clobbering a freshly loaded image with the error UI. Track an in-flight token (e.g., request id) inside `load` and ignore responses whose token no longer matches before applying `setData`/`setError`.

No cleanup / abort handling on unmount: the effect dispatches `load()` but never signals cancellation. If the component unmounts while `fetchBingDaily` is pending, the resolved/rejected handler still calls `setData`/`setError`, triggering React's "set state on unmounted component" warning and a memory leak. Add an `AbortController` (preferred — pass to `fetchBingDaily` if supported) or a `mountedRef` flag, and bail out in `.then/.catch` when aborted/unmounted; also return a cleanup from the effect that aborts.

Project standard requires async/await over Promise chains. Both `load` and `open` use `.then/.catch`; converting to `async/await` with `try/catch` produces linear, easier-to-read control flow and makes the new abort/mounted guards above easier to express.

In any non-UTC zone the baseline shifts by one day, so a task completed on the active local day can silently fail to match (while the `planStart.slice(0,10) === dayKey` branch just above uses a correct locale-independent string compare). Make both branches consistent — e.g. compare `new Date(t.completedAt).toISOString().slice(0,10) === dayKey` (or normalize both to a local-day key), instead of mixing UTC-parsed `toDateString()` with a YYYY-MM-DD string.

Self-loops crash `layoutGraph`: the guard `!g.hasEdge(l.source, l.target)` does not filter the `l.source === l.target` case, and graphology's `addEdge` throws on self-loops in an undirected graph — any dependency edge pointing at itself in `buildTaskGraph` will blow up the whole card. The effect fires once after mount regardless of whether `filters` actually changed by the user; when the initial state came from `loadGraphFilters()` the effect immediately writes the same payload back to storage. The countdown `useEffect` calls `respond(false)` without listing it as a dep (eslint-disable). The invariant that makes this safe - `respond` only reads refs and uses no render-local state - should be made explicit in the comment so a future maintainer doesn't "fix" it by adding the dep and inadvertently close over stale state. Also worth noting that `respond` is recreated every render so the `void respond(false)` on the `remaining<=0` branch actually calls the version from the same render where remaining hit 0 (safe because of refs, but a reader may not realise).

Subtle concurrency hazard around `pendingRef` after a response completes: `respond()`'s `finally` only clears the React `pending` state (`setPending((p) => (p === cur ? null : p))`). The `pendingRef` itself is only re-synced to state on the next render. If a new `bot-confirm` event lands in the microtask window between this `finally` and the subsequent render commit, the `useTauriListen` callback will read a stale `pendingRef.current`, see `stale.id !== p.id && !busyRef.current` as true, and `auto-reject` a payload that has already been responded to. The inline callback passed to `useTauriListen` is recreated on every render. Even though the captures (`setPending`, `setRemaining`, `pendingRef`, `busyRef`, `invoke`) are identity-stable, the function itself is not. If `useTauriListen` subscribes via `useEffect(() => { listen(cb); return () => unlisten(cb); }, [cb])` - which is the conventional implementation - this will unsubscribe and resubscribe on every parent render, causing a `Tauri` channel churn. Worth either (a) wrapping the callback in `useCallback` (with `[pendingRef, busyRef]` deps - both stable, so it would memoise), or (b) verifying `useTauriListen`'s implementation handles subscription stability internally.

comments.content: Pending setTimeout is never cleared: if the component unmounts within 5s/3s of these calls, setNotice("") will fire on an unmounted component (React warning + retained closure). Track the id in a useRef, clear it before scheduling a new one, and clear on unmount in a cleanup effect (same pattern is needed in importRules on the line below).

Disabling exhaustive-deps here masks a stale-closure footgun: `refresh` is recreated on every render and captures the current `rules`/`running` snapshot via the setter closures. Any future change that makes refresh depend on state (e.g., reads `rules` directly) will silently desync, because the effect only ever runs once on mount. Either wrap refresh in `useCallback` with `[]` deps (only setters are used, which are stable) or move the body into the effect.

Race window between `await confirm(...)` and `setRunning(true)`: a second rapid click enters runNow, awaits its own confirm, and both then pass the `if (running) return` check — emitting two concurrent `migration_run` invocations on a destructive operation (file delete/move). Worse, the backend's auto-poll mentioned in the UI ("后台每 X 分钟自动检测一次") is not coordinated with this local `running` flag, so manual and auto runs can overlap. Disable the button synchronously at the top of the handler (before any await) and add a ref-based lock; ideally also have the backend enforce a single-flight lock.

The log modal has no Escape-key handler, no backdrop click-to-close, no focus trap, and no `role="dialog"` / `aria-modal`. Keyboard-only users cannot dismiss it. Add a useEffect that registers a `keydown` listener (Escape closes) while `logOpen` is true, allow clicking the outer `bg-black/40` div (`e.target === e.currentTarget`) to close, and add `role="dialog"` `aria-modal="true"` for screen readers.

comments.content: `refresh()` swallows all errors silently. If `migration_rules_load` or `migration_status` fails on mount (e.g., Tauri IPC error, backend unavailable), the user sees an empty rules list with no diagnostic and may wrongly conclude there are no rules. The other handlers in this file surface failures via `setError(formatCommandError(e))` — do the same here, or at minimum keep a boolean indicating the load failed.

Linked-hover handlers (`hoverDay`, `hoverTask`) and every `onMore={() => onNavigate(...)}` are recreated on each render. HomePage's `nowState` ticks every 30s and other state (traces/notifications/archiveDays) also updates, so the four linked-hover children (`WeeklyChart`, `DayGridMini`, `PoolPager`, `GraphMini`) and the three bottom-row panels (`BotPanel`, `RecentArchivedPanel`, `ArchivePulsePanel`) re-render each tick even though they don't observe `now` at second resolution. `HomePanels` doesn't use `React.memo` (confirmed via search), so the new function references are not skipped. Wrap the hover callbacks in `useCallback` (with `[dayKeys]` deps for `hoverTask`) and pre-bind `onMore` to stable handlers (or accept `onNavigate` as a stable prop and memoize per-target helpers) to stop the cascade.

The header comment for HomePage claims both traces and notifications use "30s 轻轮询 + 变更广播", but only `traces` has the polling fallback; `notifications` is reloaded only once on mount plus the `NOTIFICATIONS_CHANGED_EVENT` broadcast. If the Tauri event stream ever drops (app backgrounded/resumed, listener detach window) or a notification is created/resolved in the moment between the mount effect and `useTauriListen` attaching (effects 1 and 2 race on mount), the pending list silently goes stale — even worse, `notifError` only gets cleared on the success path of `loadNotifications`, so a missed refresh leaves no UI signal. Mirror the trace pattern: add `setInterval(loadNotifications, REFRESH_MS)` with matching cleanup so the UI converges regardless of event delivery.

`trace_list` is invoked with a bare `limit: 200` magic number. There is no constant, no comment explaining the choice, and no UI-side guard if executions genuinely exceed 200 between polls — the polling cycle will silently drop older rows while `traceError` stays empty (because each fetch itself succeeds). Promote to a named `TRACE_LIST_LIMIT` (or read from settings) and ideally surface a banner or mark the panel stale when `rows.length === limit` so the truncation is visible.

`runNow` never calls `reload()` after success, so the row's `lastStatus` / `schedLast` / upcoming-time summary stay stale until the next `sched-status` or `tasks-changed` event arrives. If those events are delayed or missed, "立即执行" leaves the list showing the previous run's data (and the "下次" countdown doesn't update). Every async step in `jumpToSession` is silenced with `.catch(() => {})`, so IPC regressions (failed `emit`, rejected `w.show()`, failed `setFocus`, missing `WebviewWindow.getByLabel`) are invisible. `formatDuration` doesn't guard against `NaN`, `Infinity`, or negative values from backend. Corrupt `durationMs` would render as "NaNms", "Infinitys", or "-100ms" in the failure-triage history list — undermining the very surface designed for diagnosing scheduling problems. The `payload.sessionId!` non-null assertion is needed because TypeScript doesn't narrow object-property optionality across statements. Same anti-pattern recurs at `r.cardId!` (history row), `a.nextRunAt!`/`b.nextRunAt!` (upcoming sort) and `e.nextRunAt!` (render). Either mask env the same way, or apply selective masking by key (`*TOKEN*`, `*SECRET*`, `*KEY*`) and document why env is treated differently.

`startEdit` does not set `busy=true` (nor `form` non-null) until `bot_get_config` resolves, so during the in-flight window the remove/toggle/添加服务器 buttons remain enabled. The `editLoadingRef` guard only blocks re-entering edit; a click on another row fires a parallel `mcp_server_delete` / `mcp_server_toggle`, racing the eventual `setForm(...)` and corrupting list state (e.g. edit form opens after a sibling row was already deleted). Set `busy=true` at entry and clear it in `finally`, so the existing `disabled={busy}` guards on Remove/Toggle/Add cover the window too.

`maskHeaderValue` is too aggressive for short values: any value ≤8 chars collapses to plain `"••••"` so the user cannot visually verify what is about to be persisted/sent (e.g. `Bearer x`, short API keys, `Key ab`). The confirm step is the only safety net, yet it shows nothing to confirm. Consider length-aware masking (always show at least the first 1–2 and last 1–2 chars, falling back to `"••••"` only for values where the math is impossible) so the user can sanity-check the secret without seeing it in full.

The avatar rendering uses a nested ternary (`src ? A : kind === "bot" ? B : C`) which violates the project rule against nested ternaries. Refactor to an `if`/`else if`/`else` chain or extract a small `renderAvatar()` helper for readability and easier diffing.

`pick`, `remove`, and `saveName` all repeat the same skeleton: `if (busy) return; setBusy(true); setError(""); try { … } catch (e) { handleCommandError(e, label, { silent: true }); setError(formatCommandError(e)); } finally { setBusy(false); }`. Extract a single `runProfileAction(label, fn)` helper so the busy/error wrapping is defined once and the three call sites stay focused on their specific Tauri calls.

All three async handlers resolve state in their `finally`/post-`await` blocks with no unmount guard. If `ProfileRow` unmounts while an `await open()/setProfileAvatar/removeProfileAvatar/setProfileName` is in flight, the subsequent `setBusy`, `setError`, `setSaved`, and `setDirty` calls still fire on an unmounted component, and the `savedTimer` scheduled just before unmount can clobber state if React reuses the slot. Track a `mountedRef` (or accept an `AbortSignal` from a per-mount controller) and bail out of any `setState` after unmount.

`src` comes straight from `entry.avatarDataUrl` (a path chosen via the Tauri `open()` dialog) and is passed verbatim into ``. React will escape the attribute, but the *value* itself must be guaranteed safe — confirm `setProfileAvatar` strictly enforces a `data:image/*;base64,…` URL (rejecting foreign schemes, oversized payloads, or arbitrary paths) before storing. Otherwise a malformed entry from any other caller could be rendered here or reused by downstream copy/export paths.

comments.content: openDir is missing the `busy` guard that importSkill and removeSkill both apply, so a user can fire skills_open_dir concurrently with an in-flight import or delete (and double-click the open-dir button itself). Even though opening a directory is idempotent at the OS level, the inconsistency lets multiple invoke calls land at the Rust side while another mutation is still settling. Gate with `if (busy) return;` (and optionally setBusy/finally) to match the sibling handlers.

refresh() never clears the prior `error` (or `notice`) before fetching skills_list. If a previous action stashed an error and a later code path re-enters refresh (e.g., a future auto-refresh, retry button, or event listener that doesn't go through importSkill/removeSkill), the stale message persists and can misrepresent the current state. Reset both at the top of refresh so the UI status always reflects this fetch's outcome.

refresh() (and the handlers that await it) have no isMounted / AbortController guard. If the panel unmounts while skills_list, skills_import, or skills_delete is in flight, the resolved promise will still call setSkills/setError/setNotice on a torn-down instance and could clobber a freshly mounted instance's state. Track a `mounted` ref (set true in a mount effect, false in its cleanup) and early-return from the setters when it flips, or pass an AbortController down to invoke so the in-flight request is cancelled.

removeSkill silently calls refresh() on success with no user feedback, while the sibling importSkill emits a localized `技能「${name}」已安装` toast plus auto-dismiss timer. The user has no confirmation that the delete applied beyond the row disappearing. Extract the notice+timer into a small helper (e.g., `flashNotice(text)`) and invoke it from both import and delete paths so feedback is consistent and the timer/setNotice wiring isn't duplicated.

Cross-contaminated `error` state and missing overview race token. `loadOverview` calls `setError(null)` on every retry, so a previously surfaced `loadModelDays` failure is wiped out by an unrelated overview refresh; conversely a transient `loadModelDays` failure paints its error on top of an otherwise healthy overview. `loadOverview` also has no sequence token (only `modelDaysSeqRef` exists), so rapidly clicking 刷新 (which fires both via `refresh`) lets a stale overview response overwrite a newer one with potentially different totals. Either (a) split the error into `overviewError`/`modelDaysError`, or (b) drop the leading `setError(null)` in `loadOverview` and use a sequence token mirroring `modelDaysSeqRef` for both fetchers.

`isEmpty` falsifies when an error is set, but the template below unconditionally renders the 5-cell metric grid in the `!isEmpty` branch — so on `loadOverview` failure with no data yet, the user sees the red error line followed by a grid of zeros that look like real aggregated values (累计 0 / 峰值 0 / 当前连续天数 0 …). Treat error as a separate terminal state and skip the grid (or show an explicit empty-data hint) whenever an error is shown.

comments.content: Day-string parsing has no defensive validation. `parseInt(d.day.slice(5, 7), 10)` and the `[, m, dd] = d.day.split("-")` in `TokenTrendChart` both assume the Rust side always returns strict `YYYY-MM-DD`. A single malformed row (e.g. an empty string, a partial timestamp, or a bad ingest record) yields `NaN`, producing labels like "NaN月" or "NaN月NaN日" and a month-label `col - lastCol` comparison against `NaN` which silently suppresses nearby month labels. Add `YYYY-MM-DD` validation and skip / substitute a placeholder for bad rows instead of silently emitting "NaN月".

`heatColor` returns `color-mix(in srgb, var(--brand) X%, var(--surface))` with no fallback. Tauri's WebView can ship older Chromium / WebKit revisions on some platforms (and some users remain on older OS versions), where `color-mix` is unsupported — in that case `backgroundColor` falls back to the CSS default `transparent`, so every active heat cell becomes invisible (overlay only the empty `--inset-bg` 0-cell is visible). Either set a deterministic baseline (`background-color: var(--brand); background-image: linear-gradient(...)`) or compute the mix at the JS layer so the resolved color is always a concrete value.

Heatmap cells are decorative `<div>`s and convey per-day data only via the native `title` tooltip — no `role`, no `aria-label`, no `tabIndex`, no focus ring. Keyboard users cannot reach any cell, and screen readers announce nothing. Add `role="grid"` (or `role="list"` on the wrapper + `role="gridcell"` on each cell), an `aria-label` mirroring the title (e.g. `${d.day} ${fmtTokens(total)} tokens`), and `tabIndex={0}` plus a focus style so the per-day tooltip is reachable without a mouse.

Vertical viewport edge is not clamped. Only horizontal clamping is applied; `top: tip.y - 6` places the chip 6px above the element's top edge with no upper bound. When the host is near the top of the viewport (e.g., the first row in a scrollable grid well, which the comment says is `overflow-hidden`), the chip is clipped or rendered off-screen. Clamp the top as well, and consider flipping the chip below the element when there isn't enough room above.

```tsx
top: Math.max(8, tip.y - 6), // and decide below vs. above based on available space
```

Clamp math assumes a fixed 280px chip width. Long unbroken text, bold/large fonts, or theme differences can push the actual rendered width well beyond 280px, causing the chip to overflow the right edge despite the clamp, or to be visibly misaligned with the trigger. Measure the chip after render (`useLayoutEffect` + `ref`) and use the measured `offsetWidth` in the clamp instead of the hardcoded constant, or rely on CSS `max-width` with a flexible clamp.

comments.content: `skipTip` is a ref that is only ever reset in `onPointerLeave`. When the user starts a drag (`onPointerDown` flips it to `true`) pointer capture often prevents `pointerleave` from firing until release, and if the block unmounts mid-drag (e.g. task removed, layout re-flows) no `pointerleave` ever fires for the next instance to inherit — actually each instance has its own ref, but for the *current* instance the flag stays `true` for the rest of its lifetime and the tooltip silently breaks. Either reset on `onPointerUp` / `onPointerCancel`, or use `useState` so a re-render after `onPointerDown` is forced and the flag can't outlive the gesture. Same flag also depends on hover firing first — if `pointerenter` was skipped (programmatic focus, keyboard nav), `skipTip.current = true` is set unconditionally, so the very first real hover never shows the chip.

`tip.show(task.title)(e)` calls `tip.show`, ignores the returned function's return value, and only invokes it synchronously with the pointer event. This couples this component to `HoverTitle`'s curried contract: if the hook ever returns a cleanup disposer or expects the caller to await a promise, this call site silently drops it. Prefer the simpler `tip.show(task.title, e)` shape (or whatever the hook documents) and verify that the chip's lifecycle is owned by the hook rather than by this component rendering `{tip.chip}` unconditionally inside every block — the latter means every visible block ships the chip node in the DOM at all times.

This is a list-row component rendered once per plan segment per day, yet it is not wrapped in `React.memo` and the three pointer handlers are reallocated on every render. With a busy week (dozens of segments) and frequent parent re-renders (drag layout updates, scroll sync, hover state), every block re-runs the geometry math and churns closures. Wrap the export in `React.memo` (or memoize via `displayName`) and `useCallback` the handlers with `[tip, onPointerDown]` deps so unchanged segments skip rendering entirely.

comments.content: Race between fire-and-forget `startEdit` and `remove`: startEdit is invoked as `void startEdit(t.name)` so the click handler runs to its first `await` without an `if (busy) return;` guard. If the user clicks "编辑" and then confirms "删除" on the same template before the params_get invoke resolves, `remove` runs `if (editing?.name === name) setEditing(null);` against a still-null `editing` (closure snapshot), then completes. When startEdit's invoke finally resolves, it calls `setEditing({name, params})` and resurrects the editing pane for a template that no longer exists, leaving the user staring at stale edits of a deleted file. Fix: add `if (busy) return;` at the top of startEdit/saveEdit/reextract/remove (matching importTemplate and setDefault), or store an ignore-token in a ref so late callbacks skip setState.

Stale-closure / `...null` bug in reextract: `setEditing({ ...editing, params })` re-spreads the closure-captured `editing` after the `await invoke`. If the user clicks "取消" or deletes the currently-edited template while reextract is in flight, `editing` becomes `null`; when the invoke resolves, `{ ...null, params }` evaluates to `{ params }` with no `name` field. The UI then renders the editor for an unnamed (and possibly deleted) template, and the next save would call `word_template_params_update` with `oldName: undefined`. Fix: read fresh state from a ref, or guard the post-await setState with a "still editing this name" check, e.g. `setEditing(prev => prev && prev.name === name ? {...prev, params} : prev)`.

Inconsistent `if (busy) return;` guard across handlers: `importTemplate` and `setDefault` early-return on `busy`, but `startEdit`, `saveEdit`, `reextract`, and `remove` do not. Because the buttons rely solely on `disabled={busy}` for gating and state updates are async, two rapid clicks (or programmatic invocation) can slip past the disabled prop and run concurrently, causing interleaved setBusy/setError/refresh sequences and the race conditions noted above. Add the early-return at the top of every command handler for consistency.

`saveEdit` only rejects `editName.trim() === ""` client-side. A user can rename a template to a name that already exists in `items`, contains path separators (`/`, `\`), trailing dots, or otherwise collides with the built-in default — the request is then forwarded to the backend, where it surfaces as an opaque `word_template_params_update` error. Pre-validate against `items` for uniqueness (excluding the currently-edited entry), strip path separators, and reject the empty/unchanged cases so the user gets immediate, actionable feedback before the round-trip.

Exported `loadPoolOpen` / `savePoolOpen` access `localStorage` with no error handling. comments.content: `sortPoolTasks(tasks)` runs on every render (drag hover, tooltip state change, parent re-render, etc.) even though `tasks` is reference-stable from the parent. For a typical pool this is negligible; for large lists / frequent parent re-renders (drag tick, hover-tip state machine) it becomes O(n log n) per render. Wrap in `useMemo(..., [tasks])` (and rely on `tasks` reference equality; if the parent mutates in-place, ask it to shallow-copy before passing). Avoids over-rendering while the panel animates.

comments.content: `useHoverTitleTip()` portals the tooltip to `document.body`, so the `tip.chip` rendered at the bottom of the `<aside>` lives outside the aside entirely. If the user hides the pool mid-hover (e.g., via `onToggle` or `evaded` triggering from a drag) without an intervening `pointerleave`/`pointerdown` on the row, the chip's internal `tip` state stays set and a floating tooltip is left on screen over an invisible origin point — and the scheduled 350ms `setTimeout` can still fire `setTip(...)` after unmount, racing React. The hook doesn't subscribe to the panel's open state; either pass `open`/`evaded` into `useHoverTitleTip` and call `hide()` from a side-effect when it flips false, or wrap `setTip` in a `mounted` ref cleanup so late timers don't write state.

Global Escape listener discards in-progress draft edits in note/tags/subtask inputs. Pressing Escape while editing any of these fields fires the window keydown handler, calling onClose() and unmounting the panel before the local onBlur commit runs. Users lose unsaved changes (e.g., a half-typed note) on a single Escape keypress. Also note that this handler does not guard against IME composition in any meaningful way (e.nativeEvent.isComposing would be safer than e.isComposing for cross-browser IME handling). Consider only closing on Escape when the active element is not a text-editing element (e.g., check document.activeElement is the panel root / not an INPUT/TEXTAREA / not e.target.matches('input,textarea')).

Title draft useEffect overwrites in-progress edits whenever task.title changes for any reason. Because `task.title` is in the dependency array, any external `onUpdate({ title: ... })` round-trip, sibling re-render that recomputes task props, or websocket/state-sync event that re-emits the task will reset the textarea to the new task.title even while the user is mid-keystroke. This is a data-loss / edit-clobber bug. Reset only when the task identity actually changes, or skip while the field is focused: `useEffect(() => { if (document.activeElement !== titleRef.current) setTitleDraft(task.title); }, [task.id, task.title]);` (and still reset on task.id change).

toLocalDT emits a local wall-clock datetime with no offset or 'Z' marker (e.g. '2026-10-12T09:00'). Rust parsers commonly interpret such strings as UTC, so any planStart/planEnd stored this way will be re-rendered as the local time minus the user's UTC offset (e.g. 09:00 written in UTC+8 becomes 01:00 in UTC). This silently shifts scheduled tasks across days and corrupts timeline rendering. Either explicitly append the offset (`...T${fmtMin(min)}${offsetStr}`) or send epoch millis / a tagged enum that conveys "local time" semantics to the backend. The `parsePlanDT` round-trip can't paper over this if the backend stores the literal string.
comments.existing_code:
const toLocalDT = (day: Date, min: number) =>
  `${day.getFullYear()}-${pad2(day.getMonth() + 1)}-${pad2(day.getDate())}T${fmtMin(min)}`;

comments.content: The success and error branches of copyOneFile duplicate the same setState + clearTimeout + new timer pattern verbatim, including the hard-coded 1600 ms and the `_drop` destructure. If one branch is later modified (e.g. to also reset after the timer fires on an unmounted component), the other won't, and the 1600 ms will drift into two different constants. Extract a helper, e.g. `const flashCopy = (p: string, ok: boolean) => { setCopyState(m => ({ ...m, [p]: ok ? "ok" : "err" })); clearTimeout(copyTimers.current[p]); copyTimers.current[p] = setTimeout(() => setCopyState(m => { const { [p]: _, ...rest } = m; return rest; }), COPY_FEEDBACK_MS); };` and call it from both branches.

copyTimers are only cleared on unmount. If the parent keeps TaskDetailPanel mounted and just swaps the `task` prop, an in-flight 1600 ms timer from the previous task will still fire against the new task's `copyState`. If the new task happens to have a file at the same path (e.g. user copies a file, switches to another task that also has the same path bound, timer fires), the user sees a phantom '✓ 已复制' / '复制失败' badge even though no copy happened for this task. Clear pending timers whenever `task.id` changes (or whenever `copyState` itself is reset on task change).

Tags onBlur fires an unnecessary `onUpdate` whenever the user types an equivalent tag list with different separator/whitespace, because the comparison is on the raw input string rather than the parsed tag array. e.g. stored `['设计','改造']` joined to `'设计，改造'` differs from user input `'设计, 改造'` even though both produce the same parsed tags. This triggers a backend roundtrip + emits a 'task updated' event for a no-op change, which can race with concurrent edits. Compare parsed arrays instead: `if (JSON.stringify(tags) !== JSON.stringify(task.tags ?? [])) onUpdate({ tags });`.

Two places use nested ternaries, which violates the project's "Nested ternary expressions are not allowed" rule. (1) The completedAt status line chains `cond ? A : cond2 ? B : C`. (2) `dueVal` chains `cond1 ? v1 : cond2 ? v2 : ""`. Extract a small helper or use an if/else (or `??` chains) so the conditions are linear and easier to audit; the `dueVal` one is especially error-prone because `parsePlanDT(task.due)` is called twice and the string-shape branch silently drops any time component the backend may have included.

comments.content: The file header comment is garbled/typo'd: "漂移面极小（ 决策留档" appears truncated mid-phrase and contains a stray space inside the parenthesis. The "(similar)" token is also unexplained — it reads as a typo for something like "(similar to GNU diff)" or a reference to the `similar` library, but without context it confuses readers. Clean this comment up so the design rationale (no third-party diff lib, backend emits unified text, frontend only colors lines) is clear and free of placeholder text.

`diff.split("
")` on a string that ends with a newline yields a trailing empty element (e.g. `"a
b
"` → `["a", "b", ""]`). That last entry falls through to the `return ""` branch but still renders an empty `<div>`, producing a blank row at the bottom of the diff block. Strip the trailing empty line (or filter on `l.length === 0 && i === lines.length - 1`) so trailing newlines from the backend don't add phantom rows.

Tailwind arbitrary-value classes of the form `bg-[var(--ok,#22c55e)]/10` mix a CSS comma (the `var()` fallback) with Tailwind's opacity slash modifier. The comma inside `[...]` is a known tripping point for Tailwind's type inference — in many setups the `/10` opacity is silently dropped or the class fails to compile, leaving the +/- rows without a tinted background. Either move the fallback out of the arbitrary value (e.g. set `--ok` unconditionally on `:root`) or use the explicit modifier form `bg-[color:var(--ok)]/10` together with a separate CSS rule that provides the fallback.

`lineClass` is invoked for every line on every render of `DiffView`. Although `truncated` keeps the input bounded, this is still pure-string prefix matching re-run on each parent re-render. Cheap to fix and removes a per-line allocation hot spot: pre-compute the class array once alongside `lines` so the render path is just a map over a precomputed array (no per-line function call).

**Race condition on stale `cur` snapshot**: `const cur = taskFiles(task)` is captured before the awaited `open(...)` dialog and `invoke('bind_files', ...)` calls. If `task.files` is updated concurrently (e.g., another card action, an external event, or the user re-clicking "bind file" rapidly) while the picker is open, the subsequent `mergeFiles(cur, added)` operates on a stale base list and the final `onUpdate(task.id, filesPatch(files))` will overwrite the external change — a data-integrity bug that can silently drop file bindings.

**Same race condition as `pickFile`**: `cur = taskFiles(task)` and `cur.some((f) => f.isDir)` are evaluated synchronously before the awaited `open({ directory: true })` call. Between the synchronous guard and the await, another binding action can change `task.files`. The guard may then either let through a duplicate folder binding or let the user's folder replace an external update via `mergeFiles(cur, [...])`.

**Draft state never resyncs with `task` prop changes**: `noteDraft`, `tagDraft`, and `subtaskDraft` are initialized once via `useState("")` and only seeded when the user opens the corresponding editor (e.g., `setNoteDraft(task.note ?? "")`). If `task` is mutated externally (Tauri event, bot result, sync) while an inline editor is mounted, the in-memory draft no longer matches `task`, and `commitNote`/`addTag`/`commitSubtask` will resurrect the stale value, clobbering the external update. Consider syncing drafts in an effect, or seeding on every render with `useMemo`/ref guard.

**`runWithBot` silently swallows emit/window failures**: The user explicitly clicked "交给机器人" — a primary action. `emit('execute-task', ...)` errors are discarded with `.catch(() => {})` and the widget `show()`/`setFocus()` chain also drops errors. If the widget webview isn't registered yet or `emit` fails, the click appears to do nothing and the bot never runs, with zero user feedback. At minimum surface a toast on emit failure; ideally await emit before the widget show.

**Silent error handler lacks justification**: `copyOneFile` below has an explicit comment explaining why failures are swallowed (non-critical UX). `openOneFile` uses `silent: true` with no comment, but unlike copy it's a clickable chip explicitly advertised as "点击打开" — silent failure on a missing/revoked/path-out-of-scope file leaves the user with no feedback and no way to diagnose. Either drop `silent: true` (so errors surface via the existing toast pipeline) or add a comment matching the `copyOneFile` rationale and confirm it's truly safe.

**Inconsistent error/feedback UX via `window.alert`**: Both `pickFile` and `pickFolder` use the blocking native `window.alert` for the "超出部分已忽略" / "已绑定文件夹" messages, while the rest of the app surfaces errors via `handleCommandError` and the toast system. Native `alert` blocks the renderer thread, can't be themed, and is jarring against the neumorphic UI. Route these through the same toast/notification path the rest of the app uses.

**Same `window.alert` inconsistency in `pickFolder`**: the duplicate-folder guard uses `window.alert("该任务已绑定文件夹，请先移除再重新绑定")`. Same fix as the truncation alert — use the app's toast pipeline to stay consistent with the rest of the UI and avoid blocking the renderer.

Dead fallback branch: `.filter((t) => t.deletedAt)` already guarantees every surviving item has a truthy `deletedAt`, so the `?? 0` in the comparator can never trigger. This is misleading dead code — readers may think `deletedAt` can be null/undefined here. Either drop the `?? 0` (and tighten the type to `number` for filtered items) or filter explicitly with `!= null` if you want to keep numeric-string/null tolerance.

Sort has no tiebreaker, so tasks deleted within the same millisecond (batch deletes, automated cleanups, identical timestamps) render in non-deterministic order — exactly the symptom the inline comment warns about. Add a stable secondary key (e.g. `t.id` or the original `order` field) so the list is deterministic.

`filter + sort` rebuilds a new array on every parent render. For a trash view that accumulates entries this is wasted work and defeats any future `React.memo` on `TodoCard`. Wrap the derivation in `useMemo` keyed on `tasks`.

The two-line comment describes a historical bug ("原 filter 不打排序...导致顺序...") instead of explaining the current logic. Future readers won't know which version is in the tree. Replace with a comment that states the present intent.

The `<select>` for `line_rule` swaps the meaning of `line_line` between two unit systems without converting the stored value:
- When `line_rule === "auto"`, `line_line` is the OOXML "240ths-of-a-line" (e.g. 240 = 1.0×, 360 = 1.5×, 480 = 2.0×).
- When `line_rule === "exact"` or `"atLeast"`, `line_line` is plain twips (1pt = 20 twips).

The conditional input below the select (`{lineIsMultiple ? ... : ...}`) reads/writes `line_line` with different functions in each branch, but the `line_rule` select itself only calls `set({ line_rule: next })`. As a result, flipping the dropdown silently re-interprets an existing integer (e.g. 1.5× = 360 is then read back as a 360-twip ≈ 18pt fixed gap) and that bogus value is what eventually ships to the backend. Either convert on transition using a documented approximation, snap to a sensible default for the new regime, or store both forms on `WordTextStyle` and pick at submit time.

comments.content:
The `<details>` "accordion" is not really single-open. `<details>` is uncontrolled in React — `open={openGroup === key}` is reassigned every render, and `onToggle` only handles the *opening* branch (`e.currentTarget.open && setOpenGroup(key)`). So when the user collapses the currently-open group via the native collapse action:

1. The handler skips the state update.
2. `openGroup` still points at the collapsed key.
3. Any subsequent re-render (e.g. the user typing in an adjacent font input, which propagates through `onChange`) makes React re-apply `open={true}` to that key, snapping the panel back open against the user's intent.

Net effect: once any group is expanded the user can only make it stay open — there's no way to land in an "all closed" or "switched focus" state. Make `openGroup` nullable and handle the close event explicitly:
comments.existing_code:
<details
          key={key}
          open={openGroup === key}
          onToggle={(e) => e.currentTarget.open && setOpenGroup(key)}
        >

comments.content: `align` and `line_rule` are typed as the catch-all `string`. The `<select>` options happen to whitelist a fixed set, but `set({...})` accepts any `Partial<WordTextStyle>`, so future programmatic patches or refactors that bypass the dropdown can inject invalid OOXML tokens with no compile-time check (e.g. `set({ align: "centre" })` would silently be persisted and round-trip through the backend). Tighten the types to string-literal unions and let TypeScript refuse unknown values at every patch site.

`num(v, step)` handles `NaN`/negative inputs but assumes `step > 0`. With `step === 0` the call path becomes `Math.round(v / 0) * 0 === NaN`, which would then be assigned verbatim into `style.line_line` / `indent_chars` / `before` / `after` (since the controlled input treats NaN-y back-conversions — e.g. `twipsToPt(NaN)` — silently as 0 in the display but the raw NaN would survive in state if any code path bypasses the converters). Guard the helper and/or assert at call sites; today the callers all pass `0.25` / `0.5` so this is purely defensive, but the helper is used in 5 places and the next caller may forget.

The body of `StyleGroup` repeats the same `<label><input/></label>` shape nine times (font_east, font_ascii, font size, align, line, indent, before, after, bold) with identical wrapper className and event-handling boilerplate. The duplication is what hides bugs like finding #1 — six of the nine fields silently mix twips vs 240ths converters, and one number field (`indent_chars`) is the only one that *doesn't* convert units, yet every block looks identical at a glance. Extracting a small `<NumberField label unit value step onChange>` (or a `<TwipsField>` / `<MultiplesField>` variant) would give each conversion a single home and surface any future unit-handling mismatch in a single diff.

comments.content: Comment is factually wrong about Vite/TS module resolution priority, and the file is effectively dead code. Standard TypeScript module resolution (which Vite follows) for `./components/WidgetApp` first tries `./components/WidgetApp.{ts,tsx,js,jsx,...}`; only when that fails does it fall back to the directory form (`./components/WidgetApp/index.{ts,tsx,...}`). Since `./components/WidgetApp/WidgetApp.tsx` exists, the resolver picks it directly — `src/main.tsx`'s `import WidgetApp from "./components/WidgetApp"` never loads this `index.tsx`. No file under `src/` does an explicit `./components/WidgetApp/index` or `./components/WidgetApp/` import either, so this file is never executed. Either (a) delete this file and import `./components/WidgetApp/WidgetApp` directly from `main.tsx`, or (b) drop the sibling `WidgetApp.tsx` so this `index.tsx` becomes the actual entry. The current shape (sibling `.tsx` plus a never-loaded barrel) just invites the next maintainer to assume the barrel is the source of truth and edit the wrong file.

comments.content: Project rule prefers async/await over Promise chains. The `void Promise.all(...).then(...).catch(...)` pattern obscures control flow (e.g. the `startPos` assignment timing is hidden inside an arrow body) and forces `unknown` error typing. Refactoring to an IIFE with async/await makes the "resolve → assign → fail fast" sequencing obvious.

The `move` handler closes over `onDelta` captured at pointerdown time. If the parent ever passes a non-stable (recreated each render) callback — which is easy to do accidentally — every drag after the first re-render will invoke a stale implementation that references old props/state. Pinning `onDelta` to a ref keeps the gesture aware of the latest callback without forcing every consumer to memoize.

The same `{ x; y; w; h; sw; sh }` shape is declared inline twice (here in the prop type, and again inside `onDown` for `let startPos`). Any future field added to one site but not the other will silently break the contract. Extract a single named type alias and reuse it in both positions.

The `as NonNullable<SortableHandleProps>` cast suppresses a genuine TS conflict (DraggableAttributes.role vs. DraggableSyntheticListeners' index signature) and silently masks any future spread key collision — e.g. if `attributes` and `listeners` ever contribute the same key (role, aria-*, etc.), `...listeners` silently overwrites `...attributes`. Consider either (a) replacing the cast with a tiny typed merge helper that picks only the safe keys from each side, or (b) restructuring `SortableHandleProps` so callers receive a `Partial<...>` and merge via `Object.assign` without a cast, so future collisions surface at compile time.

The `listeners ? ... : undefined` branch is asymmetric: `attributes` is destructured and spread unconditionally, but `listeners` is null-checked. `useSortable` consistently returns a defined (possibly empty) `listeners` object whenever a sensor is wired up, so this branch is effectively dead in normal setups and only fires when the entire draggable is misconfigured — yet the docstring doesn't explain what `undefined` semantically means to the caller ("no sensor attached"? "not yet activated"?). Either drop the check (treat empty listeners as valid) or document the contract so the caller knows how to degrade the handle (e.g. hide the grip vs. render an inert one) when `undefined` is received.

comments.content: `settle()` discards `screenSize().h` (only destructures `{ w: sw }`), so vertical anchoring is impossible. If the user drags the strip below the bottom of the monitor (or after a monitor is unplugged / resolution changes), nothing snaps it back: `ny = y` is passed straight through and `saveAnchor(anchor)` persists the off-screen Y. Two concrete consequences: (a) the widget becomes unreachable on screen yet `expandedRef`/`expanded` logic still works, and (b) the next mount picks the same off-screen Y from `loadAnchor()`. Fetch the screen height and clamp `ny` to `[0, sh - STRIP_W]` (with the same MARGIN-based bottom-snap the X axis already does).

When resizing from the **west** or **north** side, `resizePanel` recomputes `nx`/`ny` and sends it to `setPosition` without re-clamping. `Math.min(w, startPos.x + startPos.w)` only protects size growth on the inner side; it does not bound the new origin. Result: drag the window to the left edge of the screen, then resize west — `nx` becomes negative — and the strip exits the viewport (a second resize from south can hide it entirely because `ny` can go negative too). Clamp `nx`/`ny` to `[0, sw - w]` / `[0, sh - h]` after the west/north branch.

Unlike the `applyLocal` + `invoke().catch(rollbackOptimistic)` pattern used for `toggleCollapsed`/`toggleSubtask`/`commitTitle`, the `applyAndSync` path treats the `emit` failure as fire-and-forget. When the backend rejects (Tauri IPC error, channel closed during shutdown, main-window detached) the local `tasks` state has already diverged from the DB and there is no recovery code — the user's change just vanishes on the next 5s poll. Either (a) snapshot `prev` like `applyLocal` and roll back on `.catch`, or (b) emit with an ack/timeout so optimistic state can be reconciled. At minimum log the emit rejection through `handleCommandError` so silent drift is debuggable.

`toggleWsCollapsed` and `handleWsDragEnd` both emit `workspace-updated` and swallow failures with `.catch(() => {})`. There is no rollback path and no log; identical drift problem as `applyAndSync`. With `swallow on no-op` the user silently loses collapse-toggle / drag-reorder on a transient IPC error. At minimum route the error through `handleCommandError`; ideally snapshot `prev` and roll back on failure.

`load()` runs every 5 s for the lifetime of the widget and on every `tasks-changed` event. The dedup path does `JSON.stringify(list) === JSON.stringify(prev)`, which is an O(N) full-tree stringify of the entire `Task[]` payload on both sides per poll, plus garbage from the resulting string. For a user with a few hundred tasks (and sizeable `subtasks`/`files`/`notes`) this is a steady ~kilobyte allocation every 5 s. Compare by `id`/length/updatedAt or by reference-hash instead, or move the compare into the read pipeline (`diffTaskRows` already exists). Also avoids `setTasks` returning the new array when `same` is true, so the prior pointer is preserved.

Two render-phase side effects in this component disable `react/refs` to write a ref directly during render:

  1. `expandedRef.current = expanded` — supposed to keep the ref aligned with state for `chat-focus-session`. The oxlint comment claims this avoids a stale window when an event fires in the same tick as a commit, but the event listener is registered in a `useEffect([])` that runs after the first commit anyway, so by the time it can fire the effect closure has already been installed with `expandedRef.current = false` from the initial render. A `useEffect(() => { expandedRef.current = expanded; }, [expanded])` (or, cleaner, `useSyncExternalStore`) is functionally equivalent and stays inside the rules of hooks.
  2. `setTasks((prev) => { ... tasksRef.current = list; ... })` — the updater mutates a ref. Under StrictMode the updater may be invoked twice; idempotent here, but a class of footgun waiting to happen.

  Move both ref writes into `useEffect` with the appropriate deps so the project rule "render side effects prohibited" is honored and concurrent-mode replay is safe.

`handleWsDragEnd` mutates `changed` items in-place via `forEach((w) => (w.updatedAt = now))`, but those items are the same object references already living in the `next` array (and via `byId`, the original `workspace` array). Nothing crashes today because React's setState will simply commit the (already-mutated) `next` array, but it (a) violates the no-mutate-shared-state expectation that downstream consumers rely on, and (b) makes the code impossible to reason about under React 18 concurrent rendering if `next` is ever passed to a memoised child — the child will see a new `order` on the next render even though the reference is unchanged. Build a new object for each changed item before mutating.

`expand()` performs up to three awaited Tauri calls when the user mouses over the collapsed strip: `setPosition` (only on right edge), `setSize`, `setPosition` again. The second `setPosition` is unconditional even though its arguments have not changed since the first call (for non-right edge) or since the right-edge branch (for right edge). Each IPC roundtrip is on the order of a few ms, but on rapid hover-in/out the user can chain multiple expands. Collapse it to a single `setPosition` (only when needed) and one `setSize`.

project_summary:
Let me analyze this massive collection of 1587 comments across 317 files. I need to identify cross-cutting patterns and the most consequential findings.

Let me categorize by file area:

**Rust Backend (src-tauri/):**
- Database layer: Heavy criticism across `src-tauri/src/db/` - SQL correctness, transaction safety, mutex poisoning, error type flattening to String, missing enum/CHECK constraints, string-typed enums
- API handlers: Many issues with error handling, panic safety, async/sync mixing, missing cleanup
- Bot system: Long files, dead code, TOCTOU races, performance issues
- MCP: Race conditions, validation gaps
- Skills: State machine bugs, rollback logic issues
- Evolution system: Many file-locking concerns, mutex poison recovery
- Migration: Encoding bugs, race conditions, error swallowing
- Memory: Race conditions, capacity invariants, SQL injection-style issues
- Tools: Path validation, async runtime blocking

**Frontend (src/, src/components/, src/ui/, src/lib/):**
- React hooks: Missing dependencies, stale closures, race conditions
- Type safety: Loose `string` types where unions exist, redundant `?:` + `| null`
- State management: Race conditions, missed cleanup
- UI components: Nested ternaries (banned by project rules), accessibility (a11y) issues
- localStorage: Silent error swallowing
- Tauri command bindings: Type drift, missing error normalization

**Cross-cutting patterns:**
1. **String-typed enums** - massive pattern across Rust + TS
2. **Mutex poisoning recovery via `into_inner()`** - pervasive across Rust
3. **Silent error swallowing** - empty `catch`, `eprintln!` only, `.catch(() => {})` etc.
4. **TOCTOU races** - check-then-act without re-validation
5. **Async/sync mixing** - blocking I/O on async runtime
6. **Nested ternaries** - explicitly banned, repeated violation
7. **Loose equality (`==`/`!=`)** - explicitly banned, repeated violation
8. **Project scaffolding** - `index.html`, `vite.svg` branding leaks
9. **Diagnostic gaps** - missing error context, audit logging
10. **Test hygiene** - leaked resources, non-atomic test cleanup

**Module hotspots:**
- `src-tauri/src/db/` - extremely high comment density
- `src-tauri/src/bot/` - large module with many concerns
- `src-tauri/src/api_handlers/` - lots of unsafe patterns
- `src-tauri/src/memory/` - race conditions and capacity invariants
- `src-tauri/src/evolution/` - file locking and dedup concerns
- `src/components/` - React issues throughout

**Quick wins:**
- Replace nested ternaries with maps
- Use strict equality throughout
- Add `unwrap` safety comments for unsafe blocks
- Centralize magic strings (file paths, command names)
- Add explicit `busy` guards
- Add `role="button"` to clickable divs

Let me structure the summary now.

### Top Issues

1. **String-typed enums replace type-checked invariants throughout the stack.** Closed sets (`TaskStatus`, `MemKind`, `Source`, `McpSlotStatus`, `SlotState`, `ChangeStatus`, `ScheduledJobRun.status`, `WorkflowAuditKind`, `TaskFile.kind`, `ReviewVerdict`, `BotConfirmPayload.kind`, `MutationOrigin`, `ProposalTarget`, `meta_provider.source`, etc.) are stored as bare `String`/`TEXT` with the closed set enforced only by comments or `if/else` ladders. Cited paths: `src-tauri/src/db/tasks.rs`, `src-tauri/src/db/skill_out.rs`, `src-tauri/src/db/schedule_jobs.rs`, `src-tauri/src/db/workflow_audit.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot/mcp/manager.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot_skills/parse.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot/config/types.rs`, `src/components/EvolutionPanel/types.ts`, `src/components/SettingsPage/types.ts`, `src/lib/mutationOrigin.ts`, `src/lib/errorHandler.ts`. Fixing this prevents drift between frontend and backend.

2. **Silent mutex-poisoning recovery via `into_inner()` is the default pattern.** This pattern is repeated in ~30 sites: `src-tauri/src/api_handlers/{ratelimit,commands,sse,util}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/api_server.rs`, `src-tauri/src/app_state.rs`, `src-tauri/src/db/{bot_history,brief,subagents,memory/store,consolidate}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot/{mcp/commands,registry,reasoning,scheduler,skills/scheduler,skills/state}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/evolution/{emit,observe/shadow,policy}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/workflow_runner.rs`, `src-tauri/src/exec_steps.rs`, `src/components/ConfirmMap/ConfirmMap.tsx` (not poisoned, but analogous). After a panic mid-operation the lock is reused as if healthy, with only an `eprintln!` and no rollback.

3. **TOCTOU / check-then-act races are pervasive.** Examples: `WmDocxRevisions` auto-dispose vs explicit create, `lookup_tool_rule` first-match-wins, `file_rollback` multi-step race, `validate_schedule` vs display, `task_autotag` lock-acquired skip path, `tool_extract_text` symlink swap, `due_notify` window scheduling, `subagents` transition state, `trace_export` memory-load-then-write, `extract.rs` SELECT-COUNT then INSERT, `events.rs` dedup, `history.lock()` vs `clients.lock()` ordering in `api_server.rs`. The pattern is nearly always: `check → release → act`, with no re-validation under the held lock.

4. **Async functions perform blocking I/O on the Tauri runtime.** Many `#[tauri::command]` and `pub async fn` paths call `std::fs::*`, `std::sync::Mutex`, and `std::process::Command` directly without `spawn_blocking`. Cited: `src-tauri/src/api_handlers/{commands,util}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bing.rs` (4 functions), `src-tauri/src/bot_fs.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot_skills/{builtin,manage,files}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot/orchestrator.rs`, `src-tauri/src/trace_sink.rs`, `src-tauri/src/db/{tasks,workflow_audit,bot_sessions}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/migration/run.rs`, `src-tauri/src/ocr.rs`, `src-tauri/src/meta/sync.rs`, `src-tauri/src/evolution/{observe/shadow,policy}.rs`, plus `src-tauri/tests/llm_integration.rs`.

5. **Async/sync mutex hierarchy is broken across the request lifecycle.** `std::sync::Mutex` guards are held across `.await` in `src-tauri/src/app_state.rs` (`pending`, `confirm_requests`, `question_waiters`, `ask_contexts`), and over file I/O / blocking syscalls in `src-tauri/src/bot/config/{io,commands}.rs` (`CONFIG_WRITE_LOCK` over keyring + fsync), `src-tauri/src/audit.rs`, `src-tauri/src/py/{audit,env}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot_mcp.rs`, `src-tauri/src/due_notify.rs`, `src-tauri/src/evolution/mod.rs`. `src-tauri/tests/skill_e2e.rs` even relies on `#[allow(clippy::await_holding_lock)]` for serialization.

6. **Error context is destroyed at every FFI/DB boundary.** `rusqlite::Error`, `io::ErrorKind`, `reqwest::Error` chains, and JSON parse errors are funneled through `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())`/`format!("...{e}")` at the call site, then re-wrapped as `CommandError::Internal` or `CommandError::DbError(String)`. Cited: `src-tauri/src/error.rs` (`From<String>`/`From<&str>` both → `Internal`), `src-tauri/src/db/{brief,bot_history,bot_sessions,skill_out,subagents,schedule_jobs,people,trace,workflow_audit,workflow_settings,workspace,tasks}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot_web.rs` (inconsistent `err_chain` usage), `src-tauri/src/bing.rs`, `src-tauri/src/audit.rs`. Frontend then surfaces unparseable strings.

7. **`#![warn(...)]`/`#![deny(...)]` are not enforced; `clippy.toml` threshold without level config.** `clippy.toml` only sets `too-many-lines-threshold = 200`; lint levels are not declared. Result: the documented "禁止为过 lint 拆函数" rule is unenforceable, and clippy warnings are routinely suppressed inline (e.g., `#[allow(dead_code)]`, `#[allow(clippy::await_holding_lock)]`).

8. **Public mutable identity fields bypass encapsulation.** `MemStore.tasks`, `TauriStore.app`, `BotConfig`'s 4 `pub` `Option<String>` fields, `McpSlotStatus.state: String`, `KillSwitch`'s three `pub` booleans (despite documented contradictions), `SubagentSessionCtx` fields, `AppShadowSink.changes_path/app`, `ChangeStatus` exposes `pub status`. Cited: `src-tauri/src/api.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot/config/types.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot/mcp/manager.rs`, `src-tauri/src/evolution/{candidate/entry,sandbox/kill_switch}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/tool_guard.rs`, `src/components/ProfileRow.tsx`.

9. **Audit/forensics gaps.** The `audit` and `bot.log` pipeline has many divergent sinks (`eprintln!` vs `write_event` vs `audit_event!` vs `audit_log`), many panic-recovery paths that lose the original event, and several Tauri commands emit fire-and-forget events with no observer. Cited: `src-tauri/src/audit.rs` (`tool_call_failed` discards `name`; `panic_message` collapses three cases to one), `src-tauri/src/bot/{dispatch,tools,fs}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot_skills/{scheduler,runtime}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/evolution/observe/shadow.rs`, `src-tauri/src/api_handlers/{util,commands}.rs`.

10. **Test isolation and CI infrastructure leak resources and assume ordering.** `Box::leak(mock_app)` is used pervasively (`tests/skill_e2e.rs`, `tests/exec_trace.rs`, `tests/llm_integration.rs`, `tests/memory_conflict.rs`, `tests/bot_test_connection.rs`, `tests/memory_eval.rs`); shared DB writes without `cleanup()` runs (notably `tests/task_chat_exec.rs`); `tests/memory_v2_degraded.rs` mutates `WMESSAGE_BGE_MODEL_DIR` for the whole process without restoring; `scripts/test-all.sh` has a broken `-j num-cpus` literal.

### Module Hotspots

- **`src-tauri/src/db/`** — highest comment density in the project. `tasks.rs`, `workflow.rs`, `workflow_audit.rs`, `workflow_settings.rs`, `subagents.rs`, `trace.rs`, `workspace.rs`, `brief.rs`, `bot_sessions.rs`, `skill_out.rs`, `schedule_jobs.rs`, `people.rs`, `migrations.rs`, `paths.rs`, `bot_history.rs` all share the same anti-patterns: `String`-typed enums, `.to_string()`-flattened errors, missing CHECK constraints, missing transactions, N+1 SQL, full-table scans in hot paths.

- **`src-tauri/src/bot/`** — large subsystem with intertwined correctness concerns. Highest-density files: `bot_skills/{scheduler,runtime,parse,manage,files,vars,recommend}.rs`, `bot/config/{schema,commands,keyring,io,types}.rs`, `bot/{dispatch,registry,tools,fs,scheduler,reasoning,params,mcp/*}.rs`. - **Time-source inconsistency** — `chrono::Utc::now().timestamp_millis()` vs `crate::memory::now_ms()` vs `std::time::SystemTime::now()` mixed within the same file. Cited: `src-tauri/src/evolution/{derive,apply,panel/commands}.rs`, `src-tauri/src/bot_skills/{scheduler,recommend}.rs`, `src/components/GraphPage/graph-build.ts` (local-tz `getFullYear()`).
